01-001.json.summary: The Purana opens with praise of the self-born Creator who takes the three qualities (gunas) for creating, keeping and ending the world, and of Hari who upholds the worlds. It gives the line of teachers: Brahma taught this Purana to Vasishtha, Vasishtha to his grandson Parashara, Parashara to Jatukarnya, Jatukarnya to Dvaipayana (Vyasa), and Vyasa to five pupils, Jaimini, Sumantu, Vaishampayana, Paila and the bard (suta) Lomaharshana. Lomaharshana, having learnt it, comes humbly to a long sacrificial session at Kurukshetra; the sages welcome him and ask him to tell the sacred, Veda-like story of the world's origin and of all the family lines. The bard agrees to tell what Vyasa told him, the Purana once spoken by the Wind-god (Matarishvan, Vayu) to the sages of the Naimisha forest. He says a Purana has five marks: creation, re-creation, family lines, the ages of the Manus (manvantaras) and the deeds of the dynasties, and that this one has four parts (padas): Prakriya, Anushanga, Upodghata and Upasamhara. He then gives a long table of contents: the unmanifest cause and the golden cosmic egg with its seven coverings; Brahma's birth and creations; Vishnu's sleep on the waters and the lifting of the earth by the Boar; castes and stages of life; the stars, planets and the sun's chariot; the continents (dvipas), seas, mountains and the land of Bharata; the ancestors (pitris) and the shraddha rite; the four ages (yugas); the Manus and their sages; Daksha, the Maruts, demons, nagas, apsaras and other beings; the families of Bhrigu, Angiras, Kashyapa, Atri and Parashara; the solar and lunar kings, Yayati, the Yadus, the Syamantaka jewel and Krishna's birth to Devaki; Shukra's penance to Shiva; the coming kings of the Kali age; the three kinds of dissolution, the hells, and the hard path to liberation; Vasishtha, Shakti, Parashara, Vyasa and Shuka; and Vyasa's division of the one Veda into four. It also tells briefly how Brahma gave the sages a wheel and told them that where its rim broke the land was holy, which became Naimisha. One who studies this first part with self-control has as good as studied the whole Purana; the Veda should be filled out with the epics and Puranas, for the Veda fears a man of little learning. The name Purana means 'what existed of old', and knowing this frees from all sins; Narayana is this whole Purana, creating and ending the world.

01-002.json.summary: The sages ask the bard where the long sacrifice of the Naimisha sages took place, how long it lasted, and how the Wind-god came to tell the Purana. The bard says that Brahma, wishing to create the world, once held a thousand-year sacrifice in which Ida was the wife and Death the slaughterer; where the rim of the wheel of Dharma broke, the place became famous as Naimisha. It is where the holy Gomati river flows, where Vasishtha's son Shakti was born of Arundhati, where King Kalmashapada met Shakti, where the feud of Vishvamitra and Vasishtha arose, and where Parashara was born of Adrishyanti. There the sages held a twelve-year session while Pururavas ruled the earth. Pururavas, who was never content with jewels though he enjoyed eighteen islands of the ocean, came there while hunting with Urvashi; Vishvakarma had made the sacrificial ground of gold from the golden seed that the Ganga bore from Fire. Seeing the golden enclosure, the greedy king tried to take it, and the angry sages, urged by the gods, struck him with blades of kusha grass hard as thunderbolts and he died. They then set up his son Ayu, father of Nahusha, as king and finished their session in great splendour, with gandharvas singing Samans, apsaras dancing, learned debate, and no demons or faults to spoil it. At the end they questioned the lord Vayu, Brahma's pupil, who sees all, holds the worlds, works as the seven Marut groups and as the five breaths in bodies, and with gentle speech he told them the Purana. The bard says he will now tell that Purana, first spoken by Brahma, which frees gods and sages from all sins, in full and in order.

01-003.json.summary: The bard says this story frees from all sins, and one who keeps it in mind or hears it often is honoured in heaven; it brings wealth, fame, long life and victory over enemies. Bowing to Hiranyagarbha, the self-born Brahma, he begins the account of creation. The unmanifest cause, called Pradhana or Prakriti by those who think on the principles, is eternal, without beginning or end, without smell, form, taste, sound or touch, made of the three qualities, the womb of the world and the supreme eternal Brahman; at first all was pervaded by it and was dark, the qualities being in balance. At the time of creation, guided by the knower of the field (kshetrajna), the qualities lose their balance and the Great Principle (Mahat) appears, rich in goodness (sattva). Its two functions are resolve and decision; it is also called mind, Brahma and other names, and the text explains several of them (for example, Brahma because he makes things grow, brimhana). The first embodied being, the four-faced Hiranyagarbha, appears in the cosmic egg. In this egg are the seven worlds, the earth with seven continents and seven seas, mountains and rivers, sun, moon and stars. The egg is covered outside by water, fire, wind, space, the element-source (bhutadi), Mahat and Pradhana, each ten times larger than the one before; these seven natural coverings hold one another up. The unmanifest is called the field and Brahma the knower of the field. This first, natural creation came about without thought, like a flash of lightning; one who truly knows this birth of Hiranyagarbha gains long life, fame, wealth and wisdom.

01-004.json.summary: The bard explains how creation begins. When all things are drawn back into the self, Pradhana and Purusha stand in balance; balance of the qualities means dissolution, and excess of one means creation. Rajas sets things moving, like water in seeds. When the qualities are stirred, three eternal beings arise: sattva is Vishnu, rajas is Brahma, and tamas is Rudra. These three are the three worlds, the three qualities, the three Vedas and the three fires; they depend on and support one another and are never apart even for a moment. Brahma, the knower of the field, appears first, with unmatched knowledge and detachment, and has three states: as Brahma (rajas) he creates the worlds, as Time (Kala, rajas and tamas) he destroys them, and as Purusha (sattva) he remains detached; Brahma is lotus-eyed, Time is black as collyrium, and Purusha is lotus-eyed in the form of the Supreme Self. As a master of yoga he takes one, two, three or many bodies; he is called threefold, four-formed, Atma, Vishnu (because he enters all), Bhagavan, and Narayana. Dividing himself in three, he creates, devours and protects. He is called Aja (unborn) and Hiranyagarbha. The life of Brahma, a half (parardha) made of many kalpas, cannot be counted even in hundreds of years of Manus; at its end he wakes again. The present kalpa is the Varaha (Boar) kalpa, which lasts a thousand ages ruled by kings.

01-005.json.summary: The bard says that at first water covered everything; in that single ocean, with all moving and still beings destroyed, Brahma as the thousand-headed, thousand-eyed Purusha called Narayana slept on the water. The text explains the name: water is called nara, and since it is his resting place (ayana) he is Narayana. After a thousand ages he woke, saw the world empty, knew the earth lay under the water, and to lift it took the form of a huge Boar, ten yojanas wide and a hundred long, dark as a rain cloud, with white tusks; the Boar's body is described as the sacrifice itself (Vedas for shoulders, fire for tongue, kusha grass for hair, and so on). He entered the nether world, raised the earth, levelled it, and set up again the mountains that had melted in the fire of the last dissolution; with Vishvakarma he arranged the seven continents, seas and the four worlds beginning with Bhu. Brahma then created by thought. First came ignorance with five parts (tamas, moha, mahamoha, tamisra and andhatamisra), and the 'chief' creation of immovable things like trees. Next came the animals, whose flow is crosswise (tiryak-srotas), full of darkness and ignorance. Displeased, he created the gods, whose flow is upward and who are full of joy, and then humans, whose flow is downward, full of activity and sorrow. The nine creations are listed: three natural ones (Mahat, the subtle elements, the senses) and six derived ones (plants, animals, gods, humans, the 'favour' creation, and the Kumara creation). He then made the mind-born sages; the first ones turned from creating, so he made others: the deities of places (waters, fire, earth, sky, seasons, time units), Bhrigu, Angiras, Marichi, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Daksha, Atri and Vasishtha, the nine Brahmas, then Rudra from his anger, and Dharma and Sankalpa, each born from a part of his body or breath. Sanatkumara and Ribhu (Kratu) remain celibate. From his mouth he made gods, from his chest the ancestors, from his loins humans and from his hips the demons, and also lightning, clouds, rainbows and the three Vedas, and yakshas, pishachas, gandharvas, apsaras, kinnaras, rakshasas, birds, beasts and snakes. Beings take on again the deeds they had in earlier creations. The world is likened to a Brahma-tree growing from the unmanifest seed, with intellect as trunk, the senses as hollows, merit and sin as flowers and joy and sorrow as fruit. Brahmins came from his mouth, kshatriyas from his chest, vaishyas from his thighs and shudras from his feet. At the end of a kalpa the perfected go to Brahma's world and do not return, while the sun's seven rays burn the three worlds, rain floods the earth into one ocean, and after Brahma's night of a thousand ages he wakes again and sees the empty world. So ends the first part (pada) of the Purana.

01-006.json.summary: This chapter begins the second part, the Anushanga-pada. Pleased with the first part, the sage Kapeya asks the bard about the junction (pratisandhi) between the past kalpa and the present one. The bard says the present kalpa is the Varaha (Boar) kalpa; between two kalpas there is no continuous link, since all creatures are cut off at a kalpa's end, while within a manvantara the ages follow one another without a break. He explains Brahma's two halves of life (parardhas) and that the present kalpa is the first of the second half. At the end of the last kalpa, when the time of burning came, the gods who live in celestial cars, the stars, planets, sun and moon, numbering many crores in each manvantara, together with the sages, ancestors and their families, grew anxious, left their places and went up to Maharloka, then to Janaloka, and after ten kalpas to Satyaloka, Brahma's world, from which there is no return; there they become equal to Brahma in power and form and are freed together with him. Those left on earth, gandharvas, pishachas, humans, animals, birds, plants and snakes, are burnt when the sun's thousand rays become seven suns, after a long drought; freed of sin, they are born again in the next creation as Brahma's mind-born children. Rain then floods the earth into a single dark ocean, and the bard explains the words for water. Brahma, the thousand-headed Purusha called Narayana, sleeps on it through the night of a thousand ages. He creates with rajas at the start of a kalpa as Brahma, devours with tamas at its end as Time (Kala), and preserves with sattva as Narayana. The great sages (maharshis) in Maharloka, such as Bhrigu, see Time asleep; the word maharshi is explained. Because Brahma 'shapes' (kalpayati) fourteen orders of beings at its start, the period is called a kalpa.

01-007.json.summary: The bard says that after his night of a thousand ages Brahma moved over the dark waters as wind, knew the earth lay beneath, took the form of a Boar, raised the earth, levelled it and heaped up the mountains again from the remains of those melted in the last fire; the words for mountain (achala, parvata, giri, shiloccaya) are explained. He arranged the seven continents with their regions (varshas) and mountains, the four worlds, sun, moon and planets, and created again the deities of places (waters, fire, earth, wind, sky, quarters, seas, rivers, plants, time units) and the four ages: Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Tishya (Kali). Beings who did not reach the higher worlds return in each kalpa with names and forms set by their past deeds. Brahma first created a thousand couples from his mouth (full of sattva), a thousand from his chest (full of rajas, fiery), and a thousand from his thighs (rajas and tamas); from then on beings were born in pairs. In the Krita age people lived by thought alone, without houses, enjoying the earth's juice, with equal life, beauty and joy, no castes or stages of life, no love or hate, no merit or sin, no animals or snakes, and no extremes of heat and cold; the Krita age lasts four thousand divine years with twilights of four hundred each. Knowledge is the mark of Krita, sacrifice of Treta, war of Dvapara, and theft of Kali. As the age declined, the mental power faded; in Treta rain began, and 'house-trees' (kalpa-vrikshas) gave people shelter, clothes, ornaments and honey. Women began to have monthly courses, sexual union started, and the trees vanished; when they reappeared, people grabbed them and their honey out of greed, and they were lost for good. Suffering from cold, wind and heat, people built shelters, forts, villages, towns and cities, and fixed measures: finger, span (pradesha, vitasti), cubit (hasta), kishku, bow-length (dhanu), gavyuti and yojana (eight thousand bow-lengths). Rules are given for forts, the sizes of towns and villages and the widths of roads, and the words shala (hall, from shakha, branch) and prasada (palace) are explained. Then plants grew from rain without ploughing, fourteen kinds of cultivated and wild grains; when greed made them disappear, Brahma, making Mount Meru the calf, milked the earth for seeds, and seventeen cultivated grains (rice, barley, wheat, chickpea, sesame, millets, beans, lentils and others) and fourteen wild ones appeared. He taught farming and trade, fixed boundaries, and set up the four classes: the strong who protected others became kshatriyas, those who spoke truth became brahmins, those who farmed and traded became vaishyas, and those who served and were weak became shudras. He gave each their duties (teaching, sacrifice and gifts for brahmins; force and war for kshatriyas; cattle, trade and farming for vaishyas; crafts and service for shudras) and their worlds after death (Prajapati's world, Indra's, the Maruts', the gandharvas'). He then set up the four stages of life: householder, student, forest-dweller and renouncer, with their rules and ten virtues, and their higher worlds, and the four paths of the gods (through the sun) and of the ancestors (through the moon). When people still did not increase, in the middle of Treta Brahma created more mind-born beings, gods, ancestors, sages and Manus, along with all creatures who return from the past kalpa according to their deeds.

01-008.json.summary: The bard tells how Brahma created the four groups: demons, gods, ancestors and humans. Meditating, he took a body full of tamas and from his hips (jaghana) the demons (asuras) were born, so called because they came from his breath (asu); the body he cast off became night. Taking a body of sattva, he created the gods from his mouth while at play (from div, 'to play' or 'shine'), and that body became day; so gods are strong by day and demons by night. Thinking of them as a father, he created the ancestors (pitris) from another body of sattva, which became twilight, honoured between night and day by gods, demons, sages and twice-born. From a body of rajas he created humans by thought (manushya, from manana, thinking), and that body became moonlight. Night, day, twilight and moonlight are thus his four cast-off bodies, signs that recur in every manvantara. Then, in darkness, he created hungry beings: those who said 'let us guard (raksh) the waters' became rakshasas, and those who said 'let us eat (ksh) them' became yakshas. His hair, falling from displeasure, became snakes, whose names (vyala, ahi, pannaga, sarpa) are explained, and the poisonous fire of his anger entered them. From anger came fierce flesh-eating bhutas and pishachas; from his singing and drinking came the gandharvas. He made birds from his vigour, goats from his mouth, sheep from his chest, cattle from his belly and sides, and horses, elephants, donkeys, deer, camels, boars and dogs from his feet, and plants from his body hair. Seven domestic animals (cow, goat, man, sheep, horse, mule, donkey) and seven wild kinds are listed. From his four mouths came the Vedas, metres, stomas, chants and sacrifices: the Rig, Gayatri and Agnishtoma from the first; the Yajus, Trishtubh and Brihat Saman from the southern; the Samans, Jagati and Atiratra from the western; the Atharva, Anushtubh and Aptoryama from the fourth. He also made lightning, clouds and rainbows. Creatures return to the same deeds and natures they had before. Some say human effort decides results, others fate, others nature; the wise see that these are not separate. At the start, Brahma gave all beings their names and forms from the words of the Veda.

01-009.json.summary: The bard says Brahma created by thought five more agents who keep creatures in being: Rudra, Dharma, Manas (mind), Ruchi and Akuti. Rudra restores the plants again and again when they fail, and is worshipped with offerings in three cups, so he is called Tryambaka; the name is explained through the three metres and the three-cup rice cake. When the creatures still did not increase, Brahma saw tamas at work in himself; grieving, he drove it out, and from it came a pair, Adharma (wrongdoing) and Himsa (violence), with sorrow. He then made the nine mind-born sons (Bhrigu, Angiras, Marichi, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Daksha, Atri, Vasishtha), the 'nine Brahmas', and Dharma and Ruchi, each born from a part of him (Bhrigu from his heart, Daksha from his breath, Marichi from his eyes, Rudra from his pride, and so on); with Rudra they are the twelve sons. When creatures still did not grow, Brahma split his body in two: half became a man and half the woman Shatarupa, who did ten thousand years of penance and won as husband the first man, Svayambhuva Manu (also called Viraj); a manvantara is seventy-one ages. Their children were Priyavrata and Uttanapada and two daughters, Akuti and Prasuti. Akuti was given to Ruchi and bore the twins Yajna and Dakshina, whose twelve sons were the Yama gods. Prasuti, given to Daksha, bore twenty-four daughters. Thirteen (Shraddha, Lakshmi, Dhriti, Tushti, Pushti, Medha, Kriya, Buddhi, Lajja, Vasu, Shanti, Siddhi, Kirti) married Dharma; the other eleven married Bhava (Sati), Bhrigu (Khyati), Marichi (Sambhuti), Angiras (Smriti), Pulastya (Priti), Pulaha (Kshama), Kratu (Sannati), Atri (Anasuya), Vasishtha (Urja), Fire (Svaha) and the Ancestors (Svadha). Dharma's sons are virtues such as Kama, Darpa, Niyama, Santosha, Shruta, Shama and Dama, Bodha, Vinaya, Kshema, Sukha and Yasha. From Adharma came Himsa, Nikriti and Anrita, then Fear, Hell, Maya, Pain, Death, sickness, old age, grief, anger and envy, who have no wives or sons. Told to create, Rudra (Nilalohita) made by thought thousands of beings just like himself: tawny, matted-haired, three-eyed, blue-necked, armed, fierce and mighty. Brahma told him not to create beings equal to himself, but mortal ones, since immortal beings do not act. Rudra refused to create beings subject to death and old age and said 'I stand still (sthito'smi)'; these beings would be the Rudras, worshipped in the Shatarudriya and given a share of sacrifice. Brahma agreed; from then on Rudra created no more and remained celibate, and so is called Sthanu ('the motionless'). Because he surpasses gods, demons and sages in power, strength and knowledge, he is Mahadeva.

01-010.json.summary: The sages ask how Mahadeva Rudra appeared in this kalpa. The bard says that at the start of the kalpa Brahma meditated on a son like himself, and a blue-red (nilalohita) boy appeared in his lap, crying loudly. When Brahma asked why he cried, he asked for a name; Brahma called him Rudra (from rud, to weep), and he cried again and asked for more names until he had eight: Rudra, Bhava, Sharva, Ishana, Pashupati, Bhima, Ugra and Mahadeva. He then asked for a place for each, and Brahma gave him eight bodies: the sun, water, earth, wind, fire, sky, the consecrated brahmin (dikshita) and the moon. With each body the text gives rules of conduct so the god does no harm: do not look at the rising or setting sun, worship Rudra at the two twilights with the Rig, Yajur and Sama Vedas, and do not pass urine facing him; do not pass urine or excrement, spit, bathe naked or have sex in water, and do not block water flowing to the sea; do not soil the earth in shade or on roads, but cover the head and the ground with grass; do not speak ill of the blowing wind; do not burn impure things in fire, warm the feet at it or step over it; do not eat, drink or relieve oneself in the open sky; do not speak ill of a consecrated brahmin; and do not cut trees or plants on the new-moon day. As the sun he gives light, as water he nourishes, as earth he holds, as wind he is the breath, as fire he digests, as sky he is the body's hollows, as the consecrated one he is the sacrificer, and as the moon he is the mind, drunk by gods and ancestors. Each body has a wife and son: Suvarchala and Shanaishchara (Saturn); Dhatri and Ushanas (Venus); Vikeshi and Angaraka (Mars); Shiva and Manojava (with Avijnatagati); Svaha and Skanda; the Quarters and Svarga; Diksha and Santana; and Rohini and Budha (Mercury). One who knows the god by these names and bodies and worships him in them gains children and union with Bhava.

01-011.json.summary: The bard gives the families of the sages in the Svayambhuva manvantara. Bhrigu's wife Khyati bore the gods Dhata and Vidhata, who give joy and sorrow, and a daughter, the goddess Shri, who married Narayana and bore Bala and Unmada. Dhata and Vidhata married Ayati and Niyati, whose sons were Prana and Mrikanda; Mrikanda's son was Markandeya, and his son Vedashiras, from whom came the Markandeya sages; Prana's line went through Dyutiman. Marichi's wife Sambhuti bore Purnamasa and four daughters (Krishi, Vrishti, Tvisha, Upachiti); Purnamasa's son Virajas had a son Sudhama, guardian of the east, and his other son Parvasha had Yajurdhaman and Stambha Kashyapa. Angiras's wife Smriti bore four daughters, Sinivali, Kuhu, Raka and Anumati, and two sons, Bharatagni and Kirtiman; Parjanya, guardian of a quarter, belongs to this line. Atri's wife Anasuya bore five sons (Satyanetra, Havya, Apomurti, Shanaishchara and Soma) and a daughter Shruti, wife of Kardama and mother of Shankhapada. Pulastya's wife Priti bore Danagni (in a former birth Agastya), Devabahu and Atri, and a daughter Sadvati, mother of Parjanya. Pulaha's wife Kshama bore Kardama, Urvarivan, Sahishnu, the sage Kanakapitha and a daughter Pivari; Kardama's son Shankhapada became guardian of the south, and his daughter Kamya married Priyavrata and bore ten sons and two daughters from whom the warrior class spread. Kratu's wife Sannati bore sixty thousand celibate Valakhilyas, who travel before the sun's charioteer Aruna. Vasishtha's wife Urja bore seven Vasishthas (Rajas, Gartra, Urdhvabahu, Savana, Pavana, Sutapas and Shanku), who are the seven sages of that age, and a daughter Pundarika, wife of Prana; Ketuman, guardian of the west, is of this line. The bard says he will next tell of Fire's offspring.

01-012.json.summary: The bard describes the fires. Agni, Brahma's mind-born son in the Svayambhuva age, had by Svaha three sons: Pavamana (fire produced by friction), Pavaka (lightning fire, born of water) and Shuchi (the sun's fire). Their sons are Kavyavahana (who carries offerings to the ancestors), Saharaksha (fire of the demons) and Havyavahana (who carries offerings to the gods); with their sons and grandsons the fires number forty-nine. The worldly fire, Brahma's first son, is Bharata, whose son Vaishvanara carried offerings for a hundred years; Atharvan (Bhrigu) brought it forth in a lotus lake, and it is called Atharvana and Dadhyan. Pavamana is the householder's fire (garhapatya); his son Shamsya is the offering fire (ahavaniya), who loved sixteen rivers (Kaveri, Krishnavena, Narmada, Yamuna, Godavari, Vitasta, Chandrabhaga, Iravati, Vipasha, Kaushiki, Shatadru, Sarayu, Sita, Sarasvati, Hladini, Pavani) and by them had the sixteen dhishnya fires of the Soma sacrifice. The text names these sacrificial fires and their places at the Soma-pressing day: Samrat (Krishanu), Parishad, Nabhas, Havya, Ritudhaman, Vishvavyachas, Brahmajyotis, Ajaikapad, Ahirbudhnya and the eight movable ones such as the hotri's fire, Prashanta, Vaishvadeva, Ushik, and others. Pavaka's line includes the fire in water used at the final bath with Varuna, Hricchaya the digestive fire, the fierce Samvartaka who lives in the sea as the mare's-mouth fire drinking water, Kshama who burns houses, and Kravyad who eats the dead. Shuchi's line includes Ayu, the fire made by rubbing sticks; Sahasa, fire of the simple household rites; Adbhuta and Vividhi, fires of penance rites; and Arka with his sons Anikavan, Vajasrik, Rakshoha, Pitrikrit, Surabhi, Vasu, Annada and Rukmarat. These fires lived in the first manvantara with the Yama gods, and in all manvantaras the fires return with the same names and functions alongside the gods of that age. Next the ancestors will be described.

01-013.json.summary: The bard tells of the ancestors (pitris). When Brahma had made gods, demons and humans, beings who thought of him as a father were born from his sides; these are the six seasons, and the Veda says 'the seasons are the ancestors and gods'. There are two kinds: the Agnishvattas, householders who did not keep the sacred fires or sacrifice, and the Barhishads, who kept the fires and drank Soma. The months are paired into seasons with qualities (Madhu and Madhava are sap, Shuchi and Shukra fiery, and so on). The seasons are sons of Brahma and preside over time units; since all beings are born from the seasonal times (artava), the seasonal beings are fathers, the seasons grandfathers and the year great-grandfather; the year is Prajapati and its son Agni is Rita, from whom the seasons (ritus) came. From the ancestors and Svadha were born two yogini daughters: Mena, mind-born daughter of the Agnishvattas, married to Himavan, and Dharani, daughter of the Barhishads, married to Meru. Mena bore Mainaka (whose son Krauncha gave his name to Krauncha-dvipa) and the river Ganga, wife of the salt ocean. Dharani bore Mandara and three daughters, Vela, Niyati and Ayati; Vela bore Savarna, who married Prachinabarhis and bore the ten Prachetases, and Daksha was born as their son through Shiva's curse. The sage Shamshapayana asks how this happened. The bard tells that Daksha called his daughters home and honoured them, but did not invite his eldest, Sati, wife of Tryambaka (Shiva), because he hated Rudra, who never bowed to him. Sati came uninvited and was given less honour than her younger sisters; when she protested, Daksha said her sisters' husbands, the great sages Vasishtha, Atri, Pulastya, Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhrigu and Marichi, were better than Shiva, who always rivalled and insulted him. Sati, saying she would give up the body he had given her and in her next birth be Tryambaka's wife again, sat in yoga, and a fire from within burnt her to ashes. Shiva, angry, cursed the sages to be born again, not from wombs, at Brahma's sacrifice in the Vaivasvata age, and cursed Daksha to be born a human king, son of the Prachetases and grandson of Prachinabarhis, by Marisha, daughter of the trees, and said he would spoil his sacrifice there too. Daksha cursed Rudra in return: brahmins would not worship him with the other gods, would touch water after giving him an offering, and he would live on earth; so Rudra is worshipped separately. Sati was reborn as Uma, daughter of Himavan and Mena, and is always Bhava's wife, as Aditi is Kashyapa's, Shri Narayana's, Shachi Indra's and Arundhati Vasishtha's. The lesson is that one should never carry enmity, for it follows a being into other births. The bard then lists the gods of the Svayambhuva age: the Yamas, Ajitas and Shukras, thirty-three Soma-drinkers in all, with Vishvabhuk as Indra; the seven sages Bhrigu, Angiras, Marichi, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri and Vasishtha (as given here); and Manu's ten sons Agnidhra, Agnibahu, Medha, Medhatithi, Vasu, Jyotishman, Dyutiman, Havya, Savana and Satra. Asked by the sages what Time is, the bard says Time has the sun as source, the twinkling (nimesha) as smallest part, number as its eye, day and night as body, and the year as its essence. The five-year yuga has five kinds of year: samvatsara (Agni), parivatsara (the Sun), idvatsara (the Moon), anuvatsara (Wind) and vatsara (Rudra). The text explains each: the Sun is the source of all time divisions, the Moon lord of plants and of the lunar days and ancestors, Wind the breath that moves all beings, and Rudra, born from Brahma's mouth, the soul of the ages who destroys and blesses, and is worshipped as Tryambaka with the three-cup cake. Time runs like a river's current, carrying all away; one who recites this line of the lords of creatures gains great success.

01-014.json.summary: The bard says that in every manvantara the gods, sages and Manus are born with the same roles. He tells the line of Svayambhuva Manu. Priyavrata, by Kamya, daughter of Kardama, had two daughters, Samrat and Kukshi, and ten heroic sons: Agnidhra, Agnibahu, Medha, Medhatithi, Vasu, Jyotishman, Dyutiman, Havya, Savana and Satra (Sabhra). He made seven of them kings of the seven continents: Agnidhra of Jambu, Medhatithi of Plaksha, Vapushman of Shalmala, Jyotishman of Kusha, Dyutiman of Krauncha, Havya of Shaka and Savana of Pushkara. Each king's seven (or two) sons gave their names to the regions of his continent: Savana's sons Mahavita and Dhataki in Pushkara; Havya's sons Jalada, Kumara, Sukumara, Manivaka, Kusumottara, Modaka and Mahadruma in Shaka; Dyutiman's sons Kushala, Manonuga, Ushna, Pavana, Andhakara, Muni and Dundubhi in Krauncha; Jyotishman's sons Udbhijja, Venuman, Vairatha, Lavana, Dhriti, Prabhakara and Kapila in Kusha; Vapushman's sons Shveta, Harita, Jimuta, Rohita, Vaidyuta, Manasa and Suprabha in Shalmala; and Medhatithi's sons Shantabhaya, Shishira, Sukhodaya, Ananda, Shiva, Kshemaka and Dhruva in Plaksha. In the five continents from Plaksha to Shaka there is the order of castes and stages of life, with lasting happiness, long life, beauty and strength for all. Agnidhra, king of Jambudvipa, had nine sons and gave each a region: Nabhi the southern land called Hima, Kimpurusha Hemakuta, Harivarsha Naishadha, Ilavrita the middle land around Meru, Ramya Nila, Hiranvan Shveta, Kuru the land north of Shringavan, Bhadrashva Malyavan and Ketumala Gandhamadana; then he went to do penance. The eight regions other than Bharata are naturally happy, without old age, death, merit or sin, high or low, or the cycle of ages. Nabhi by Merudevi had Rishabha, foremost of kings, and Rishabha's eldest of a hundred sons was Bharata; Rishabha crowned Bharata, gave him the southern land and became a wandering renouncer, and from Bharata the land is called Bharatavarsha. Bharata's line runs through Sumati, Taijasa, Indradyumna, Parameshthi, Pratihara, Pratiharta, Unneta, Bhuma, Udgitha, Prastavi, Vibhu, Prithu, Nakta, Gaya, Nara, Virat, Mahavirya, Dhiman, Mahan, Bhauvana, Tvashta, Virajas, Rajas and Shatajit, who had a hundred sons, all kings; their descendants ruled Bharata through the seventy-one ages of that manvantara. Thus the Svayambhuva creation filled the world with sages, gods, ancestors, gandharvas, rakshasas, yakshas, humans, beasts and birds.

01-015.json.summary: Shamshapayana asks about the size of the earth, its continents, seas, mountains, regions and rivers, and the movements of sun and moon. The bard says the thousands of sub-continents cannot be told one by one; he will describe the seven continents, and warns that things beyond thought should not be judged by reasoning. Jambudvipa is a hundred thousand yojanas across, round, full of countries, cities, mountains and rivers, and ringed by the salt ocean. Six range-mountains run east to west into the seas: Himavan, Hemakuta, Nishadha, Nila, Shveta and Shringavan; between them lie the regions, nine thousand yojanas apart. In the middle is Ilavrita with golden Meru, four-coloured: white on the east (its brahmin side), red on the north (kshatriya), yellow on the south (vaishya) and black on the west (shudra). Meru rises eighty-four thousand yojanas, goes sixteen thousand into the ground, is sixteen thousand wide at the base and thirty-two thousand at the top like a bowl; its circumference is given by different measures. Gods, gandharvas, nagas, rakshasas and apsaras live on it. The regions from south to north are Bharata (Haimavata), Kimpurusha, Harivarsha, Ilavrita, Ramyaka, Hiranmaya and Kuru; Malyavan and Gandhamadana run north-south on the east and west of Meru. Around Meru lie four lands: Bhadrashva, Bharata, Ketumala and the Northern Kurus. In Ketumala, by Gandhamadana, the people are dark and strong, the women lotus-like, and they live ten thousand years drinking the juice of a great jackfruit tree. In Bhadrashva, by Malyavan, the people are white, the women moon-faced, and they stay young drinking the juice of a great black mango tree. In Ramanaka the pure, fair people live eleven thousand five hundred years on the fruit of a red banyan. In Hairanvata, where the Hairanvati river flows, strong, rich yaksha-like people live eleven thousand five hundred years on the fruit of a lakucha tree; Shringavan has three peaks, of jewels, gold and all gems. In the holy land of the Northern Kurus, trees give honey, clothes and ornaments, 'milk trees' give a nectar-like milk, the ground is jewelled with golden sand, and people fallen from the world of the gods are born there as couples who grow up together, love each other like chakravaka birds, never seek other partners, and live thirteen thousand five hundred years without sickness or sorrow.

01-016.json.summary: The sages ask about Bharatavarsha, where the fourteen Manus bring forth creatures. Lomaharshana says Bharata is the land north of the sea and south of the Himalaya; it is named after Manu called Bharata because he sustains (bharana) the people. Only here, and nowhere else on earth, are deeds performed by which mortals reach heaven, liberation or the lower states. Bharata has nine parts separated by sea: Indradvipa, Kasherumat, Tamravarna, Gabhastiman, Nagadvipa, Saumya, Gandharva, Varuna, and this ninth island, a thousand yojanas from Kanyakumari to the source of the Ganga. Its borders are held by outsiders (mlecchas): Kiratas in the east and Yavanas in the west; in the middle live brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, living by sacrifice, arms, trade and service. One who conquers it all is called samrat. Its seven chief mountain ranges are Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Shuktiman, Riksha, Vindhya and Pariyatra, with many lesser hills such as Mandara, Vaihara, Raivataka, Shriparvata and Chitrakuta. The text lists the rivers by the ranges they flow from: from the Himalaya the Ganga, Sindhu, Sarasvati, Shatadru, Chandrabhaga, Yamuna, Sarayu, Iravati, Vitasta, Vipasha, Gomati, Kaushiki, Gandaki and others; from Pariyatra the Vedasmriti, Vetravati, Charmanvati, Shipra and others; from Riksha the Shona, Narmada, Mandakini, Tamasa and others; from Vindhya the Tapi, Payoshni, Nirvindhya, Vaitarani and others; from Sahya the Godavari, Bhimarathi, Krishnavena, Tungabhadra and Kaveri; from Malaya the Kritamala and Tamraparni; from Mahendra the Trisama, Rishikulya, Langulini and Vamshadhara; and from Shuktiman the Rishikulya, Kumari and others. All these rivers are holy, mothers of the world and removers of sin. It then lists the peoples: of the middle country (Kuru, Panchala, Shalva, Shurasena, Matsya, Kashi, Koshala, Magadha, Utkala and others); the pleasant region north of the Sahya on the Godavari, where Rama built the town of Govardhana and the sage Bharadvaja planted heavenly trees for Rama's pleasure; the northern peoples (Bahlika, Abhira, Gandhara, Yavana, Sindhu-Sauvira, China, Tushara, Pallava, Shaka, Kekaya, Kamboja, Darada, Barbara and others); the eastern (Anga, Vanga, Kirata, Kashmira, Huna, Pragjyotisha, Pundra, Videha, Tamralipta, Malla, Magadha); the southern (Pandya, Kerala, Chola, Maharashtra, Kalinga, Vidarbha, Dandaka, Ashmaka, Konkana, Andhra and others); the western (Shurparaka, Nasika, Kaccha, Surashtra, Anarta, Arbuda and others); those of the Vindhya (Malava, Karusha, Mekala, Dasharna, Bhoja, Koshala, Vidisha, Nishadha, Avanti and others); and the mountain peoples (Trigarta, Kirata and others). The sages say four ages, Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Tishya, prevail in Bharata, which will be described later.

01-017.json.summary: The sages ask about Kimpurusha, Harivarsha and the other regions. The bard says Kimpurusha has a great plaksha (fig) grove like Indra's Nandana garden; its people are golden, its women like apsaras, free of sickness and sorrow, and they live ten thousand years drinking the juice of a honey-flowing tree. In Harivarsha the people are silver-coloured, fallen from the gods' world, drink sugarcane juice and live eleven thousand years without old age. In Ilavrita, the middle region, the sun does not burn and sun, moon and stars give no light there; its people are lotus-coloured and lotus-scented, live on the juice of the jambu fruit, wear silver garments and live thirteen thousand years. The sizes of Ilavrita, Meru, Gandhamadana (to the west) and Malyavan (to the east) are given. A river of jambu juice, dark as collyrium, crosses Ilavrita. South of Meru and north of Nishadha stands the eternal jambu tree Sudarshana, eleven hundred yojanas high, always in flower and fruit, after which Jambudvipa is named. Its fruits are huge (eight hundred and sixty-one aratnis) and fall with a loud noise; their juice becomes a river that circles Meru and returns to the tree's root, and those who drink it suffer no old age, hunger, tiredness or death. The juice hardens into Jambunada gold, shining red, which the gods wear. By the Lord's grace the earth swallows the waste and the dead of these people. Rakshasas, pishachas and yakshas live on the Himalaya, gandharvas and apsaras on Hemakuta, the nagas Shesha, Vasuki and Takshaka on Nishadha, the thirty-three gods on Meru, siddhas and brahmin sages on Nila, daityas and danavas on Shveta, and the ancestors on Shringavan. Countless beings, divine and human, live in these nine regions.

01-018.json.summary: The bard describes the mountains, lakes and rivers around Kailasa. On Kailasa, in the middle of the Himalaya, lives Kubera, lord of Alaka, with rakshasas and apsaras; from its foot comes the lake Manda, source of the Mandakini, with the Nandana forest on its bank. North-east is the jewelled mountain Chandraprabha, with the lake and river Acchoda and the Chaitraratha forest, where the yaksha general Manibhadra lives with the guhyakas. South-east is the red mountain Lohita with Lohita lake, source of the great Lauhitya river and the Vishoka forest, where the yaksha Manidhara lives. South is the Vaidyuta mountain with the holy Manasa lake, source of the Sarayu, and the Vaibhraja forest, where the rakshasa son of Praheti lives with hundreds of yatudhanas. West is the golden Aruna mountain, dear to Bhava (Shiva), and the snowy Munjavan where Shiva, the smoky-eyed lord of mountains, lives; from it come the lake and river Shiloda and the Surabhi forest. North is the golden Gaura mountain and Hiranyashringa, at whose foot lies Bindusaras, where King Bhagiratha lived many years for the sake of the Ganga, so that his ancestors, washed by her water, would go to heaven. There the threefold-flowing Ganga, born from the Soma's foot and seen at night as the Milky Way, first came down. She fell on Shiva's head and was held there by his yoga power; drops that fell made Bindusaras ('lake of drops'). Angry, she thought of sweeping Shiva down into the nether world, but he, knowing her pride, held her in his hair; then, seeing the starving, wasted king Bhagiratha, who had earlier pleased him, and remembering Brahma's request, he released her. She split into seven streams: Nalini, Hladini and Pavani flow east, Sita, Chakshu and Sindhu flow west, and the seventh, the Bhagirathi, follows Bhagiratha south to the sea. The peoples watered by each are listed: the Sita through the west, the Chakshu through China, Tushara, Bahlika, Khasha and others, the Sindhu through Darada, Kashmira, Gandhara and others, the Ganga through the gandharvas, Kiratas, Kurus, Bharatas, Panchalas, Kashis, Matsyas, Magadhas, Angas, Vangas and Tamraliptas until stopped by the Vindhya, and the three eastern streams through various eastern peoples. Kubera's four followers on these hills are equal in power, and the wealth of mountain dwellers doubles from one to the next. Other lakes and rivers are named on Hemakuta, Nishadha (Vishnupada), Meru (Chandraprabha and the Jambu river), Nila, Shveta and among the Kurus (Rudrakanta lake, made by Bhava, and the twelve Jaya lakes). In Kimpurusha and the other regions it does not rain; rivers flow from springs. Twelve mountains, among them Rishabha, Dundubhi, Dhumra, Chandra, Kaka, Drona, Somaka, Varaha, Narada, Chakra, Balahaka and Mainaka, lie in the salt sea, where they fled in fear of Indra cutting off their wings; between Chakra and Mainaka the fire Samvartaka (Aurva, the mare's-mouth fire) drinks the sea. The regions grow better one after another in health, length of life, virtue, pleasure and wealth.

01-019.json.summary: The bard describes the six outer continents. Each is twice as wide as the one before and is ringed by a sea of the same width. Plaksha-dvipa surrounds the salt sea; its people live long, without famine, old age or disease. Its seven mountains are Gomedaka, Chandra (where the Ashvins gathered herbs for the nectar), Narada (where Narada and Parvata were born), Dundubhi, Somaka (where the gods stored the nectar that Garuda carried off for his mother), Sumanas or Rishabha (where the Boar killed Hiranyaksha) and the crystal Vaibhraja; its seven regions are Shantabhaya, Shishira, Sukhodaya, Ananda, Shiva, Kshemaka and Dhruva, and its seven rivers include the Anutapta, Sukhi, Vipasha, Tridiva, Kramu, Amrita and Sukrita. In Plaksha and the next four continents there are castes and stages of life, no cycle of ages, a time always like the Treta age, and lives of five thousand years. A great plaksha tree stands in its middle, and it is ringed by the sea of sugarcane juice. Shalmala-dvipa has the mountains Kumuda, Unnata, Balahaka, Drona (home of the healing herbs Vishalyakarani and Mritasanjivani), Kanka, Mahisha (where the fire Mahisha lives) and Kakudman (where Indra guards jewels), seven regions and seven rivers, a great silk-cotton (shalmali) tree, and is ringed by the sea of wine. Kusha-dvipa has the mountains Vidruma, Hema, Dyutiman, Pushpavan, Kusheshaya, Hari and Mandara, regions from Udbhida to Kapila, no thieves or outsiders, fair people and rivers such as Dhutapapa, Shiva and Pavitra; a clump of kusha grass gives it its name, and it is ringed by the sea of ghee. Krauncha-dvipa has the mountains Krauncha, Vamanaka, Andhakaraka, Divavrit, Dvivida, Pundarika and Dundubhisvana, regions Kushala, Manonuga, Ushna, Pivaraka, Andhakaraka, Munidesha and Dundubhisvana, and rivers Gauri, Kumudvati, Sandhya, Ratri, Manojava, Khyati and Pundarika; it is ringed by the sea of curds. Shaka-dvipa has the mountains Udaya, Jaladhara (from which Indra takes the rain), Raivataka (where the star Revati is fixed), Shyama (from which creatures once became dark), Asta, Ambikeya and Kesari (source of the wind), seven regions, a great shaka (teak) tree, and rivers such as Sukumari, Kumari and Nalini; its people keep the four classes without mixing, have no greed, envy, taxes or punishment, and protect one another by their own duty. It is ringed by the sea of milk. Pushkara-dvipa has only one mountain, Manasottara, round like a new moon, fifty thousand yojanas high, dividing it into two regions, Mahavita outside and Dhatakikhanda inside, where people live ten thousand years with mental powers, equal in form and conduct, without crime, punishment, greed, castes, trade, Vedas, rain, rivers, heat or cold, like the Northern Kurus; a banyan tree is worshipped there, and Brahma lives there with the Sadhyas and is worshipped as lord, giving food without effort. It is ringed by the sea of sweet water. The text explains the words samudra, varsha, dvipa, udadhi and parvata, and says the seas rise and fall with the waxing and waning moon by fifteen hundred and ten finger-widths. Beyond lies a golden land twice as wide, then the Lokaloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas high, with light on its inner side and darkness outside; beyond that is the shell of the egg. Inside the egg are the seven worlds (Bhu, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapas, Satya). There are thousands of crores of such eggs, each covered by seven natural coverings (dense water, fire, dense wind, space, the element-source, Mahat and the unmanifest), beyond which is the endless darkness and the abode of the infinite God, unknown even to the gods. Below are seven nether worlds, and Janardana (Vishnu), called Padmanabha, pervades and is worshipped in all of them. The elements arise from and support one another, like vessels inside a larger vessel. This is as much of the earth's arrangement as can be told.

01-020.json.summary: The bard describes what lies below. Earth, wind, space, water and fire are called endless; the earth, mother and bearer of all beings, is said to be endless, as are the waters, fire, space and wind, which rest on one another in layers. Below the earth are seven nether worlds, each ten thousand yojanas deep: Atala (called Tala here), Sutala, Talatala, Atala, Tala, Rasatala and Patala; their ground is in turn black, pale, blue clay, yellow, gravel, rock and gold. The first holds the cities of the demon lords Namuchi and Mahanada, of Shankukarna, Kabandha and Nishkulada, of the rakshasa Bhima Shuladanta, and of the nagas Dhananjaya and Kaliya, with thousands of other naga, danava and rakshasa cities. The second holds the cities of Mahajambha, Hayagriva, Krishna, Nikumbha, Shankha and Gomukha, of the rakshasas Nila and Megha, and of the nagas Kambala, Ashvatara and Takshaka. The third holds those of Prahlada, Anuhlada, Agnimukha, Tarakaksha, Trishiras, Shishumara, Tripura and Puranjana, of the rakshasas Kumbhila, Khara and Viradha, and of the nagas Hemaka, Pandura, Maninaga, Kapila and Vishalaksha. The fourth holds those of Kalanemi, Gajakarna, Kunjara, the rakshasa Sumali, Munja and Vrikavaktra, and a great city of Garuda (Vainateya). The fifth holds those of Virochana, Vaidyuta, Agnijihva, Hiranyaksha, the rakshasas Vidyujjihva and Mahamegha and Malin, and the nagas Kirmira, Svastika and Jaya. The sixth holds those of Kesari, Suparvan, Puloman, Mahisha, the rakshasa Surosha, and the hundred-headed Vasuki, son of Surasa and friend of Indra. The seventh, Patala, holds the joyful city of Bali and the city of Muchukunda, with many cities of daityas, danavas, nagas and rakshasas. At the end of Patala lives Shesha, the endless king of all nagas, ageless and deathless, white as a washed conch, with blue garments, a thousand shining heads and two thousand eyes, wearing one earring, worshipped by great serpents; he is the boundary set by Vishnu. Beyond lies a lightless region unknown even to the gods. Next the bard will describe the course of the sun and moon.

01-021.json.summary: The bard describes the sun's course. The sun and moon light up an area equal to the seven continents and seas, and the sky is as wide as the earth. The sun is called Ravi because he protects (avana) the three worlds. The sun's disc is nine thousand yojanas across and the moon's twice that; the size of the whole earth is given in crores of yojanas. Inside the egg are the seven worlds, set one above another like umbrellas, held by their coverings. On the Manasottara mountain, around Meru, are the cities of the four world guardians: Indra's Vasvaukasara (Amaravati) in the east, Yama's Samyamana in the south, Varuna's Sukha in the west and Soma's Vibhavari in the north. When it is noon in Amaravati, the sun rises in Samyamana, it is midnight in Sukha and the sun sets in Vibhavari, and so on round the four cities; the sun circles fast like a firebrand. Sunrise and sunset are only where people first see it and lose sight of it; at night its light enters fire, and by day the heat of fire enters the sun, and the waters are cool or warm as night or day enters them. The distance the sun travels in a muhurta, the circuits of its southern and northern courses and of the equinox, the three paths (Nagavithi to the north, Ajavithi to the south) and the nakshatras in them are given in yojanas. The sun moves through a hundred and eighty-three circles in each half-year: fast by day and slow by night in the southern course, like the rim of a potter's wheel, and slow by day and fast by night in the northern course, like the hub; the pole star (Dhruva) turns in place like the clay in the middle of the wheel. The world guardians stand on Lokaloka, beyond which there is no light; twilight (sandhya) joins day and night. At each twilight three crores of rakshasas called Mandehas, who by Brahma's curse have bodies that never decay but die daily, try to eat the rising sun; brahmins at the twilight rite throw water charged with Om and the Gayatri, and the sun, protected by them and by the Valakhilya sages, shines out and rises a hundred thousand yojanas. Time units are listed: fifteen nimeshas make a kashtha, thirty kashthas a kala, thirty kalas a muhurta, thirty muhurtas a day and night; the day is divided into five parts of three muhurtas (morning, sangava, midday, afternoon, evening). At the equinox day and night are fifteen muhurtas each. Fortnights, months, seasons, half-years and the five years of a yuga (samvatsara, parivatsara, idavatsara, anuvatsara, vatsara) are explained, with four systems of reckoning (solar, lunar, stellar and civil). The three peaks of Shringavan (gold, silver and jewelled) are described; when the sun reaches the eastern peak it is equinox, when day and night are equal and gifts should be given to the ancestors and brahmins. The months of the northern course are Tapas, Tapasya, Madhu, Madhava, Shukra and Shuchi, and of the southern Nabhas, Nabhasya, Isha, Urja, Sahas and Sahasya. The four world guardians on Lokaloka are Sudhaman, Kardama's son Shankhapa, Hiranyaroman (Parjanya) and Ketuman. South of Ajavithi lies the path of the ancestors, where eighty-eight thousand householder sages who keep the sacred fire and beget children live till the dissolution, reborn in one another's families and re-establishing dharma in each age; north of Nagavithi lies the path of the gods, where eighty-eight thousand celibate sages, who avoided sex, desire and hatred, have won deathlessness until the dissolution. Above the seven sages is Dhruva, the shining third step of Vishnu, Vishnu's highest place, where those who reach it grieve no more.

01-022.json.summary: The sages ask how the heavenly lights move without colliding, and whether something moves them or they move by themselves. The bard says Dhruva, son of Uttanapada, fixed in the tail of the Shishumara (the heavenly porpoise) like the post of a threshing floor, turns the sun, moon and planets, and the stars follow him like a wheel; they are tied to him by bonds of wind. Their conjunctions, risings and settings, portents, the two half-years, the equinox, the seasons and the good and bad fortune of creatures all come from Dhruva. The sun, guided by Dhruva, draws up water from the whole world with his rays and wind; the water passes to the moon, flows down through wind-channels, stays in plants and falls from clouds when the wind strikes them, so water is never lost but only circulates. Heat comes from the sun and cold from the moon, and together they uphold the world; the Ganga and other great rivers have the moon as their support. Water in burning bodies rises as smoke and forms clouds. The words megha and abhra are explained. Clouds are of three kinds: fiery ones born of heat and smoke, called Jimuta, which are silent, without lightning and rain only a short distance; Brahma-born ones from Brahma's breath, with lightning and pleasant thunder, which bring the rainy season that renews the earth; and Pushkaravartaka clouds, born of the wings of mountains that Indra cut off, which bring the flood at the end of the kalpa. The clouds are the pieces of the shell of the cosmic egg, and smoke nourishes them all; Parjanya and the four elephants of the quarters are chief among them and send frost in winter. The Parivaha wind holds the heavenly Ganga, whose spray the elephants of the quarters scatter as mist; it falls on the city of Pundra between Hemakuta and the Himalaya and is carried on to water the lands. The sun is the maker of rain. The sun's chariot, made by Brahma, has one wheel with three naves, five spokes and six rims; it is ten thousand yojanas long, and its parts are the parts of the year: the day is the nave, the five seasonal years the spokes, the six seasons the rim, the half-years the poles, muhurtas, kalas and kashthas other parts, night the cover and dharma the flag. Seven Vedic metres (Gayatri, Trishtubh, Anushtubh, Jagati, Pankti, Brihati and Ushnik) are its horses. The axle is fixed to Dhruva, and two reins tied to Dhruva are drawn in or let out, so the sun moves through inner circles in the northern course and outer circles in the southern.

01-023.json.summary: The bard says the sun's chariot is occupied in turn, two months each, by a group of seven: two Adityas, two sages, two gandharvas, two apsaras, two yakshas (gramanis), two nagas and two rakshasas. In Madhu and Madhava: Dhata and Aryama, Pulastya and Pulaha, the nagas Airavata and Vasuki, Tumburu and Narada, Susthala and Punjikasthala, Rathakrit and Rathaujas, and Heti and Praheti (Kamsa and Bhima are also named). In Shuchi and Shukra: Mitra and Varuna, Atri and Vasishtha, Haha and Huhu, Sahajanya and Menaka, Rathasvana and Rathachitra, Takshaka and Rambhaka, and Paurusheya and Vadha. In Nabhas and Nabhasya: Indra and Vivasvan, Angiras and Bhrigu, Vishvavasu and Ugrasena, Pramlocha and Anumlocha, Shveta and Aruna, Elapatra and Shankhapala, and Sarpa and Vyaghra. In autumn: Parjanya and Pusha, Bharadvaja and Gautama, Paravasu and Suruchi, Vishvachi and Ghritachi, Senajit and Sushena, Airavata and Dhananjaya, and Apa and Vata. In Sahas and Sahasya: Amsha and Bhaga, Kashyapa and Kratu, Chitrasena and Urnayu, Urvashi and Purvachitti, Tarkshya and Arishtanemi, Mahapadma and Karkotaka, and Vidyutsphurja and Shatayu. In Tapas and Tapasya: Tvashta and Vishnu, Jamadagni and Vishvamitra, Dhritarashtra and Suryavarchas, Tilottama and Rambha, Ritajit and Satyajit, Kambala and Ashvatara, and Brahmapeta and Yajnapeta. They strengthen the sun with their power: sages praise him, gandharvas and apsaras sing and dance, yakshas hold the reins, nagas draw the chariot, rakshasas follow, and the Valakhilyas surround him from rising to setting. They give heat, rain and light, and take away the good of the wicked and the sins of the good. The sun feeds the gods with nectar by filling the moon with his Sushumna ray in the bright fortnight, which the gods drink in the dark fortnight; the ancestors drink the last portion on the new-moon day, and humans live on the plants that rain makes grow. The moon's chariot has three wheels and ten white horses, with names such as Yaju, Chandamanas, Vrisha, Hamsa and Vyoma. Thirty-three thousand, three hundred and thirty-three gods drink the moon's digits; the ancestors (Saumyas, Barhishads, Agnishvattas and Kavyas, who are the years, seasons and months) drink the svadha at the new moon. The chariots of the planets are described: Budha's of water and light, Shukra's with ten earth-born horses of many colours, Mangala's golden with eight red horses, Brihaspati's golden with eight white horses, Shanaishchara's of black iron, and those of Rahu (Svarbhanu) and Ketu with eight dark horses; Rahu goes from the sun to the moon at the junctions of the month. All are tied to Dhruva by invisible bonds of wind and turn like an oil press or a firebrand; the wind that carries them is Pravaha. The starry Shishumara is described: Dhruva is in its tail, Uttanapada its upper jaw, Yajna its lower jaw, Dharma its head, Narayana its heart, the Ashvins its forefeet, Varuna and Aryama its hind legs, the year its organ, Mitra its anus, and Agni, Mahendra, Kashyapa and Dhruva in its tail, these four never setting. Seeing it at night removes the sin done by day, and one lives as many extra years as it has stars.

01-024.json.summary: The sages ask how the heavenly bodies can be 'houses of the gods' and what the lights are. The bard explains. When Brahma's night ended and the world lay dark, Brahma, moving like a firefly, found fire hidden in earth and water and divided it in three: earthly fire (fuel-fed, put out by water), the sun's fire called Shuchi, and lightning fire born of water. The sun, lightning and the digestive fire need no fuel and are not quenched by water. At night a quarter of the sun's light enters fire, and by day the heat of fire enters the sun. The sun draws up water from rivers, seas, wells and all beings with a thousand rays: four hundred rain-giving rays called Amrita (named Chandana, Sadhya, Kutana and Akutana), three hundred snow-giving rays called Chandra, and three hundred heat-giving rays called Shukla. With them he feeds humans with plants, ancestors with svadha and gods with nectar; he gives heat in spring and summer, rain in the rainy season and autumn, and cold in winter. Twelve Adityas rule the months, from Varuna in Magha to Vishnu in Pausha, each shining with a stated number of thousands of rays, and the sun's colour changes with the season (tawny, golden, white, pale, copper, red). The sun is the source and support of the moon, stars and planets; the moon is lord of stars and the sun king of planets. Mars is Skanda, Mercury Narayana, Saturn Yama, and Shukra and Brihaspati are the teachers of demons and gods. All the worlds arise from and dissolve into the sun; without him there is no time, no rites, no seasons, no crops and no life. Like a lamp in a house, he lights all sides. Of his thousand rays, seven are the sources of the planets: Sushumna feeds the waning moon, Harikesha the stars, Vishvakarma Mercury, Vishvashravas Venus, Sampadvasu Mars, Arvavasu Jupiter and Svarat Saturn. The words nakshatra, taraka, Aditya, Savita and Chandra are explained. The moon's disc is of dense water and the sun's of dense light; the heavenly bodies are the houses where the gods of each manvantara live. In this age the sun is Vivasvan, son of Aditi; the moon is Soma, son of Dharma; Shukra is Bhargava; Brihaspati is son of Angiras; Budha is son of Soma (Tvishi); Saturn is son of Vivasvan and Samjna; Mars was born of Agni and Vikeshi; the nakshatras are Daksha's daughters; and Svarbhanu (Rahu) is son of Simhika. The sizes of the discs are given: the sun nine thousand yojanas, the moon twice that, Rahu equal to them, Venus a sixteenth of the moon, and the others smaller in turn. From below upward lie the sun, moon, stars, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the seven sages and Dhruva. The nakshatras of each planet's birth are given (the sun in Vishakha, the moon in Krittika, Venus in Tishya, Jupiter in Purva Phalguni, Mars in Purva Ashadha, Saturn in Revati, Mercury in Dhanishtha, Ketu in Ashlesha and Rahu in Bharani); planets afflicted in one's birth star bring trouble, which is removed by worshipping that planet. The first of each class is named: the sun among planets, Shravishtha among stars, the northern course, the samvatsara, Shishira season, Magha month, the bright fortnight, the first lunar day, and the muhurta ruled by Rudra. Rudra moves the sun, who is Time. The motions of the lights cannot be fully grasped by the human eye, and should be studied by scripture, inference, observation and reasoning, using sight, texts, water, drawing and calculation.

01-025.json.summary: After this teaching, at midday the Wind-god (Vayu) recited his prayer, ending 'Salutation to you, Nilakantha (blue-throated one)'. The Valakhilya sages, eighty-eight thousand celibates who travel with the sun and live on air, leaves and water, praised Vayu as the source of all speech and asked why Shiva's throat is blue. Vayu told them that in the Krita age the sage Vasishtha asked Kartikeya (Skanda) the same question, and Kartikeya told what he had heard as a child sitting in Uma's lap, a talk between Shiva and Parvati on beautiful Kailasa, which is described with its birds, music, swings and Shiva's many strange-shaped attendants (ganas). Parvati asked Shiva why his throat shone dark like a cloud. Shiva said: when the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk for nectar, a terrible poison came up first, bright as the fire of doomsday; it burnt Janardana (Vishnu) and turned him from red-fair to dark. The frightened gods and demons went to Brahma, who said this was the Kalakuta poison, which neither he nor Vishnu nor the gods could bear, but only Shankara. Brahma meditated on Om and praised Shiva with a long hymn of salutations (to the three-eyed one, bearer of Pinaka, lord of beings, destroyer of Kama and of Tripura, Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra, Sankhya and Yoga, the manifest and unmanifest, and so on). Shiva asked what he should do; Brahma asked him to drink the poison for the good of the worlds. Shiva agreed and drank it, and his throat at once became dark like a blue lotus, like the naga Takshaka coiled there. Brahma said the throat made him beautiful, so Shiva kept the poison in his throat and became Nilakantha. The amazed gods, demons and other beings praised him as Vishnu, Brahma, Death, the sun, moon, fire, wind, earth and water, creator and destroyer, and went to Meru. Shiva told Parvati the rewards of this story, first spoken by Brahma: poisons, bad dreams and evil are destroyed in one who keeps it; he is loved by women and at court, wins in disputes and battles, travels safely and prospers; after death he becomes like Shiva, blue-throated and three-eyed, and roams all worlds. A brahmin gains the Veda, a kshatriya the earth, a vaishya profit and a shudra happiness; the sick are healed, prisoners freed, pregnant women bear sons, girls find good husbands, and lost wealth is found. Hearing it gives the merit of giving a hundred thousand cows; one who keeps even a quarter verse goes to Rudra's world, and no yakshas, pishachas or vinayakas trouble a house where it is kept. Kartikeya says he heard this and told it to Vasishtha, and a twice-born who studies it reaches the sun's world.

01-026.json.summary: The sages ask about the greatness of Mahadeva. The bard says that after Vishnu bound Bali and won back the three worlds, the gods, sages, gandharvas and others came to the ocean of milk and praised Vishnu as creator and saviour. Vishnu told them that his own power came from the grace of the Lord who is the creator and Time. Long ago, after he had swallowed the three worlds, he lay alone on the waters, thousand-headed, holding conch, discus and mace. Brahma, four-faced, golden and shining, came to him and asked who he was, saying 'I am the maker of the worlds'; Vishnu replied that he was the maker and destroyer, and they argued, each wanting to win. Then they saw in the north a huge flame, and within it a shining linga, neither gold nor stone nor silver, beyond description, growing and splitting heaven and earth. Brahma said, 'You go down and I will go up, and we will find its end.' Vishnu went down for a thousand years and Brahma up, but neither found an end; they returned afraid and bewildered. Folding their hands, they meditated on the Lord and praised him: as the highest Brahman, the imperishable, Jyeshtha, Vamadeva, Rudra, Skanda and Shiva, as Om, vashat, svaha and svadha, the sacrifice and vows, the Vedas, worlds and gods, sound in space, smell in earth, taste in water, form in fire, touch in wind, knowledge in the intellect, the destroyer, Time and Death; with his eastern face he makes Indra, with the southern he draws the worlds back, with the western he is Varuna, and with the northern Soma; from him come the Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts and all beings, and goddesses such as Uma, Lakshmi, Kirti, Medha, Sarasvati, twilight and night; they hail him as golden-seeded, golden-clad, ash-smeared, holder of the Pinaka, and blue-throated. Pleased, Mahadeva appeared, bright as crores of suns, with countless faces, wearing snakes as his sacred thread, and laughed so loudly that the world was filled and they were afraid. He told them not to fear: they were born from his body, Brahma being his right arm and Vishnu his left, and he offered a boon. They asked for lasting devotion to him; he granted it, told them to create many beings, and vanished. Vishnu told the gods this was the unmanifest knowledge called Shiva, seen only by the eye of wisdom. The gods bowed to Shankara and returned home. One who recites this hymn gains all wishes and is freed from sins.

01-027.json.summary: The sages ask how Mahadeva took a strange form in the Devadaru forest and why the sages there failed to recognise him. The bard says that in the Krita age many sages did hard penance in the pine forest on the Himalaya, some living on moss, some lying in water, some standing on one toe. To bless them Shiva came there naked, smeared with ash, with wild hair, fearful teeth, red-brown eyes and a firebrand in his hand, laughing, singing, dancing amorously, weeping, begging again and again, roaring like a bull and braying like a donkey; the sages' wives were drawn to him. The angry, deluded sages cursed him to be a donkey, a rakshasa, a pishacha or a danava, but their penance had no effect on Shankara, as stars fade in the sun. The text notes that curses of sages had struck others: Daksha's sacrifice was destroyed, Vishnu had to take ten births through Bhrigu's curse, Gautama made Indra's organ fall, the Vasus were born in a womb, Nahusha became a snake, the milk ocean was made undrinkable for brahmins and Mandavya cursed Dharma; only Shiva was untouched. The sages told him this conduct was not right for householders, students, forest-dwellers or ascetics, and told him to let his linga fall, speak sweetly and wear a cloth. Shiva said that even Brahma and the gods could not make it fall by force, but he would let it fall himself; then he vanished. With the linga fallen, creatures were no longer born, the sun did not burn, fire lost its light, the stars and planets went wrong, and the sages' rites and power failed. They went to Brahma and told him how they had insulted and struck a madman who behaved wrongly with their daughters-in-law and daughters. Brahma, knowing by meditation, told them this was Mahadeva, the highest lord, who creates and destroys the world, and who is called a yogi in Krita, sacrifice in Treta, the fire of time in Dvapara and the banner of dharma in Kali; they should make an image of the linga as they had seen it and worship him with anger and senses controlled. They did so for a year on altars, mountains, caves and river banks. In spring Shiva came again in the same form; the sages, with wives and children, worshipped him with water, garlands and incense, begged pardon, and praised him at length as the source of all things, the naked one with tinkling bells, the blue-throated dweller in cremation grounds, the best among each class of things, and the one who will burn the worlds with the fire from his forehead. Shiva said that brahmins devoted to ash, self-controlled and meditating, must never be blamed or insulted; whoever blames them blames Mahadeva and whoever honours them honours him. The sages bathed him with scented water and praised him as half-woman (ardhanari), wearing elephant skin and snakes; the linga was set up again. Shiva offered a boon, and Bhrigu, Angiras, Vasishtha, Vishvamitra, Gautama, Atri, Sukesha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Marichi, Kashyapa and Samvarta asked about bathing in ash, nakedness and reversed conduct. Shiva explained: he is Fire joined with Soma (his consort Ambika); the world is made of fire and soma; ash is what remains after fire and is his own seed, which purifies and protects, so ash is put around the houses of women after childbirth. Bathing in ash with anger and senses controlled burns away thousands of wrongs and leads to him without return; one who bathes in ash at the three times becomes a leader of his ganas. The Pashupata vow was made first, before the other stages of life. All beings are born naked; those with unconquered senses are naked even in fine cloth, while patience, steadiness, non-violence, detachment and equal regard for honour and insult are the best covering. Those who meditate on Mahadeva by the northern path gain deathlessness, and those of the southern path who resort to cremation grounds gain the eight powers (anima and the rest). One who reads this pure and with faith goes to Rudra's world.

01-028.json.summary: The sage Shamshapayana asks how King Pururavas, son of Ila, went to heaven every new moon and how he satisfied his ancestors. The bard says that when the sun and moon meet in one nakshatra on the new-moon night, Pururavas went to see them, his maternal and paternal grandfathers, bowed and waited; at the moment called Sinivali or Kuhu he received the nectar (sudha) flowing from the moon and with it offered the monthly shraddha to his ancestors, the Saumyas, Barhishads, Kavyas and Agnishvattas. The ancestors are explained through time: the year (Agni) gave rise to the seasons, the seasons to the seasonal times; the half-months are fathers, the seasons grandfathers and the five-year cycle great-grandfathers. The Saumyas are born of Soma, the Kavyas of Kavi; sacrificing householders are Barhishads, non-sacrificing ones Agnishvattas, and the Kavyas are lords of the Ashtaka rites. The waning and waxing of the moon is described again: thirty-three gods drink its fifteen digits in the dark half, the ancestors drink the last portion at the new moon, and the sun's Sushumna ray fills it again till full moon. The junctions (parvan) of the fortnights are explained like the knots of sugarcane or bamboo, with the exact times for the full-moon and new-moon rites, the vyatipata moment when sun and moon face each other, and the names Anumati and Raka (two kinds of full moon), and Sinivali and Kuhu (two kinds of new moon; Kuhu is named after the cuckoo's call). The ancestors who receive the monthly shraddha are of two kinds: divine ancestors and human ancestors (father, grandfather and great-grandfather). Those who kept the duties of their stage of life and practised penance, celibacy, sacrifice, offspring, shraddha, learning and giving go to heaven and are satisfied by the offerings of their families. Those who fell from their duties, lacking svadha and svaha, become ghosts in Yama's realm, starving, thirsty, naked and driven about, and suffer in hells such as Shalmali, Vaitarani, Kumbhipaka, the burning sand and the sword-leaf forest; the three rice balls offered by relatives on darbha grass, naming their name and clan, reach and satisfy them. Those reborn as animals or plants receive the offering as the food fit for that birth: as a calf finds its mother among lost cows, the mantra carries the shraddha food to the ancestors, so a shraddha given with faith is never fruitless. Sanatkumara saw this with divine sight. For the ancestors the dark fortnight is day and the bright fortnight night. When these ancestors are pleased by shraddha, the gods and ancestors are pleased. This completes the account of the Svayambhuva creation.

01-029.json.summary: A sage asks about the four ages (yugas) of the Svayambhuva manvantara. The bard explains the reckoning of time: fifteen nimeshas make a kashtha, thirty kashthas a kala, thirty kalas a muhurta, and thirty muhurtas a human day and night. A human month is a day and night of the ancestors (the dark fortnight is their day), and a human year is a day and night of the gods (the northern course is their day); three hundred and sixty human years make a divine year. The years of the seven sages and of Dhruva are also given in human years. The four ages of Bharata are Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Kali: Krita lasts four thousand divine years with dawn and dusk of four hundred each, Treta three thousand with three hundred, Dvapara two thousand with two hundred, and Kali one thousand with one hundred, twelve thousand in all; in human years Krita is 1,440,000 plus 288,000 (as given), Treta 1,080,000, Dvapara 720,000 and Kali 360,000. Seventy-one sets of four ages make a manvantara, about 306,720,000 human years. At the start of the Treta age, Manu and the seven sages taught dharma: the seven sages the dharma of revelation (shrauta), based on marriage, the fire rite and the Rig, Yajur and Sama, and Svayambhuva Manu the dharma of tradition (smarta), based on conduct and the duties of castes and stages of life. The Vedic mantras of earlier kalpas came back to the sages by intuition; in Treta the Vedas were whole, and in Dvapara they are divided because life grows short. Kshatriyas offer sacrifices with action, vaishyas with offerings, shudras with service and brahmins with recitation. In Treta the classes were happy, followed one another (kshatriyas following brahmins, vaishyas kshatriyas, shudras vaishyas), and enjoyed long life, intelligence, strength, beauty and health. When people again fell into conflict, Svayambhuva Manu begot Priyavrata and Uttanapada, and from them came kings who bear the rod of punishment and please (ranjana) the people; Yama punishes hidden sins. The gods, led by Indra Vishvabhuk, began sacrifice. Truth, recitation, penance and giving are the dharma of Treta. In Treta, world emperors (chakravartins) are born from a portion of Vishnu: broad-chested, lotus-eyed, of equal height and arm-span (nyagrodha-parimandala), with marks such as the Shrivatsa, long arms, a lion's shoulders, the walk of an elephant, and wheel and fish signs on their feet. They have fourteen jewels, seven lifeless (wheel, chariot, gem, sword, shield, banner, treasure) and seven living (wife, priest, general, chariot-maker, minister, horse and elephant). They have strength, dharma, happiness and wealth without conflict, surpass sages and gods, live eighty-five thousand years and can travel unhindered through sky, sea, the nether world and mountains. In Treta the one Veda has four parts, the rod of punishment keeps order, and people live three thousand years.

01-030.json.summary: Shamshapayana asks how sacrifice began at the start of the Treta age in the Svayambhuva creation. The bard says that when the Krita age ended, plants grew, rain fell, farming and the householder life were set up and the castes and stages arranged, Indra Vishvabhuk began a horse sacrifice with all the gods. The great sages came, and seeing the poor animals tied for slaughter while the priests were busy, they asked Indra what kind of sacrifice this was: killing animals is a strong wrong (adharma), not dharma, for violence is never called dharma. They told him to sacrifice as scripture allows, with seeds of grain kept three years so they cannot sprout, as Brahma once ordained, a sacrifice without violence. A great dispute arose between Indra and the sages over whether one should sacrifice with moving or unmoving things. Tired of arguing, they asked King Vasu, son of Uttanapada, who could move through the sky. Vasu, without weighing the matter, recalled the Vedas and said that one should sacrifice with whatever is offered, with sacrificial animals or with seeds and fruits; violence is the nature of sacrifice, since the mantras and deities the sages saw point to it, and if the mantras are their authority they must accept this. The sages fell silent, seeing it was fated, and as soon as he had spoken King Vasu, who once moved above, sank into the nether world. So no one person, however learned, should decide a doubtful point alone, for the ways of dharma are many and subtle. Therefore the sages call non-violence the door of dharma; thousands of crores of sages reached heaven by their own penance, giving only gleaned grain, roots, fruit, greens and a pot of water. Freedom from malice and greed, penance, kindness to beings, self-control, celibacy, truth, compassion, patience and steadiness are the root of eternal dharma. Kings such as Priyavrata, Uttanapada, Dhruva, Medhatithi, Vasu, Sudhaman, Virajas, Shankha, Prachinabarhis and Parjanya went to heaven by penance. Penance is greater than sacrifice, since Brahma created the world by penance: by sacrifice one reaches the gods, by penance the Vairaja world, by renouncing action Brahma's world, by detachment victory over nature, and by knowledge liberation (kaivalya). The sages, seeing Vasu brought down by the power of dharma, ignored his words and left, and the gods finished their sacrifice. Thus sacrifice began in the Svayambhuva age, and since then it has turned with the ages.

01-031.json.summary: The bard describes the Dvapara and Kali ages. In Dvapara the powers of Treta fade; the classes become mixed, duties are reversed, and the age is marked by sacrifice, punishment, pride, hypocrisy, patience and force, under rajas and tamas. Revelation and tradition split in two, people cannot agree on what dharma is, and the one four-part Veda is divided because life grows short, by Vyasa at the start of each Dvapara; the Rig, Yajur, Sama and Atharva branches, the Brahmanas and Kalpa-sutras multiply and differ. Drought, death and disease bring sorrow, sorrow brings reflection, reflection detachment, and detachment the seeing of faults. Medicine, the Vedic limbs, astrology, statecraft, logic, commentary and law books arise as separate schools. Livelihood is won only with bodily toil, greed and trade spread, and desire, anger and killing increase. In Tishya (Kali) come violence, envy, lies, deceit and the killing of ascetics; plague, hunger and drought; tradition is no longer an authority; people die in the womb, in youth or in childhood; and the bad sacrifices and study of brahmins bring fear to all. The longest life is a thousand years at first and later a hundred.
