Twice-born men stop studying and sacrificing; shudras share beds, seats and food with brahmins; kings are mostly shudras who spread heresy; shudras act like brahmins and brahmins like shudras; kings act like thieves; women become faithless, fond of wine and meat, and few are faithful to one husband; cows decline and wild beasts grow strong; giving is the main dharma left; kings take taxes but do not protect; brahmins live by serving shudras and bow to them; people sell penance and sacrifice; there are many ascetics in ochre robes, shaven heads and false sects (Nirgranthas, Kapalikas and others); men are few and women many; people sell the Veda and holy places; shudras teach dharma and shudra-born kings perform horse sacrifices; people kill women, children and cows. Yet in Kali those who keep dharma reach success quickly: what took a year in Treta and a month in Dvapara is gained in a day. At the end of Kali, in its twilight, Pramati, born of the Bhrigu line and of the Moon's clan from a portion of Madhava (Vishnu), as in an earlier Svayambhuva age, at thirty-two years of age goes about the earth for twenty years with an army of armed brahmins and kills the outsiders (mlecchas), shudra-born kings, heretics and the unrighteous in all regions (the peoples listed include Gandharas, Paradas, Pahlavas, Yavanas, Shakas, Tusharas, Barbaras, Chinas, Kiratas, Dravidas and Simhalas), and comes to rest between the Ganga and the Yamuna. The few people left, without a king, attack one another, abandon wives, homes and farming, flee to rivers, coasts and mountains, live on meat, roots and fruits, dressed in bark and leaves, until sorrow brings reflection, calm and understanding; then in a day and night, as if waking from sleep, the Krita age begins. The siddhas and seven sages who stayed as seed teach the shrauta and smarta dharma to the new Krita people, born from the remnant of Kali as grass sprouts from burnt roots after rain. Happiness, life, strength, beauty, dharma, wealth and pleasure decline by a quarter in each age. A thousand sets of four ages make a day of Brahma, and seventy-one a manvantara; every manvantara and kalpa repeats the same pattern, and the world, like the ages, never stands still but turns through rise and fall.

01-032.json.summary: The bard says that in the Krita age demons, nagas, gandharvas, pishachas, yakshas and rakshasas are born equal in size; the eight orders of divine beings are ninety-six finger-widths tall by their own fingers. The heights of gods, demons and humans in the various ages and twilights are given; a human is eight of his own spans (tala) tall, and one who is nine spans tall with arms reaching the knees is honoured even by gods. The heights of cattle, elephants and trees are given too. Animals, birds and plants used in sacrifice are reborn in the gods' worlds in the same forms. The bard then defines the good. Sat means Brahman, so those who share in it are santah (the virtuous); those who are not angered or pleased by the ten sense objects and eight causes are self-controlled; brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas are twice-born because they keep both general and special duties; a student is a sadhu by pursuing learning, a householder by managing the house, a forest-dweller by penance and an ascetic by yoga. Dharma and adharma are good and bad action; dharma (from dhri, to hold) brings what is desired and adharma what is not. An acharya is one who practises, establishes and gathers the rules. Dharma is twofold: shrauta (from hearing), based on marriage, the fire rite and the Vedas, taught by the seven sages; and smarta (from memory), based on the conduct of castes and stages, taught by Manu, who remembered the customs of the previous manvantara. The 'shishtas' are those who remain (shesha) in each manvantara to keep dharma, Manu and the seven sages, and their conduct is shishtachara, with eight marks: giving, truth, penance, knowledge, learning, sacrifice, renunciation and kindness. The limbs of dharma are defined: truth is telling exactly what one saw when asked; penance is celibacy, recitation, silence and fasting; sacrifice is the joining of animals, offerings, mantras, priests and fees; kindness is treating all beings as oneself; patience is not striking back when abused or struck; non-greed is not taking others' goods even when unguarded; celibacy is avoiding sex in act, thought and talk; self-control is not misusing the senses; giving is giving one's dearest lawfully-won goods to the worthy, best when for liberation, middling when from compassion and lowest when for one's own gain; detachment, renunciation and knowledge (knowing the conscious from the unconscious) are also defined. In each manvantara a new Veda is set out, though the Shatarudriya stays the same, and hymns are of four kinds (praising substance, quality, fruit and lineage). Mantras appeared to the sages from discontent, fear, sorrow, joy and grief. The bard explains the five kinds of rishi from the creation of Mahat onward, the word rishi (from rish, to go) and the classes: the ten great sages (maharshis), Brahma's mind-born sons Bhrigu, Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Manu, Daksha, Vasishtha and Pulastya; the rishis, their sons, such as Kavya, Brihaspati, Kashyapa, Chyavana, Utathya, Vamadeva, Kardama, Vishravas, Shakti and the Valakhilyas; and the rishikas, born of wombs, such as Vatsara, Bharadvaja, Dirghatamas, Sharadvat, Parashara, Dadhicha and Vaishravana. It then lists the ninety mantra-makers by family: nineteen Bhrigus (Bhrigu, Kavya, Prachetas, Richika, Aurva, Jamadagni, Vainya Prithu, Divodasa, Gritsamada, Shaunaka and others), thirty-three Angirasas (Angiras, Bharadvaja, Garga, Mandhata, Ambarisha, Purukutsa, Trasadasyu, Kanva, Mudgala, Utathya, Vamadeva, Dirghatamas, Kakshivan and others), six Kashyapas (Kashyapa, Vatsara, Naidhruva, Raibhya, Asita, Devala), the Atris (Atri, Shyavashva, Gavishthira, Purvatithi and others), seven Vasishthas (Vasishtha, Shakti, Parashara, Indrapramati, Bharadvasu, Maitravaruni, Kundina), thirteen Kushikas (Vishvamitra, Devarata, Madhucchandas, Aghamarshana, Ashtaka, Lohita and others), three Agastyas (Agastya, Dridhayu, Idhmavaha), two kshatriyas (Vaivasvata Manu and Pururavas) and three vaishyas (Bhalandana, Vatsa, Sankila).

01-033.json.summary: The bard names the 'sons of sages' (rishiputras) who taught the Brahmana texts and branches of the Vedas. Among the Rigveda (bahvricha) teachers are Bhargava, Paila, Sankritya, Jajali, Mathara, Yajnavalkya, Parashara, Upamanyu, Indrapramati, Manduki, Shakali, Bashkali and others, eighty-six in all; among the Charaka Adhvaryus (Yajurveda) are Vaishampayana, Lauhitya, Kantha, Kala, Shyamapati, Palandu and Alambi; among the Sama singers are Jaimini, Bharadvaja, Kavya, Paushyanji, Hiranyanabha, Kaushilya, Laugakshi, Kusumi, Langali, Shalihotra and King Pururavas; and others such as Kaushitaki, Markandeya, Vaiyasaki Shuka, Bhurishravas, Dhaumya, Kashyapa, Aruni, Shvetaketu, Kahoda, Yajnavalkya and Shaunaka. Women who spoke of Brahman are also named: Aditi, Urvashi, Vishvayosha, Mudgala, Tara, Pratimedhi, Sujata, Lopamudra and Kaushitika. The styles of speech are distinguished: Brahma's words are commanding, unified and deep; the great sages' words state things directly with names and case-endings; the rishikas' words use many Vedic and particle forms; the words of sages' sons are unclear and full of doubt; ordinary human speech is full of reasons, examples and empty showy words; and 'mixed' sages, born across class lines, speak of past, present and future and of cures for the suffering of birth. Brihaspati, Shukra, Vyasa and Sarasvata, who wrote the law books and the shastras, are rishis by their great penance; a rishi is known by wisdom, not by age. A Rik is a verse with set metrical feet; a Yajus is a formula not measured by feet; a Saman has seven parts (hinkara, pranava, prastava, udgitha, pratihara, upadrava and nidhana), or five without the first two. Mantras are of nine kinds (form, blame, praise, abuse, satisfaction, question, permission, narrative and blessing), and twenty-four varieties are listed, such as praise, censure, lament, curse, question, answer, blessing, sacrifice, prohibition, instruction, salutation and longing. The Brahmana has ten modes: reason (hetu), explanation (nirvachana), blame, praise, doubt, injunction (vidhi), the deeds of another (purakriti), ancient tale (purakalpa), decision (vyavadharana) and comparison (upama), each explained. Mantra comes from mantray (to counsel), and a sutra is short, clear, meaningful, all-sided, without filler and faultless.

01-034.json.summary: The sages ask how the Vedas came to be divided again. The bard says that in a Dvapara age of the Svayambhuva manvantara, Brahma told Manu to protect the Veda, since the twice-born had grown weak and only a ten-thousandth of the Krita-age strength was left; if the Veda perished, sacrifice would perish, and with it everything. The first Veda had four parts and a hundred thousand verses, and the sacrifice ten times as much. Manu divided the one Veda into four. In this age Vyasa, son of Parashara, called Dvaipayana, an eternal portion of Vishnu, was urged by Brahma to do the same. He took four pupils for the Vedas: Paila for the Rigveda, Vaishampayana for the Yajurveda, Jaimini for the Samaveda and Sumantu for the Atharvaveda; and he took the bard Lomaharshana for the epics and Puranas. From the one Yajurveda he arranged the four priestly offices: the adhvaryu with the Yajus, the hotri with the Rik, the udgatri with the Saman and the brahman with the Atharva; he collected the Riks into the Rigveda and the Samans into the Samaveda, used the Atharva for the king's rites, and made a Purana collection from stories, sub-stories, songs and traditions. The Yajurveda is so named from yajana (sacrificing), and the horse sacrifice is performed with it. Paila split the Rigveda into two collections and gave them to Indrapramati and Bashkala; Bashkala made four and taught them to Bodhya, Agnimathara, Parashara and Yajnavalkya; Indrapramati taught Mandukeya, whose line ran through Satyashravas, Satyahita and Satyashri, whose three pupils Shakalya (Devamitra), Rathitara and Bashkali Bharadvaja founded branches. The proud Shakalya died at King Janaka's sacrifice. Asked how, the bard tells that thousands of sages came to Janaka's horse sacrifice; Janaka, wishing to know who was best, offered a thousand cows, gold, villages, jewels and slave women to the best among them. The sages, greedy for the wealth and proud of their learning, quarrelled over it. Yajnavalkya, born of a portion of Brahma, told his pupil to take the wealth home, saying no one equalled him in debate and anyone who disagreed could challenge him. He calmly debated the sages one by one, and none could answer him. Then he called on Shakalya, who angrily accused him of treating them all like straw and taking the prize; Yajnavalkya replied that the strength of knowers of Brahman is insight, that the prize was the king's wager, and offered to answer questions on desires. Shakalya asked over a thousand questions and Yajnavalkya answered them all before the sages. Then Yajnavalkya asked him one question, with death as the stake, on Sankhya, Yoga, the highest goal of the self or the path of meditation; Shakalya could not answer and died. Yajnavalkya took the wealth and fame and went home with his pupils.

01-035.json.summary: The bard continues the spread of the Veda branches. Shakalya made five Rigveda collections for his pupils Mudgala, Gokhala, Khaliyas, Matsya and Shaishireya; Shakapurni Rathitara made three and a fourth work, the Nirukta (etymology), taught to Paila, Ikshalaka, Shatabalaka and Gaja; Bashkali Bharadvaja made three, taught to Apanapa, Pannagari and Arjava. Vaishampayana made eighty-six Yajurveda collections and gave them to his pupils, leaving out only Yajnavalkya; they divided into northern, middle-country and eastern schools, led by Shyamayani, Asuri and Alambi. Asked why they are called Charaka Adhvaryus, the bard tells that the sages once agreed to meet on Meru, and anyone who did not come within seven nights would incur the sin of killing a brahmin. Vaishampayana alone failed to come and so bore that sin; he asked his pupils to perform the atonement for him. Yajnavalkya said he alone would do it by his own penance and the others need not. Angered, Vaishampayana rejected him and told him to give back all he had learnt; Yajnavalkya vomited the Yajus formulas, stained with blood, and gave them back. He then worshipped the Sun by meditation, and the Sun, in the form of a horse, gave him the Yajus formulas that had gone up into the solar disc; those who study them are called Vajins, while Vaishampayana's pupils, who 'performed' (charana) the atonement, are called Charakas. Yajnavalkya's fifteen pupils (Kanva, Baudheya, Madhyandina, Vaidheya, Tapaniya, Vatsa, Jabala, Kevala, Avati, Pundra, Vainaya, Parashara and others) are the Vajins; the Yajus teachers number a hundred and one. Jaimini taught the Samaveda to his son Sumantu, he to Sutvan, he to Sukarman, who learnt a thousand collections; when Indra killed pupils who studied on forbidden days, Sukarman fasted to death in protest until Indra granted him two mighty pupils, Paushyanji and the prince Hiranyanabha Kaushalya, who founded the northern and eastern Sama schools. Their pupils and sub-branches are listed (Laugakshi, Kuthumi, Kushidi, Langali, Ranayaniya, Patanjali, Krita and many others). Sumantu split the Atharvaveda and gave it to Kabandha, who split it between Pathya and Devadarsha; Devadarsha's pupils were Moda, Brahmabala, Pippalada and Shaulkayani; Pathya's were Jajali, Kumudadi and Shaunaka, whose line produced the Nakshatra-kalpa, Vaitana, Samhita-vidhi, Angirasa-kalpa and Shanti-kalpa. The bard himself made the Purana collection; his pupils were Atreya Sumati, Kashyapa Akritavrana, Bharadvaja Agnivarchas, Vasishtha Mitrayu, Savarni Somadatti and Susharma Shamshapayana, of whom Kashyapa, Savarni and Shamshapayana made three more collections, so with his own there are four root collections of four thousand verses each. The numbers of Rik, Saman and Yajus verses in various schools are given. The eighteen branches of learning are the four Vedas, six limbs, Mimamsa, Nyaya, law, Purana, medicine, archery, music and statecraft. There are three kinds of sage: brahmarshis of the families of Kashyapa, Vasishtha, Bhrigu, Angiras and Atri, who live in Brahma's world; devarshis such as Nara and Narayana, the Valakhilyas, Kardama, Kubera, Narada and Parvata, who live in the gods' world; and rajarshis of the lines of Manu, Ila, Ikshvaku and Nabhaga, who live in Indra's world. Seven marks make the seven sages: long life, making mantras, power, divine sight, wisdom, direct knowledge of dharma, and founding clans. Eighty-eight thousand householder sages take the southern path and as many celibates the northern. In the Vaivasvata manvantara the Vedas have been divided twenty-eight times; the Vyasas of each Dvapara are listed: Svayambhu (Brahma), Prajapati, Ushanas, Brihaspati, Savita, Mrityu, Indra, Vasishtha, Sarasvata, Tridhama, Trivrisha, Sanadvaja, Antariksha, Dharma, Trayyaruni, Dhananjaya, Kritanjaya, Rijisha, Bharadvaja, Gautama, Uttama, Haryavana, Vena, Vajashravas, Somamukhyayana, Trinabindu, Tataja, Shakti, Parashara, Jatukarna and Dvaipayana; the next will be Drauni (Ashvatthama). The text then praises the supreme Brahman, the one syllable Om, beyond creation and dissolution. The length of a manvantara is given again (306,720,000 human years), fourteen of which make Brahma's day. At the end of a manvantara the gods, sages, ancestors and Manu go up to Maharloka; the seven sages and Manu who remain start the next manvantara at the beginning of a Krita age, as Krita follows Kali, setting up the Vedas, livelihood, punishment, the castes and stages; new gods fill the empty places. Reciting this account of the Manus is holy, brings heaven, sons and long life, and should be recited on great festival days.

01-036.json.summary: Shamshapayana asks about the other manvantaras. The bard names the six past Manus (Svayambhuva, Svarochisha, Uttama, Tamasa, Raivata and Chakshusha) and says eight are to come (Savarni, Raucya, Bhautya and others, besides Vaivasvata). For each he gives the gods, Indra, seven sages and Manu's sons. In the Svarochisha age the gods were the Tushitas, sons of Kratu, and the Paravatas, sons of Vasishtha, twenty-four Soma-drinkers; Indra was Vipashchit; the seven sages were Urja, Stamba, Prana, Rishabha, Datta, Nishchala and Arvarivan; Manu's nine sons included Chaitra and Kimpurusha. In the Uttama age there were five groups of twelve gods (Sudhamans, Vashavartins, Pratardanas, Shivas and Satyas); Indra was Sushanti; the seven sages were the sons of Vasishtha; Manu had thirteen sons. In the Tamasa age the gods were the Satyas, Surupas, Sudhis and Haris, sons of Pulastya, in groups of twenty-five; Indra was Shibi; the sages were Kavya, Prithu, Agni, Jyotirdhama, Charaka, Pivara and Chaitra; Manu's sons included Janujangha, Shanti and Nara. In the fifth age (Raivata) the gods were the Amitabhas, Abhutarajasas, Vaikunthas and Sumedhas, fourteen each; Indra was Vibhu; the sages were Devabahu, Sudhaman, Hiranyaroman, Vedashri, Urdhvabahu, Parjanya and Satyanetra. Svarochisha, Uttama, Tamasa and Raivata were of Priyavrata's line. In the Chakshusha age the gods were the Adyas, Prasutas, Bhavyas, Prithukas and Lekhas, eight each; Indra was Manojava; the sages were Uttama, Havishman, Sudhaman, Virajas, Atinaman, Sahishnu and Madhu; Manu's ten sons by Nadvala were Uru, Puru, Shatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavak, Kriti, Agnishtut, Atiratra, Sudyumna and Abhimanyu. The bard then gives Chakshusha's ancestry. Uttanapada, given in adoption to Atri, had by Sunrita, daughter of Dharma, the sons Dhruva, Kirtiman, Ayushman and Vasu. Dhruva fasted and did penance for ten thousand divine years seeking great fame, and Brahma gave him the highest place among the stars, which neither rises nor sets until the dissolution; Ushanas sang a verse in wonder that the seven sages circle him. Dhruva's line ran through Shishti, Prachinagarbha, Udaradhi (once Indra), Divanjaya, Ripu, Ripunjaya and Chakshusha, father of Chakshusha Manu by Pushkarini, called Varuni because her brother had become Varuna. From Uru came Anga, whose son by Sunitha, daughter of Death, was Vena. Asked to tell Pritu's birth in full, the bard warns that it should be told only to the pure and devoted. Vena, through the fault of his maternal grandfather, abandoned dharma, stopped study and sacrifice, forbade sacrifice and giving, and demanded that sacrifices be made to him alone. The sages led by Marichi begged him to stop; he laughed and said none equalled him and he could burn or flood the earth at will. The angry sages seized him and churned his left hand: from it came a short, very dark man, who stood frightened; told 'sit down' (nishida), he became the ancestor of the Nishadas, and the fishermen and Vindhya peoples are said to come from Vena's sin. Then they churned his right hand like a fire stick, and from it came Prithu, blazing like fire, holding the bow Ajagava, arrows and armour; Vena, saved by this good son from the hell called Put, went to heaven. The rivers, seas, Brahma, the gods and all beings consecrated Prithu as the first king; because he pleased (ranjana) the people whom his father had harmed, he was called raja. Waters stood still when he crossed the sea and mountains made way; the earth gave crops without ploughing. At his sacrifice the Suta was born on the Soma-pressing day and the Magadha during the chanting; the Suta's origin is explained as a mixing of offerings, and his duty is to manage chariots, elephants and horses and practise medicine. The sages told them to praise Prithu for the deeds he would later do; pleased, he gave the Anupa country to the Suta and Magadha to the Magadha, and since then kings are praised by such bards. The hungry people ran to Prithu for livelihood; he took his bow and chased the earth, who fled as a cow through all the worlds, then begged him not to kill a woman, saying the people depended on her. Prithu said that killing one for the good of many is no sin and he would kill her unless she fed the people; she agreed to be his daughter if he gave her a calf and levelled her. He pushed back the rocks with his bow tip, which made the mountains grow; before this the earth was uneven and there were no towns, crops, cattle-keeping, farming or trade. Making Chakshusha Manu the calf, Prithu milked crops from the earth into his own hand. Then others milked her: the sages with Soma as calf, Brihaspati as milker, the metres as vessel and penance and the Veda as milk; the gods with Indra as calf and Savita as milker in a golden vessel, getting vigour and honey; the ancestors with Yama as calf and Death as milker in a silver vessel, getting svadha; the demons with Virochana as calf and Dvimurdha as milker in an iron vessel, getting magic; the nagas with Takshaka as calf and Vasuki as milker in a gourd, getting poison; the yakshas with Vaishravana as calf in an unbaked pot, getting the power to vanish; the rakshasas and pishachas with Sumali as calf in a skull, getting blood; the gandharvas and apsaras with Chitraratha as calf in a lotus, getting fragrances; the mountains with Himavan as calf and Meru as milker, getting herbs and gems; and the trees with the plaksha as calf in a palasha vessel, getting the power to regrow when cut or burnt. Thus the earth, mother and support of all, was milked by Prithu for the good of the worlds.

01-037.json.summary: The bard explains the earth's names: Vasudha because she holds wealth (vasu), Medini because she was once covered with the fat (medas) of Madhu and Kaitabha, and Prithivi because she became the daughter of Prithu. Prithu divided the earth into regions with towns and mines and protected the four classes; he should be honoured by all: by brahmins, by kings seeking fame, by warriors seeking victory (a soldier who names Prithu before battle comes through safely) and by vaishyas, since he gave livelihood. The earth was first milked by Brahma, with Vayu as calf, for seeds; then in each manvantara with its Manu as calf (Svayambhuva, Svarochisha, Uttama, Tamasa, Charishnava, Chakshusha), and in the present Vaivasvata age by Prithu. Prithu's sons were Antardhi and Pavana; Antardhana by Shikhandini had Havirdhana, whose sons by Dhishana were Prachinabarhis, Shukla, Gaya, Krishna, Vraja and Ajina. Prachinabarhis, so called because his kusha grass pointed east, became sole king of the earth; by Savarna, daughter of the ocean, he had the ten Prachetases, masters of archery, who did penance for ten thousand years lying in the sea. While they did so the unprotected earth was covered by trees, the wind could not blow, the sky was hidden and creatures perished. Angered, the Prachetases sent out wind and fire from their mouths; the wind uprooted the trees and the fire burnt them. When only a few trees were left, King Soma came and asked them to give up their anger: trees would grow again, and he offered them as wife Marisha, a jewel of a girl born of the trees, whom he had borne in his womb; from her, with half their power and half his, would be born the wise Daksha, who would again increase the creatures. The Prachetases accepted her, and Daksha was born from the ten brothers and Marisha with a portion of Soma. Daksha first created beings by thought, then by sexual union; he gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kashyapa, twenty-seven (the lunar mansions) to the Moon, four to Arishtanemi, two to Bahuputra, two to Angiras and one to Krishashva, and from them came gods, birds, cows, nagas, daityas, danavas, gandharvas, apsaras and other races of the Vaivasvata age; from then on creatures were born by union, whereas earlier they arose by will, sight or touch. A sage asks how Daksha, said earlier to be born of Brahma's breath, could again be born a son of the Prachetases, and how Soma's daughter's son became his father-in-law. The bard says birth and dissolution go on always; Daksha and the others are born in every age and the wise are not confused, for in those times penance and power, not age or seniority, were what counted. One who knows this creation of the Chakshusha age has children, long life and honour in heaven. So the six creations from Svayambhuva to Chakshusha have been told in brief; the bard will now tell the present Vaivasvata creation.

01-038.json.summary: The bard describes the seventh, Vaivasvata, manvantara. Its gods were born of Kashyapa, son of Marichi, and of others: the eight groups are the Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, Maruts, Bhrigus and Angirasas; the Adityas, Maruts and Rudras are Kashyapa's sons, the Sadhyas, Vasus and Vishvedevas Dharma's, and the Bhrigus and Angirasas the sons of Bhrigu and Angiras. Their Indra is the mighty one called Tejasvin. All the Indras of the manvantaras, past and future, share the same marks: they are lords of past, future and present, thousand-eyed, holding the thunderbolt, each having performed a hundred sacrifices, and surpass all beings in power, penance, wisdom and strength. The bard explains 'lords of past, future and present': Brahma first uttered 'Bhuh' and the earth (Bhurloka, the 'past' or existing world) came to be; then 'Bhuvah' (from 'bhavat', becoming) and the atmosphere arose; then 'Bhavya' (what is to be) and heaven arose; these are the three vyahritis; and since natha means protector, the Indras are lords of the three worlds. The gods, yakshas, gandharvas, rakshasas, pishachas, nagas and humans are their glory, and they protect creatures by dharma like kings, teachers and fathers. The seven sages of this age are Vishvamitra son of Gadhi, Jamadagni son of Aurva, Bharadvaja son of Brihaspati, Gautama Sharadvan son of Utathya, Atri, Vasuman son of Vasishtha, and Vatsara of Kashyapa's line. The nine sons of Vaivasvata Manu are Ikshvaku, Nriga, Dhrishta, Sharyati, Narishyanta, Nabhaga, Dishta, Karusha and Prishadhra (with Pamshu named as the ninth). This ends the second part (Anushanga-pada) and the first section (Purva-bhaga) of the Brahmanda Purana.

02-001.json.summary: This chapter opens the middle section (Madhya-bhaga) and the third part, the Upodghata-pada. Shamshapayana asks for the third part in full, and the bard begins the present Vaivasvata creation. The seven sages of the Svayambhuva age, cursed by Bhava (Shiva), had gone to Janaloka; there they agreed to be born again as Brahma's sons at Varuna's sacrifice in the Chakshusha age. At the great sacrifice of the god (Brahma) bearing the form of Varuna, attended by all the gods, the Vedas in bodily form (the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda with the gandharvas, and the fierce Brahmaveda or Atharva), the parts of sacrifice, the goddess Ila, the quarters and the goddesses, Brahma saw the beautiful divine women, and his seed fell on the ground. He took it up with the ladle and offered it into the fire with mantras, and the great sages were born, blazing. From the flame came Bhrigu (Brahma said 'bhrigus tvam'), and Mahadeva claimed him as his son, so the Bhrigus are called Varunas. From the coals (angara) came Angiras, whom Agni claimed. From six more offerings came Marichi (from the rays), Kratu (from the sacrifice), Atri ('I am the third'), Pulastya (from heaped hair), Pulaha (from long hair) and Vasishtha (from the midst of wealth); these are the mind-born sons who increased the creatures. These sages also produced the seven groups of ancestors (the Maricas, Bhargavas, Angirasas, Paulastyas, Paulahas, Vasishthas and Atreyas) and three others (Amurtas, Aprakashas and Jyotishmans), ruled by Yama. Other lords of creatures were born too: Kashyapa, Kardama, Shesha, Vikranta, Sushravas, Bahuputra, Kumara, Vivasvan, Prachetas, Arishtanemi and others; the Valakhilyas from the kusha grass, the Vaikhanasas from the ash, the Ashvins from his nose, and other beings, seasons and times from other parts of him. The gods asked Brahma that these be lords of creatures and continue his line, and he agreed. The bard first gives the line of Bhrigu. Bhrigu's wives were Divya, daughter of Hiranyakashipu, and Pauloma (Puloma), daughter of Puloman. Divya bore Shukra (Ushanas, Kavya), teacher of gods and demons, whose wife Go, mind-born daughter of the ancestors, bore Tvashta, Varutri, Shanda and Amarka. Varutri's sons, priests of the demons, tried to destroy sacrifice by making Manu sacrifice for them; Indra drove them off, freed Manu's wife from a demon's grip, and burnt them on the southern half of the altar, and their heads became date palms. Shukra's daughter by Jayanti was Devayani; Tvashta's sons were Trishiras Vishvarupa and Vishvakarma. Bhrigu had twelve sons called the Bhrigu gods (Bhuvana, Bhavana and others). Pauloma's son was dropped from the womb in the eighth month when a rakshasa attacked, so he was called Chyavana, and he burnt the man-eaters in anger. By Sukanya he had Apravana and Dadhicha; Dadhicha's son by Sarasvati was Sarasvata; Apravana by Ruchi had Aurva, born by splitting the thigh (uru); Aurva's son was Richika; Richika's son by Satyavati was Jamadagni, born through the exchange of the two rice dishes (one for Rudra, one for Vishnu); Jamadagni and Renuka had Rama (Parashurama), with both brahmin and warrior nature. The Bhargava sub-clans are the Vatsas, Vidas, Arshtishenas, Yaskas, Vainyas, Shaunakas and Mitrayus. Then the line of Angiras: Atharvan (Angiras) married Surupa daughter of Marichi, Svarat daughter of Kardama and Pathya daughter of Manu, and had Brihaspati, Gautama, Ayasya, Vamadeva, Utathya, Ushija, Dhrishni and Samvarta; their descendants include Bharadvaja (son of Brihaspati), Sharadvan, Dirghatamas, Brihaduktha, Sudhanvan and the Ribhus, the divine chariot-makers; the fifteen Angirasa sub-clans include the Bharadvajas, Gargas, Kanvas, Mudgalas, Haritas and Kapis. Marichi, seeking a son, meditated in the waters for seven thousand years and begot Arishtanemi, called Kashyapa, equal to Brahma in power, who is born in every manvantara from a portion of Brahma. The name Kashyapa is explained: when Daksha spoke harshly to him over his daughters, he angrily drank kashya (wine), or because of harsh speech (kasha). Daksha gave him his daughters, all mothers of the world. One who knows this creation of the sages lives long and is freed from all sins.

02-002.json.summary: The bard says that after the sixth (Chakshusha) creation, Daksha, told by Brahma to create, first made gods, sages, gandharvas, humans, nagas, rakshasas, yakshas, pishachas, birds and beasts by thought; when these did not increase, he decided to create by union and married Asikni, daughter of the patriarch Virana, a woman of great penance who upholds the world. A verse is quoted that a million proud serpents followed Daksha as he married her. By Asikni he had a thousand mighty sons, the Haryashvas. Narada, Brahma's son, who was later born again as a mind-born son of Kashyapa because of Daksha's curse, destroyed them. Asked how, the bard tells: when the Haryashvas met to increase creation, Narada told them they were foolish, since they did not know the size of the earth above, below and within, so how could they create? They went off in every direction to find out and never came back, like rivers into the sea. Daksha then had another thousand sons, the Shabalashvas; Narada told them the same, they agreed to follow their brothers' path, and they too never returned. Since then a brother who goes searching for a lost brother soon perishes, so the wise should not do it. Daksha in anger cursed Narada to perish and to live in a womb. Brahma, with the brahmin sages, pleaded with Daksha, and they agreed that Narada would be born as Daksha's daughter's son; Daksha gave a daughter to Brahma (Parameshthi), and from her Narada was born again. Daksha then had sixty daughters by Asikni, who were taken as wives by Kashyapa, Dharma, Soma and other sages. One who knows this creation of Daksha lives long and gains fame, wealth and children.

02-003.json.summary: The sages ask about the birth of gods, danavas and daityas in the Vaivasvata age. The bard begins with Dharma, whose ten wives, given by Daksha, were Arundhati, Vasu, Jami, Lamba, Bhanu, Marutvati, Sankalpa, Muhurta, Sadhya and Vishva. Sadhya bore the twelve Sadhyas. The Jaya gods, made by Brahma from his mouth, have mantras for bodies and are named after rites (Darsha, Paurnamasa, Brihat, Rathantara and others); through Brahma's curse they were born again as the Jitas, Tushitas, Satyas, Haris, Vaikunthas and Sadhyas in successive manvantaras. The Tushitas of the Svarochisha age decided to enter Sadhya and be born again; Nara and Narayana were also born then. Vasu bore the eight Vasus, Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Apa (Aya), Anala, Anila, Pratyusha and Prabhasa; their sons include Kala (son of Dhruva), Varchas and Budha (sons of Soma), Kumara (Skanda, son of Anala by Svaha, with Shakha, Vishakha and Naigameya), Manojava (son of Anila), the sage Devala (son of Pratyusha), and Vishvakarma, son of Prabhasa by Brihaspati's sister Bhuvana, a yogini. Vishva bore the ten Vishvedevas; Marutvati the Marutvans; Bhanu the Bhanus; Muhurta the Muhurtas; Lamba Ghosha; Sankalpa Sankalpa; Jami the nine paths of the stars; and Arundhati all earthly things. The fifteen day muhurtas (Raudra, Sarpa, Maitra, Pitrya, Vasava, Apya, Vaishvadeva, Brahma, Prajapatya, Aindra, Aindragna, Nairrita, Varuna, Aryamna, Bhaga) and fifteen night muhurtas (Ajaikapad, Ahirbudhnya, Pushan, Ashvin, Yama, Agneya and others) are named. The planets move in three regions, northern (Airavata), middle (Jaradgava) and southern (Vaishvanara), each with three 'paths' of three nakshatras (Nagavithi, Gajavithi, Airavati; Arshabhi, Govithi, Jaradgavi; Ajavithi, Margi, Vaishvanari). Daksha gave twenty-eight daughters, the nakshatras, to Soma. Kashyapa took fourteen: Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kashtha, Arishta, Anayus, Khasha, Surabhi, Vinata, Tamra, Muni, Krodhavasha, Ira and Kadru. The Sadhyas of the Chakshusha age entered Aditi and were born as the twelve Adityas: Dhata, Aryama, Mitra, Varuna, Amsha, Bhaga, Indra, Vivasvan, Pusha, Parjanya, Tvashta and Vishnu (youngest but not least); Indra and Vishnu were Nara and Narayana again. Gods too are born and die like the rising and setting sun, because of attachment to sense objects and powers. Surabhi, by Shiva's grace and her penance, bore the eleven Rudras (Angaraka, Sarpa, Nirriti, Sadasaspati, Ajaikapad, Ahirbudhnya, Jvara, Bhuvana, Ishvara, Mrityu and Kapali), and daughters Rohini and Gandharvi; Rohini's daughters bore cows, buffaloes and sheep; Gandharvi bore the flying horses such as Uchchaihshravas; and Surabhi bore the moon-bright bull who became Shiva's banner. The bard then explains that the one Self-born has three bodies: the rajasic body of Brahma, which creates; the sattvic body (Purusha), which protects; and the tamasic body of Time, which destroys, appearing as Kashyapa, Vishnu and Rudra respectively. Some say Brahma is the cause, some Prajapati, some Bhava, others Vishnu; but praising one praises all and blaming one blames all, so the wise should not hate any god; the one God divides into three and deludes creatures, and those who argue 'this is higher, not that' are like yatudhanas and pishachas. Worshipping one is worshipping the three. Vishnu, born of Brahma's sattvic body, appeared in each manvantara: as Yajna of Akuti, Ajita of Tushita, Satya of Satya, Hari of Harini, Vaikuntha with the Vidhutarajasas, and in the Vaivasvata age as the son of Kashyapa and Aditi, who as Trivikrama won the three worlds in three steps and gave them to Indra. Whatever is mighty, glorious or splendid comes from a portion of Vishnu's power. A verse on lords of yoga is quoted: one who gains yoga power may enjoy sense objects and then, by further penance, withdraw everything as the sun withdraws the stars.

02-004.json.summary: The bard tells the story of the Jaya gods. Brahma created twelve gods from his mouth, with mantras for bodies and named after rites (Darsha, Paurnamasa, Brihat Saman, Rathantara, Chiti, Suchiti, Akuti, Kuti, Vijnata, Vijnatri, Manas and Yajna), told them to marry, keep the fire and sacrifice, and vanished. They did not accept his command: seeing the faults of action and the waning of its fruits, they disliked birth, gave up wealth, dharma and pleasure, and turned to the highest knowledge, longing never to be born. Angry, Brahma said he had created them only to have offspring and sacrifice; since they ignored him and sought deathlessness without doing their duties, they would be born seven times. When they begged forgiveness, Brahma said no one in the world is independent: everything is pervaded and bound by him through the bond of hope, he knows all that beings do and think, and none can escape him. Still, since they had acted out of renunciation, their births would be happy and of their own choosing, in the seven manvantaras from Svayambhuva to Vaivasvata, after which they would come to him. He sang an old verse: the three Vedas, offspring, shraddha, penance, sacrifice and giving, with constant effort, are what the Lord dwells in. Cursed by him, the twelve Jayas became the Ajitas (or Jitas) in the Svayambhuva age; then the Tushitas in the Svarochisha age; the Satyas, sons of Uttama Manu by Satya; the Haris, born of Harini, in the Tamasa age; the Vaikunthas, born of Vikuntha, in the Raivata (Charishnava) age; the Sadhyas in the Chakshusha age; and finally, in the present Vaivasvata age, the twelve Adityas born of Kashyapa and Aditi. One who hears this with faith always wins victory (jaya).

02-005.json.summary: A sage asks about the birth of daityas, danavas, gandharvas, nagas, rakshasas, pishachas, birds and plants. The bard says Diti bore two sons and a daughter to Kashyapa, the eldest of all beings. At Kashyapa's horse sacrifice at holy Pushkara, five golden seats were set for the chief priests; the unborn child came out of Diti's womb, sat on the golden hotri's seat and recited the narrative, so the sages named him Hiranyakashipu ('golden cushion'). His younger brother was Hiranyaksha and his sister Simhika, wife of Viprachitti and mother of Rahu. Hiranyakashipu did penance for a hundred thousand years, fasting and hanging head down, and asked Brahma that he be immortal and unkillable by any being, rule over gods, danavas and asuras, and not be killed by anything wet or dry, by day or by night; Brahma granted it with a limit. He then pervaded the world in many forms, shining as sun and moon, blowing as wind, acting as herdsman, farmer, teacher and priest, and all gods bowed to whichever direction he looked. Vishnu as Narasimha (man-lion), born from a man and with a man's body, was his death: on the seashore the god called Sudarshana fought him hand to hand and tore him with his nails, which are neither wet nor dry. Hiranyaksha had five sons, Shambara, Shakuni, Kalanabha, Mahanabha and Santapana, whose descendants were killed in the Tarakamaya war. Hiranyakashipu's four sons were Prahlada, Anuhlada, Samhlada and Hlada. Hlada's sons Sunda and Nisunda were brahmin-killers; Sunda's son by Tataka was Maricha, killed by Rama in the Dandaka forest; Muka was killed by Arjuna in the Kirata episode. The Nivatakavachas were born in Samhlada's line. Bashkala's sons were Jambha, Shatadundubhi, Daksha and Chanda; Kalanemi's sons were Brahmajit, Kratujit, Devantaka and Narantaka; Shambhu's were Rajaja and Goma. Virochana's son Bali had a hundred sons, chief of them the thousand-armed King Bana, with Kumbhagarta, Daya, Bhoja and Kunchi, and two daughters, Shakuni and Putana; Bana's son was Indradhanva. Diti, whose sons had been killed, pleased Kashyapa and asked for a son who would kill Indra. Kashyapa, sad, agreed on condition that she stay pure for a full thousand years. She did penance at Kushaplavana. Indra came, offered to serve her, and with a hidden wicked purpose fetched fuel, flowers and fruit and massaged her limbs. When ten years were left, Diti, pleased, told him he would soon see a brother with whom he would share the three worlds. At noon she fell asleep with her head on her knees and her hair at her feet, which made her impure. Seeing this opening, Indra entered her womb, and finding the mighty embryo, split it into seven with his thunderbolt; as it wept he said 'ma ruda' (do not weep), and split each part again into seven. Diti woke and cried 'do not kill', and Indra came out, explained that she had been impure, and begged pardon. Diti said it was her own fault and asked that her sons have seven places in the sky: the seven wind-zones (Avaha from earth to the clouds, Pravaha to the sun, Udvaha to the moon, Samvaha to the stars, Vivaha to the planets, Anuvaha to the seven sages, and Parivaha to Dhruva), each ruled by a group of seven. Their forty-nine names are given (Shakrajyotis, Satya, Satyajyotis, Chitrajyotis, Ritajit, Satyajit, Sushena, Senajit, Dhatu, Dhanada, Ugra, Bhima, Varuna and others). Indra agreed that the Maruts, named from his words, would be gods who share the sacrifice and his younger brothers. Mother and son went to heaven content. One who hears or reads the birth of the Maruts wins in debate.

02-006.json.summary: The bard lists the sons of Danu, the danavas, led by Viprachitti: mighty, strong in penance, boon-holders, cruel and full of magic. Among them are Dvimurdha, Shambara, Shankukarna, Dundubhi, Ayomukha, Kapila, Vamana, Maya, Marichi, Mahamaya, Vikshobha, Suketu, Indrajit, Ekachakra, Taraka, Vaishvanara, Puloman, Svarbhanu, Vrishaparvan, Jambha, Ashvagriva, Shatagriva, Sharabha, and the asura Surya and Chandramas (distinct from the gods of those names). Daityas are Soma-pressers and danavas are not. Other descendants of Danu, born of daitya-danava unions and killable by humans, include Ekaksha, Arishta, Pralamba, Naraka, Keshi and Talaketu. Simhika's fourteen sons by Viprachitti, the Saimhikeyas, are Shala, Shalabha, Ilvala, Namuchi, Vatapi, Kalanabha, Bhauma, Kanaka and others, the eldest being Rahu, who torments the sun and moon; their ten thousand descendants were killed by Parashurama. The daughters are named: Prabha daughter of Svarbhanu, mother of Nahusha; Shachi daughter of Puloman, mother of Jayanta; Sharmishtha daughter of Vrishaparvan, mother of Puru; Upadanavi, mother of Dushyanta; and Puloma and Kalaka, daughters of Vaishvanara, wives of Kashyapa, whose sixty thousand sons, the Paulomas and Kalakeyas living in Hiranyapura, could not be killed by the gods but were killed by Arjuna. Maya's sons by Rambha were Mayavi, Dundubhi, Mahisha, Kalika and Ajakarna, and his daughter was Mandodari. Anayusha's five sons were Araru, Bala, Vritra, Vijvara and Vrisha; Araru's son Dhundhu was killed in a cave by Kuvalashva at Uttanka's request; Bala's sons were Nikumbha and Chakravarman (in a past birth Karna); Vijvara's were Kalaka and Khara; Vrisha's four cruel sons were Shraddhada (eater of shraddha offerings), Yajnaha, Brahmaha and Pashuha. While Vritra fought Indra, a hundred thousand rakshasas called Bakas were born from him; they became Indra's followers, knowers of Brahman, gentle and righteous, living hidden among people. Krodha bore the divine gandharvas, fine singers: Siddha, Purna, Barhi, Purnamsha, Brahmachari, Shataguna, Suparna, Vishvavasu, Bhanu and Suchandra.

02-007.json.summary: This long chapter completes the families of Kashyapa's wives. Muni bore sixteen divine gandharvas (Bhimasena, Ugrasena, Suparna, Varuna, Dhritarashtra, Suryavarchas, Chitraratha, Parjanya, Kali, Narada and others) and many apsaras (Aruna, Mishrakeshi, Alambusha, Tilottama, Rambha, Manobhava and others); Haha, Huhu and Tumburu are also named. Other apsaras are listed: the ten Panchachudas (Menaka, Sahajanya, Parnini, Punjikasthala, Kritasthala, Ghritachi, Vishvachi, Purvachitti, Pramlocha, Anumlocha), Urvashi born of Narayana, and fourteen groups of apsaras born of Brahma's mind, the Maruts, Arishta, fire, sun rays, moon rays, sacrifice, nectar, wind, earth, lightning, Death and Kama. Apsaras are free to all; from the touch of divine sages came Narada, Parvata and Arundhati. Vinata bore Aruna and Garuda; Kadru bore a thousand nagas, chief of them Shesha, Vasuki and Takshaka, with Airavata, Mahapadma, Kambala, Ashvatara, Elapatra, Shankha, Karkotaka, Dhananjaya, Dhritarashtra, Kaliya, Nahusha and others. Khasha bore two monstrous sons at dusk and dawn; at once grown and hungry, the elder said to their mother 'let us eat her' (bhakshava), and the younger 'protect her' (raksha); Kashyapa named them Yaksha and Raksha, and gave them blood and fat as food, strength at night and weakness by day. The rakshasa, seeking food at night, met two pishachas, Aja and Shanda, who caught him with their daughters' help and gave him the two girls, Brahmadhana and Jantudhana, in a pishacha marriage. From Jantudhana came the yatudhanas (Heti, Praheti, Ugra, Paurusheya, Vadha, Vidyut, Sphurja, Vata, Vyaghra, Surya), and their descendants such as Malyavan, Sumali, Puloman, Madhu and his son Lavana; from Brahmadhana came the brahma-rakshasas (Yajnapeta, Brahmapeta and others). The yaksha, desiring the apsara Kratusthala, took the form of the gandharva Vasuruchi, united with her in the Nandana garden, and a son was born who said 'I am king' (rajan); his father named him Rajatanabha, grandfather of the guhyakas, who live in the red banyan. Rajatanabha married Bhadra, daughter of the daitya Anuhlada, and had Manivara and Manibhadra; by Punyajani, Manibhadra had twenty-four Punyajana yakshas, and by Devajani, Manivara had the guhyakas (Purnabhadra, Haimavata and others). Khasha's other rakshasa sons (Lalavi, Kratha, Bhima, Sumali, Madhu and others) and seven daughters (Alamba, Utkacha, Utkrishta, Nirrita, Kapila, Shiva, Keshini) produced further rakshasa hosts, including the Nairritas who follow Shiva under Virupaksha, and many lesser earth-rakshasas, child-seizing spirits such as Skanda-graha, and Putanas. Kubera, lord of Alaka, rules yakshas, rakshasas and Nairritas. Gandharvas fall short of the gods by three quarters in every quality, yakshas and rakshasas short of the gandharvas, and pishachas short of the rakshasas. Krodha's twelve daughters, wives of Pulaha, bore the animals: deer, antelopes, bears, buffaloes, camels, boars, rhinoceroses, monkeys, kinnaras, kimpurushas, lions, tigers, snakes, crocodiles, cats, mice and others. Hari bore ten great monkey chiefs, and Shveta others; the monkeys are countless, cannot be killed by fire, weapon or poison, wear divine ornaments, perform sacrifices, know the Vedas and live in the mountains around Meru in cities built by Vishvakarma; they were created by Brahma to help Rama. The line goes Urdhvadrishti, Vyaghra, Sharabha, Shuka, Riksha; Riksha married Viraja, by whom Indra fathered Vali and the Sun Sugriva; Vali, crowned king, married Tara, daughter of Sushena, and had Angada; Sugriva married Ruma. Kesari married Anjana, and from Vayu she bore Hanuman, a lifelong celibate, eldest of Kesari's sons; Nala was born of Agni; many other monkey leaders (Tara, Panasa, Gandhamadana, Gavaya, Sushena, Mainda, Dvivida, Kumuda, Gavaksha and others) are named. Vali, king in Kishkindha, once caught Ravana under his arm and in a moment touched the four oceans; he revived the faint Ravana with cold water and asked how he, conqueror of all gods, could be overcome by a monkey; Ravana asked for friendship, and they made a pact; Vali then performed many great sacrifices, and Narada sang that none equalled him. Asked why the sun is called Martanda, the bard says Prajapati placed supreme light in Aditi's womb inside an egg; the gods, losing their power, asked him to reduce it; he split the egg, put the strength into the shell and the light into the child, and since the child came from a 'dead egg' (mrita-anda) he is Martanda; the two shell halves were given to Iravati, who bore the four elephants of the quarters; keeping this story at home prevents untimely death. Riksha's sister Raksha bore Jambavan, king of bears, whose daughter Jambavati married Vasudeva (Krishna); his sons and the cats, and Sarama's sons Shyama and Shabala (Yama's dogs) are listed; hearing this frees from fear of fanged animals and thieves. There are eleven kinds of 'monkey' (panthers, sharabhas, lions, tigers, nilas, porcupines, bears, cats, monkeys and others), whose king is Vali. The elephants are described: Bhauvana sang the Rathantara over the egg halves, and Iravati bore Airavata, four-tusked, Indra's mount, and the other quarter elephants (Anjana, Supratika, Vamana, Padma), whose lines, marks and forest regions are given, with the meanings of the elephant names (dvirada, hastin, karin, varana, dantin, gaja, kunjara, naga, matanga, dvipa, samaja). Bhuta bore Rudra's countless ghost attendants, of every strange shape, celibate and devoted to Shiva. Kapisha bore the kushmandas and the sixteen pairs of pishachas (Chhagala, Vakra, Dushpura, Suchimukha, Vipada, Kumbhapatra, Ulukhala and others), whose looks and habits are described; Brahma gave them invisibility, shape-changing, the twilights and haunts such as ruined houses, crossroads and cremation grounds, and made the unrighteous, cheats and traitors their livelihood, with offerings at the junctions of the month; Shiva is their lord. Damshtra bore lions, tigers and leopards; Risha's five daughters bore fish, crocodiles, shell creatures, frogs, snails, cowries and leeches; insects, lice, ants and worms are born from sweat, dirt, rotting food and dung. Sarama bore dogs; Surasa bore snakes, with Takshaka king of serpents and Vasuki of nagas. Tamra's six daughters bore the birds: Gridhri bore Sampati and Jatayu to Aruna; Shuki bore Garuda's six sons, whose fourteen thousand snake-eating descendants live on Shalmali-dvipa and many mountains; Bhasi bore owls, crows, peacocks, pigeons, partridges and other birds; Dhritarashtri bore swans and water birds; Shyeni bore hawks. Ira bore the mothers of trees, creepers and grasses. Each mother's nature passed to her children: Aditi righteous, Diti strong, Surabhi ascetic, Danu full of magic, Kadru angry, Vinata a carrier, Tamra a killer, and so on. Because gods and others are born of Daksha's daughters as of human mothers, and the gods are born among humans in every age, humans are the best, being able to win dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation. One who reads this line regularly gains children, wealth and a good end.

02-008.json.summary: The bard says that when Kashyapa's creatures were established, Prajapati (Brahma) appointed kings over each class: Soma over brahmins, plants, stars, planets, sacrifices and penance; Brihaspati over the Angirasas; Kavya (Shukra) over the Bhrigus; Vishnu over the Adityas; Pavaka over the Vasus; Daksha over the patriarchs; Indra over the Maruts; Prahlada over the daityas; Narayana over the Sadhyas; Shiva (bull-bannered) over the Rudras and over all bhutas and pishachas; Viprachitti over the danavas; Varuna over the waters; Vaishravana (Kubera) over kings, yakshas, rakshasas and wealth; Yama over the ancestors; Himavan over mountains; the Ocean over rivers; Chitraratha over the gandharvas; Uchchaihshravas over horses; the tiger over beasts; the bull over cattle; Garuda over birds; Vayu over scents and bodiless beings; Shesha over fanged creatures; Vasuki over nagas; Takshaka over serpents; Parjanya over seas, rivers and clouds; Kama over apsaras; and the Year over seasons, months and time units. As guardians of the quarters he made Sudhanva (east), Shankhapada (south), Ketuman (west) and Hiranyaroman (north), and Vaivasvata Manu king of humans; Prithu was consecrated as emperor by these. These kings are appointed anew in each manvantara. Kashyapa then did penance for sons to found clans and had Vatsara and Asita; from Vatsara came Naidhruva and Raibhya, and from Asita by Ekaparna came Devala, best of the Shandilyas. In a later Dvapara, Marutta's line runs down to Trinabindu, whose daughter Ilavila (born of Alambusha) married Pulastya's son and bore Vishravas. Vishravas married Brihaspati's daughter Devavarnini, Malyavan's daughters Pushpotkata and Vaka, and Mali's daughter Kaikasi. Devavarnini bore a three-legged, ugly, yellow-bearded son whom his father called Kubera (ku, bad, and bera, body), also Vaishravana; Kubera's son by Riddhi was Nalakubara. Kaikasi bore Ravana (ten-necked, twenty-armed, dark, mighty, so named for making the world cry), Kumbhakarna, Shurpanakha and Vibhishana. Ravana was Hiranyakashipu in a former life, ruled for thirteen sets of four ages, tormented gods and sages, and when his penance was spent was killed with his followers by Rama son of Dasharatha in the twenty-fourth Treta age. Pushpotkata bore Mahodara, Prahasta, Mahaparshva, Khara and Kumbhinasi; Vaka bore Trishiras, Dushana, Vidyujjihva and Anupalika. Kubera rules the Paulastya rakshasas and others; the rakshasas are of seven kinds (yatudhanas, brahmadhanas, Vartas, day-walkers, Paulastyas, Nairritas, Agastyas and Kaushikas) and their fearful common appearance is described. Pulaha's offspring are the beasts and others named before; Kratu had no wife or children in this age. Atri had ten devoted wives, apsaras born of Bhadrashva and Ghritachi; by Madra he had Soma. When Svarbhanu struck the sun and it was falling from the sky, Atri said 'svasti' (may it be well) and it did not fall; he founded the Atri clans, and by penance had ten sons, the Svastyatreyas, chief of them Datta (Dattatreya, said to be a form of Vishnu) and Durvasas, and a daughter Abala. The Atri sub-clans are Shyavashvas, Mudgalas, Vagbhutakas and Gavishthiras. Kashyapa, Narada, Parvata and Arundhati were mind-born; Narada, celibate through Daksha's curse, gave Arundhati to Vasishtha. In the Tarakamaya war, when drought struck, Vasishtha revived creatures with plants by his penance. Vasishtha's son by Arundhati was Shakti; Shakti's son by Adrishyanti was Parashara; Parashara's son by Kali was Krishna Dvaipayana (Vyasa); Vyasa's son by Arani was Shuka; Shuka's sons by Pivari were Bhurishravas, Prabhu, Shambhu, Krishna and Gaura, and his daughter Kirtimati was wife of Anuha and mother of Brahmadatta. The eight Parashara sub-clans and the line of Indrapramati (Kuni), Vasu and Upamanyu are given, with the Kundinas descended from Mitra and Varuna; there are eleven Vasishtha sub-clans. So these eight mind-born sons of Brahma fill the three worlds with their descendants.

02-009.json.summary: The sages ask how Bhavani was born twice, first as Sati daughter of Daksha and then as Uma daughter of the mountain king and Mena, who the ancestors are whose mind-born daughter Mena was, and about the rite of shraddha: who the ancestors are, how offerings named for father, grandfather and great-grandfather reach them, how those in hell can give rewards, and why even the gods worship ancestors. The bard says the ancestors are born in every manvantara as sons of the gods, and Manu, called Shraddhadeva, began the shraddha rite. Brahma created gods to worship him, but they abandoned him and worshipped themselves for rewards; he cursed them to lose their understanding. When they begged, he told them to do penance and ask their own sons; the sons taught them the atonements and the knowledge of dharma, and the gods said to their sons 'you are our fathers (pitarah)'. Brahma said that since they spoke the truth, their sons would be the ancestors; so sons became fathers and fathers sons. He added that if anyone offered shraddha to undesired ancestors, rakshasas and danavas would get the fruit; the ancestors, fed by shraddha, nourish the moon, which nourishes the world; and those who offer the three rice balls by name and clan receive prosperity and children. So gods and ancestors are ancestors of each other. The sages ask how many groups of ancestors there are. The bard relates how Shamyu asked his father Brihaspati the same, and about where and when shraddha gives lasting fruit. Brihaspati said that before heaven, earth, stars and time existed, Brahma alone did penance, which was yoga; by it he made the worlds, knowledge and Vedas, the bright worlds called Santanaka and the Vairaja gods, and the first gods (Adidevas), yogis of great power. Of their seven groups, three are formless and four have subtle forms; they live above the gods. They send rain, which produces food, and nourish the moon and food by yoga, so the worlds called them pitris; they are swift as mind, eat svadha, and are free of greed, delusion, fear and sorrow. If they give up yoga they go to bright worlds, and after a thousand ages are born again as knowers of Brahman, regain yoga and reach liberation, vanishing like a meteor or a flash of lightning, as a river enters the sea. Pleased by shraddha, these yogi ancestors nourish the moon, by which the three worlds live, so shraddha should be offered with care to yogis. The power of the ancestors is yoga. One who knows mantras is worth a hundred thousand ordinary brahmins at a shraddha, a snataka worth many mantra-knowers, and a teacher of yoga saves from great danger; yoga surpasses a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers and a thousand students. Even an unbeliever, sinner or thief is saved by feeding yogis, and his ancestors are pleased as farmers by good rain. One should feed a meditator; failing that a celibate student; failing that a detached householder; a yogi who meditates is greater than one who stood on one foot living on air for a hundred years. This is the first group of ancestors; the others will be described next.

02-010.json.summary: Brihaspati describes the seven groups of ancestors in heaven, four with form and three formless, with their worlds, daughters and daughters' sons. The formless Vairajas, sons of Viraja Prajapati, live in the bright Santanaka worlds and nourish the moon by yoga when fed by shraddha. Their mind-born daughter Mena married Himavan and bore Mainaka (whose son is Krauncha) and three daughters, Aparna, Ekaparna and Ekapatala. They did penance for a hundred thousand years: Ekaparna ate one leaf of the banyan, Ekapatala one patala flower, and Aparna ate nothing; her grieving mother tried to stop her, saying 'u ma' (oh, do not), and so she became famous as Uma. The world is created by the penance of these three maidens, all eternally young, celibate, yoginis. Uma, the best, went to Mahadeva; Ushanas (Shukra) was her adopted son. Ekaparna married the yoga teacher Asita and bore Devala; Ekapatala married Jaigishavya, son of Shatashalaka, whose sons Shankha and Likhita were not born of a womb. While Uma and Shankara were joined in love, Indra, fearing the child they might have, sent Agni to disturb them; Shiva let his seed fall on the ground, and Uma angrily cursed Agni to carry it in his womb. After many years Agni asked the Ganga to bear it; she did so, burning, and at last released a child bright as a hundred suns, son of Rudra, Agni and Ganga. Gods rejoiced with drums and flowers. The wives of the seven sages (except Arundhati), going to bathe, saw him and loved him like mothers; to drink from all of them at once he made six faces, so he is Shanmukha; because he scattered (skandita) the danavas he is Skanda; and because the Krittikas raised him he is Kartikeya. A flame came from his mouth as his spear (shakti); Vishnu gave him a peacock and a cock, Vayu a banner, Sarasvati a great vina, Brahma a goat and Shiva a ram. After he split the Krauncha mountain and killed the demon Taraka, the gods made him their general; he is followed by pramathas, bhutas, Mothers and vinayakas. The Barhishad ancestors, Soma-drinking sons of Marichi, live in the Somapada worlds; their mind-born daughter Acchoda, a river from the Acchoda lake, had never seen her fathers and chose another, the sky-roaming Amavasu son of Ila, who was with the apsara Adrika; for this wrong she lost her yoga and fell. Falling, she saw the tiny ancestors in three heavenly cars and cried for help; they told her that deeds done by gods bear fruit at once, but she would have the fruit of her penance later: in the twenty-eighth Dvapara she would be born from a fish as the daughter of King Amavasu and Adrika (as Satyavati, daughter of a fisherman, at the meeting of Ganga and Yamuna), bear Vyasa to Parashara, who would divide the Veda, and bear Vichitravirya and Chitrangada to Shantanu, and then regain these worlds. The Agnishvatta ancestors, sons of Pulaha, live in the Viraja worlds; their daughter Pivari, a yogini, will marry Shuka, son of Vyasa, and bear five sons and the daughter Kirtimati, mother of Brahmadatta, and Shuka will reach liberation through the sun's rays. The four groups with form are: the Kavyas, sons of Kavi born of Svadha, whose daughter Ekashringa (Yogotpatti) married Shukra; the Upahutas, sons of Angiras, worshipped by kshatriyas, whose daughter Yashoda was mother of Khatvanga (Dilipa), about whose sacrifice the sages sang that those who see him win heaven; the Ajyapas, sons of Kardama, worshipped by vaishyas, whose daughter Viraja was wife of Nahusha and mother of Yayati; and the Sukalas, sons of Vasishtha, worshipped by shudras, living in the Manasa worlds, whose daughter is the Narmada river, wife of Purukutsa and mother of Trasadasyu. Manu starts the shraddha rites at the beginning of each manvantara. Shraddha should be offered with faith in silver vessels; the ancestors' rite is greater than the gods', since the ancestors are fed first. The gods, Indra, the sages, yakshas, nagas, suparnas and kinnaras all worship the ancestors. Pleased by shraddha, the ancestors give all desires: release from old age and death, yoga, liberation (which cannot be won without yogic power, as a bird cannot fly without wings), jewels, horses, celestial cars full of apsaras, children, strength, memory, intelligence, kingdom and health.

02-011.json.summary: Brihaspati continues the rules of shraddha. Silver or silver-trimmed vessels are best for the ancestors, since the earth was once milked of svadha in a silver vessel; even seeing or speaking of silver at shraddha gives unending merit. A black antelope skin protects from rakshasas; gold, silver, a daughter's son, the kutapa time and sesame are purifying. An altar is set in the south-east, a cubit square, with three pits a span long and four fingers deep and three cubit-long khadira staffs decorated with silver; they are purified with water, goat's milk and cow's milk; one who worships the ancestors there after bathing three times a day gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice, prosperity, long life, offspring and in time liberation. The mantra 'Salutation to the gods, the ancestors and the great yogis, to Svaha and Svadha, always' should be said three times at the start and end of shraddha and when offering the rice balls; the ancestors come at once and rakshasas flee; it is also for those wanting kingship. The 'Saptarchis' hymn is given, bowing to the formless and embodied ancestors, the leaders of Indra and the gods, the seven sages, Manu, the sun and moon, stars, planets, wind, fire, heaven and earth, Prajapati, Soma, Yama, the lords of yoga, the seven groups of ancestors and Brahma; one who recites it daily with devotion becomes sole ruler of the earth, and the ancestors give food, long life and sons. Nothing cooked at home should be eaten before offering it there. The fruits of different leaf-vessels are listed: palasha gives Vedic radiance, ashvattha wealth, plaksha lordship, nyagrodha prosperity and children, kashmari protection, madhuka good fortune, phalgu all wishes, arka brilliance, bilva Lakshmi and long life, bamboo rain. Flowers, scents, incense (guggulu with honey and ghee gives the fruit of an Agnishtoma), and lamps should be offered, then the brahmins honoured with food, clothes, jewels, cows, horses and villages, since the ancestors enter them as wind at shraddha. The procedure follows: marking and sprinkling the ground, offering collyrium, unguent and thread, and placing three rice balls mixed with ghee and sesame for father, grandfather and great-grandfather, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder and the right knee down, saying 'salutation to you, ancestors'; some also offer three to the maternal ancestors. Linen, hemp or cotton thread is used, not silk or wool; white fragrant flowers and lotuses are good, scentless or strong-smelling ones are avoided. Brahmins face north and the sacrificer south. Kusha and kasha grass are best (kasha grew from the hair of the patriarch Ashva); certain grasses are forbidden. A mantra driving away all impure things, demons, yakshas, pishachas and yatudhanas is said while marking the altar, and rakshasas avoid the place where it is recited. Unclean food and wicked people should not be looked at. The fire is lit and three offerings made: to Agni Kavyavahana and Angiras with svadha (south), to Soma with the ancestors (north), and to Yama Vaivasvata (between). Offering into a well-lit, smokeless, bright, clockwise-turning flame brings success; offering into an unlit fire makes the sacrificer blind in the next world, and a dark, smelly, sparking fire bodes defeat. Bilva and udumbara leaves and fruits are especially pure. Fuel sticks of palasha, plaksha, nyagrodha, ashvattha, vikankata, udumbara, bilva, sandal, sarala, devadaru, shala and khadira are approved; shleshmantaka, naktamala, kapittha, shalmali, nipa, vibhitaka, kovidara and trees where birds nest are forbidden. 'Svadha' is the word for the ancestors and 'svaha' for the gods.

02-012.json.summary: The bard reports Brihaspati's teaching that gods and ancestors depend on each other; the ancestors should be worshipped first and the gods after, and even the gods worship the ancestors first. The ten Vishvedevas, sons of Dharma by Daksha's daughter Vishva, did hard penance on the Himalaya; the ancestors and Brahma, pleased, offered a boon, and they asked for a share in shraddha. Brahma granted it, and the ancestors agreed that the Vishvedevas would eat with them: at shraddha people would first honour them with garlands, scents and food, then the ancestors; the ancestors would be sent off first and the gods after; protecting the shraddha and hospitality are the two duties. The five great daily sacrifices of the Veda should always be performed; givers reach Brahma's fearless, sorrowless world; even shudras should perform them without mantras, and one who cooks only for himself eats sin and lives in debt. Offerings (bali) are thrown to the north-east and toward water. A rice ball is to be offered even for a living father, some say. Some teachers want the rice balls offered after feeding the brahmins, but Brihaspati says the balls should be offered first and the brahmins fed after, because the ancestors are yogis who nourish the moon; feeding one yogi is like an offering made directly to the ancestors and carries host and guests across like a boat; honouring the bad and slighting the good brings the gods' punishment at once, and one who feeds a fool in place of a worthy man ruins himself. The rice balls bring different fruits when placed in different places: in fire for enjoyment, the middle one with mantras for offspring, to cows for beauty, in water for wisdom, fame and glory, to crows for long life, to cocks for delicacy; or they may be thrown into the sky or water facing south, since the sky and the south belong to the ancestors. The first portion of flowers, fruits, food and drink is offered into the fire, then the balls to Yama and Soma, then water, and then the brahmins are fed with warm, rich, fragrant food while the host stands attentive with folded hands; the ancestors then grant generosity, gratitude, kindness, refined speech, penance, sacrifice and giving. After the brahmins have eaten, the ground is sprinkled, food is scattered, svadha is announced, the brahmins are given generous fees, permission is asked for the leftovers, and they are honoured and seen off with folded hands.

02-013.json.summary: Brihaspati lists holy places where shraddha pleases the ancestors forever and leads to heaven and in time to liberation. Amarakantaka, where Angiras did penance for countless years and where there is no death, demon or misfortune, is foremost; its soft, golden kusha grass south of the Narmada, the Jvala lake, the Vishalyakarani river and the well on Malyavan are described, and Ushanas sang that those who offer shraddha there reach success with little penance. Other places named include Mount Mahendra; Vailata peak (which gives divine sight); Saptagodavara and Gokarna (where the Savitri recited by a non-brahmin loses its power); the sandal-forest source of the Tamraparni, whose conches and pearls carried in water save even sinful ancestors; Chandratirtha, Kumari, the source of the Kaveri, Shriparvata, Vaikrita and Ushira mountains; the Narmada, daughter of the ancestors; Mathara's forest; the Vindhya, where only the good can see a certain stream; Matanga's pool on Kailasa; Shurparaka, Pandukupa, Pindaraka, Chitrakuta, Jambumarga and Asita's mountain; Pushkara, Prabhasa and the ocean; the Vrisha well in the Devika, whose water rises at the lowing of cows, with the stone of Agni; the Dashashvamedhika, Panchashvamedhika and Hayashiras fords; Sunda-Nisunda; the Viraja tree; the Madrava, Shiva lake, Vyasa lake and Brahma lake; Mount Urjanta with Vasishtha's hermitage; Pundarika and Brahmatirtha; the meeting of Sindhu and the sea and the Panchanada; Saptanada and Manasa; the Sandhya river, which comes only to the faithful; the 'heaven-path' ford where the seven sages left their bark garments; Nandi's shrine; Kurukshetra and Sannihita, where shraddha frees a son from debt; the Sarasvati at Vinashana, Plakshaprasravana, Drishadvati and Triplaksha; the Ganga at Shakravatara, the source of the Yamuna (sister of Yama); Brahmatunda lake, where Vasishtha stood like a post and a balance shows dharma; the hermitage of Gandhakali (Satyavati), born from Acchoda, who will bear Vyasa; Nanda, Viraja and Mahalaya, which save ten generations before and after; Kakahrada, Kumara's lake, Umatunga, Bhrigutunga and Brahmatunga; Shalagrama, whose naga king accepts the offerings of the good only; Karavati, Shandili and Vamana's cave; Kashyapa's Kalasarpi; Devadaru forest; the Bhagirathi at Prayaga, Kalanjara, Dasharna, Naimisha, Kurujangala and Varanasi, where the lord of yoga always dwells; the Lauhitya, Vaitarani and Svargavedi; Gaya with Dharmaprishtha, Brahma's lake and the Gridhravata; Bharata's hermitage; Matanga's forest; the Dandaka forest with the Vishalya ford; Mahahrada and the Kaushiki; Mundaprishtha, where Shiva set his foot, which frees from sin as a snake sheds its skin; Kanakanandi, from which men reach heaven in their own bodies; Manasa lake, where the heavenly Ganga is seen with a golden arch; the Chandrabhaga and Sindhu; and the Sushumna pool on the Himalaya, which gives ten thousand years of life. All the Himalaya, the Ganga, the rivers and seas are holy; shraddha may also be done on clean, cow-dung-plastered ground, mountain slopes, river banks, cowpens and quiet houses, facing south-east. Even a sinner is purified by visiting holy places with faith and is not reborn as an animal; but the faithless, the sinful, the unbeliever, the doubter and the mere arguer get no fruit. The guru is the highest ford, and meditation higher still, the eternal ford of Brahman; meditation is higher than fasting. Controlling the breath, the senses, mind and intellect (pratyahara) is the means to liberation; when faults and senses are worn out, the pure self is extinguished like a fire without fuel, beyond the manifest and unmanifest, neither being nor non-being.

02-014.json.summary: Brihaspati describes what is fit and unfit for shraddha. Shraddha should not be done at night, except during an eclipse, when it should be done at once with all one has; one who fails to do so sinks like a cow in mud. Rhinoceros meat (without the horn) is the best offering. Shyamaka millet and sugarcane arose from drops from Indra's nose when he drank Soma at Tvashta's sacrifice, so they are imperishable offerings; certain grains (prasatika, priyangu, green mudga, black gram, sesame, barley and rice) are good, while others (mahayava, nishpava, black and red grains, rajamasha, masura) are to be avoided. A long list of good fruits, roots and vegetables is given (bilva, amalaka, grapes, jackfruit, mango, pomegranate, dates, lotus stalk, long pepper, black pepper, patola, brihati, dry ginger, radish and others). Garlic, onion (grinjana), pond water and tasteless or ill-smelling foods are forbidden, because garlic and the like grew from drops of blood that fell from Bali's wounded body in the war of gods and demons; red tree resins, salt from saline soil and women in their courses are also excluded, as is the milk of sheep, deer, camels, one-hoofed animals, buffaloes and yaks. Shraddha with forest roots and fruits gives royal status and heaven. Noisy, crowded, insect-ridden or foul-smelling ground is avoided, as are the Trishanku region (twelve yojanas, north of the Mahanadi and south of Vaikata), Karaskara, Kalinga, the land north of the Sindhu and places where the stages of life have perished. Shamyu asks who the 'naked ones' (nagna) are who must not see a shraddha. Brihaspati says the threefold Veda is the covering of all beings, and those who abandon it are the naked; whoever leaves dharma and seeks liberation elsewhere is a vrishala, whatever his caste. After their defeat by the gods, the asuras created heretics: Vriddhashravakas, Nirgranthas, Shakyas, Jivakas and Karpatas; those who wear matted hair, shave or go naked without reason, keep vows or recite falsely, or abandon the duties of their family are 'naked'; a shraddha seen by them goes to the danavas. Brahmin-killers, the ungrateful, unbelievers, those who violate the teacher's bed, robbers, the cruel, the fallen, and those who revile gods, brahmins and the Veda must be sent away. Krita is the brahmin age, Treta the kshatriya, Dvapara the vaishya and Kali the shudra; in Krita ancestors were worshipped, in Treta gods, in Dvapara there were wars, and in Kali heresies. A cock, village pig or dog spoils a shraddha by its look; food seen by the diseased, fallen or unclean is unfit, and must be purified with water, white mustard and black sesame. Unfit foods are listed (food on a seat, touched by the foot, stale, burnt, undercooked, with stones, insects or hair, oilcake, and others; curd-greens, brinjal and fermented drinks), though rock salt and lake salt are pure. Rules for purifying things are given: water for stone, roots, fruits, ropes and leather; scraping for bone, wood and horn; re-firing for clay; mustard or sesame paste for gems, pearls and coral; ash for cotton; earth and water for people and animals; for land, sprinkling, plastering, scraping, sprinkling with cow urine, cows walking over it, burning and digging. Rules for relieving oneself are given: going an arrow's flight south-west of the house, head covered, ground covered with grass, facing north by day and south by night, and cleaning with set numbers of handfuls of earth and water; then washing the feet and sipping water. Fasts and penances for eating bad food or touching a dog, a dog-cooker or human bones are stated. Going to sinful lands (Karaskara, Kalinga, Andhra, Shabara, north of the Sindhu) brings their sin, which is removed by visiting Bhrigutunga, the Sarasvati, the Ganga and the Himalayan rivers. Impurity after death or birth lasts ten days (some say twelve for brahmins), a fortnight for vaishyas and a month for shudras; a woman in her courses is pure after four nights; touching such a woman, a woman after childbirth, a dog, an outcaste, a 'naked one' or a corpse-carrier requires bathing in one's clothes. The rules of sipping water (achamana) are given in detail: seated in a clean place facing east or north, hands within the knees, sipping three times, wiping twice and touching the openings of the head; without it, Veda, sacrifice and penance bear no fruit. Purity of mind, speech, body, fire and time is needed; one who mixes up the rules of purity gives his fruit to pishachas and yatudhanas, and one without faith in purity is born among outsiders; gods and ancestors bless the pure, devoted, self-controlled and compassionate.

02-015.json.summary: The sages praise the account of shraddha and ask for the rest. The bard says brahmins should not, in principle, be examined, yet at rites for gods and ancestors one should avoid a man whose faults are known; an unknown brahmin should not be examined, since siddhas wander the earth in the form of brahmins, and the gods and lords of yoga roam in many forms; so a guest should be welcomed with folded hands, water for feet and hands, oil and food. The fruits of foods are given: milk gives the fruit of an Agnishtoma, milk-rice of an Ukthya, ghee of a Shodashin, honey of an Atiratra, and feeding brahmins with all they wish gives the fruit of a Sarvamedha. One who insults a guest at shraddha is cast out by the gods, as Paravasu was; the gods and ancestors enter the guest; honoured he grants wishes, dishonoured he burns. Forest-dwellers, householders, Valakhilyas and ascetics are guests; a true guest (atithi) is a wanderer who does not cook; the thirsty, tired and hungry must always be fed, and one must never say 'there is nothing' to the hungry. Those who are not suffering, not wounded, of modest livelihood, not begging and solitary should be fed at shraddha; one who refuses food is not freed from sin even in a hundred births. Feeding all brahmins in one row removes sin. An ascetic (yati) comes first, then one who knows the five Vedas with the epics, then knowers of three, two and one Veda, then a teacher. The 'purifiers of the row' are listed: knowers of the six Vedic limbs, meditators, one who knows all systems, the wandering yayavara, masters of any of the fourteen branches of learning, those who know the Suparna hymns, keep five fires, sing Samans, have performed the Trinachiketa rite, know the three Vedas or know Brihaspati's great treatise. A brahmin invited to shraddha who sleeps with a woman makes the ancestors lie in his seed that month. Feeding a householder honours the Vishvedevas, a forest-dweller the sages, a Valakhilya Indra, and an ascetic Brahma himself. Those outside the four stages of life must not be fed, even if they live on air. The 'polluters of the row' are listed: the non-ascetic who preaches liberation, ascetics of fierce penance who revile brahmins, the Aupavastas, Sankhyas, unbelievers, Veda-revilers, those who scorn meditation, those shaven or matted without reason, the Karpatikas, the cruel, those of broken conduct, eaters of everything, artisans, singers, those who eat with shudras, liars, slanderers, hypocrites, sellers of the Veda, paid teachers and their paid pupils, buyers and sellers, the husband of a 'putrika' daughter, usurers, adulterers, thieves and those who sacrifice for anyone. For a brahmin, dragging, killing, farming, trade, cattle-keeping and serving one who is not his teacher are wrong. One who eats like a pig, from his palm, or talking, gives nothing to the ancestors; leftovers of shraddha must not be given to women or shudras, though the remaining curd and ghee may go to one's son. The ancestors eat as long as the food is hot and the guests eat in silence. Gifts, receiving, offering, eating and bali are done with the thumb, so that demons do not get them, and sipping is done with hands inside the knees.
