Shaven, matted and ochre-robed men are avoided at shraddha, but those who keep their conduct, wise meditators devoted to the gods, purify by their very sight; gifts may be given to tufted, ochre-robed tridandins, since lords of yoga fill the three worlds and see all things. One who knows the Riks knows the Vedas, one who knows the Yajus knows sacrifice, one who knows the Samans knows Brahman, and one who knows the mind knows all.

02-016.json.summary: Brihaspati describes gifts at shraddha and their fruits. Whatever is best in the world and dearest to oneself should be given to the ancestors. The giver of food gains an imperishable golden celestial car full of apsaras; one who gives new cloth with side dishes gains long life, splendour, power and beauty; a sacred thread gives the fruit of giving the Veda; a full water pot brings honey, milk, ghee and curd; a pot marked with a wheel brings a heavenly milk cow; cotton-padded sandals bring a fine vehicle; fans bring soft fragrant flowers; shoes bring a new horse-drawn car; an umbrella with garlands becomes a palace that follows the giver; a house with jewels, bed and food given to ascetics brings honour in heaven and a celestial car bright as the sun and moon. Fine golden vessels bring tasty foods and good fortune; sesame and sugarcane bring friends and success with women; vessels of metal, silver or gold bring wishes fulfilled, splendour and wealth; a milk cow with a milking pot brings cattle and prosperity; fire and firewood in winter bring bodily vigour, beauty and victory in battle; fragrant garlands bring happiness and devoted young wives; beds, seats, vehicles, land and mounts give the fruit of a horse sacrifice; vessels of ghee bring the fruit of many cows; a forest with fruit and flowers the fruit of a Gosava; wells, gardens, ponds, fields, cowsheds and houses joy in heaven as long as the moon and stars; a well-spread jewelled bed pleases the ancestors; garments of wool, silk, linen and cotton, skins and blankets give the fruit of a Vajapeya, many wives, sons and servants, and drive away misfortune as sunrise drives away darkness; clothing is dear to all the gods, and no rite can be done without it. Sweet foods, rice cooked with sesame, milk-rice, honey and ghee give the fruit of an Agnishtoma; ghee poured on the ground in an elephant's shadow and food in the rainy season and under Magha remove sorrow; flattened rice with sugar and milk is imperishable; greens and meat broth please for a year; barley meal, parched grain, cakes and gruel with curd bring the treasure Padma; new crops bring all enjoyments. Hot, fresh food given to the hungry brings a sun-bright car drawn by swans and countless maidens. No gift is higher than food, since beings are born, live and grow by food; food is Prajapati himself and the worlds rest on it. Giving shelter to guests is welcomed by the gods with thousands of divine hospitalities; one who gives all these becomes sole king of the earth. Giving is the highest dharma; through it the kingless gain a kingdom, the poor wealth and the short-lived long life, if they are devoted to their ancestors.

02-017.json.summary: Brihaspati describes the timing of shraddha. The three Ashtakas, for the sake of sons and wives, fall in the dark fortnight: the first ruled by Indra and offered with cakes, the second by Prajapati with meat, the third by the Vishvedevas with vegetables; a fourth should also be observed. One who performs these with all he has gains good here and hereafter; the ancestors come at the month's junctions as cows to a watering place, and if not honoured at the Ashtakas they go away and the person's hopes fail; givers go to the gods and non-givers to animal births. Shraddha on each lunar day brings a different fruit: the first day wealth that is not lost; the second lordship over people; the third, for those seeking boons, destroys enemies and sin; the fourth shows the enemy's weak points; the fifth brings great fortune; the sixth honour; the seventh lordship and leadership of groups; the eighth full prosperity; the ninth power and women; the tenth brahminical glory and all the Vedas; the eleventh the best gifts and lordship; the twelfth victory, kingdom, long life, wealth, offspring, cattle, intelligence, freedom and prosperity; the thirteenth long life and power. The fourteenth is for those who died young or by weapons. On the new moon shraddha brings all wishes and endless heaven, and is also for twins and those born at odd times. Shraddha under the Magha nakshatra brings all wishes and is imperishable, since Magha is ruled by the ancestors.

02-018.json.summary: Brihaspati gives the shraddhas for each nakshatra that Yama told King Shashabindu. Under Krittika one who keeps the sacred fires shines in heaven; Rohini brings offspring; Mrigashirsha brilliance; Ardra success in harsh deeds; Punarvasu land and sons; Tishya (Pushya) prosperity; Ashlesha heroic sons; Magha pre-eminence among kin; Purva Phalguni good fortune; Uttara Phalguni generosity and children; Hasta leadership in assemblies; Chitra handsome sons; Svati profit in trade; Vishakha sons; Anuradha the turning of the wheel of rule; Jyeshtha the highest lordship; Mula health; Purva Ashadha great fame; Uttara Ashadha freedom from sorrow; Shravana the highest goal; Dhanishtha kingship and great wealth; Abhijit the Vedas with their limbs; Shatabhisha success in medicine; Purva Bhadrapada many means of livelihood; Uttara Bhadrapada thousands of cows; Revati much base metal and goods; Ashvini horses; and Bharani (for the good) long life. Performing shraddha in this way, Shashabindu won and ruled the whole earth without trouble.

02-019.json.summary: Shamyu asks what offering satisfies the ancestors longest. Brihaspati says sesame, rice, barley, beans, water, roots and fruits satisfy them for a month; fish for two months; deer meat three; hare four; birds five; boar six; goat seven; mountain animals eight; ruru deer nine; gavaya ten; sheep eleven; cow's milk a year; rhinoceros meat, milk-rice with honey and ghee in an elephant's shadow, and black goat's meat forever. The ancestors sang verses: may there be born in our family one who offers on the thirteenth day, in the rainy season under Magha, with goat meat; one should wish for many sons so that at least one goes to Gaya, marries a 'Gauri' (a young bride) or releases a bull. Asked their fruits, Brihaspati says shraddha, recitation, offering and penance at Gaya are imperishable; a son born of a Gauri bride saves twenty-one generations; one who releases a bull purifies ten generations before and after, and whatever water the bull touches in a river, with its tail or any limb, and whatever ground it scratches with horn or hoof become streams of honey and imperishable gifts for the ancestors, equal to a lake a thousand nalvas wide; sesame with jaggery and honey are also imperishable. Brahmins should not be examined, though at rites for gods and ancestors examination is allowed; worthy guests are those who have completed Vedic study and vows, know languages and grammar, read the Puranas and law books, have done the Trinachiketa, keep five fires, know the Suparna hymns and the six limbs, sing the Jyeshtha Saman, have bathed at holy places and sacrifices, keep truth and their own duty, and are free of anger and greed; honouring yogis honours Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara, and the dharma of yoga is the first of all. Those unfit for the row are listed: gamblers, drinkers, herdsmen, village servants, usurers, shopkeepers, arsonists, poisoners, village priests, Soma sellers, servants across the sea, slanderers, false witnesses, one who quarrels with his father or keeps a paramour in his house, thieves, artisans, flatterers, cooks, the one-eyed, the lame, unbelievers, the mad, eunuchs, foeticides, violators of the teacher's bed, physicians, adulterers and sellers of vows; a gift to them is lost or like an offering into ash, and a one-eyed man destroys sixty, a eunuch a hundred, a leper five hundred and one with a sinful disease a thousand of the giver's fruit. Food eaten with the head covered, facing south, with shoes on, or given without respect goes to the demons. Dogs and brahmin-killers must not see it; the food is screened and sesame scattered against rakshasas; a pig destroys it by sight, a cock by the wind of its wings, a woman in her courses by touch, and an angry giver too. The ancestors are pleased by offerings on lovely river banks, lakes and quiet places. The knee is bent, silence kept, darbha held; shraddha is done in the forenoon of the bright fortnight and the afternoon of the dark fortnight, not passing the Rauhina hour. By devotion to the ancestors one gains rare yoga and by meditation liberation, the secret Brahman taught by Kashyapa and Sanatkumara. One who hears this and does not perform shraddha sinks into dark hell as an unbeliever; one who blames yogis, or even listens to such blame, becomes a worm, is cooked in Kumbhipaka and has his tongue cut again and again; so hatred of yogis must be avoided. The true master of the Veda is not one who has merely studied it but one who has gone beyond the twenty-four principles and the three qualities and knows what is to be known through yoga. One who reads this account of shraddha with faith gains the fruits of holy places and gifts, becomes a purifier of the row, and reaches the world of the gods; the speaker bows to the Self-born who taught it and to the great lords of yoga.

02-020.json.summary: Brihaspati concludes the account of the ancestors for his son Shamyu. These ancestors, sons of Prajapati, are gods even to the gods and live forever in seven places: the first group belongs to the yogis, the second to the gods, the third to the danavas and others, and the rest to the classes of men. The gods, the four stages of life, all four classes, people of mixed birth and even outsiders (mlecchas) worship them. Those who worship them with devotion receive prosperity, offspring and heaven; the ancestors' rite is greater than the gods', since the ancestors nourish the gods first. Their subtle yogic path cannot be seen even by penance, still less by the fleshly eye. Silver vessels are the best purifiers. The three rice balls offered by relatives on kusha grass by name and clan reach the ancestors wherever they are; as a calf finds its mother in a cowpen, the mantra carries the food to the being in whatever form it has taken, even after a hundred births, and becomes the food fit for it. Shamyu thanks him and promises to do all this. Brihaspati says Angiras once told this to the sages at Brahma's thousand-year sacrifice, after five thousand years had passed, where Brahma offered the first portion of food to the ancestors for the good of the worlds; the bard notes that this is how Brihaspati explained the creation of the ancestors to his son.

02-021.json.summary: The text notes that the account of shraddha is finished. The chapter then continues, without introduction, a story told by Vasishtha to a king (Sagara, as the colophons show) about Jamadagni and his son Rama (Parashurama). After some years, Rama, learned in the Vedas and devoted to his parents, asked their leave to visit his grandparents, who had often sent for him. His parents, weeping with joy, embraced him and let him go, asking him to come back soon. Rama went to the hermitage of his grandfather Richika, filled with the sound of Vedic study and peaceful animals; Richika and Satyavati, not knowing him at first, wondered who this radiant boy was; he gave his name and clan and bowed, and they embraced him with tears of joy and asked after his family. He stayed with them some months serving them, then with their blessing went on to the hermitage of Aurva and Chyavana, and then to the hermitage of his great-great-grandfather Bhrigu. That hermitage is described at length: shady trees, birdsong, Vedic chanting, the smoke of offerings, young sages carrying fuel and kusha, girls carrying flowers and water, fearless deer, dancing peacocks, rice drying, guests honoured and scriptures discussed. Bhrigu, white-bearded, sat on kusha grass teaching the subtle meaning of the Aranyakas to the sages. Rama bowed to him and to Khyati as Upendra bows to Brahma; Bhrigu asked about his family and why he had come, and Rama told him everything. After some days Bhrigu called him aside and told him to go at once to the Himalaya, build a hermitage and worship Mahadeva with penance and single-minded devotion; Shankara, pleased, would grant all he wished, and he should ask for all the divine weapons, since he would have to do very difficult deeds with weapons for the good of the gods.

02-022.json.summary: Vasishtha continues. Rama bowed to Bhrigu and Khyati, took leave of the sages and set out for the Himalaya by the road his teacher had described, passing many lands, mountains, rivers, hermitages and holy places. The Himalaya is described at great length: its peaks scraping the sky, coloured minerals and glowing herbs, forest fires lit by friction and sun-stones and quenched by melting snow, siddhas and yakshas on sunny rocks, fighting boars and tigers, rutting elephants, lions attacking elephants, sharabhas, hunters and bears, yak herds, kinnaris singing in caves, peacocks dancing, cuckoos, bees, waterfalls, and a long list of trees. Rama climbed it joyfully and thought that Brahma had rightly made it king of mountains and gave it a share in sacrifice: with its white snowy garment, its scented woods, the pearls from elephants' temples struck by lions, its cloud canopy, Kailasa as its white umbrella and its retinue of animals, it seemed like an emperor. He came to a large clear lake full of lotuses, water birds and fish, built a hermitage on its shore and began his penance, living on greens, roots and fruits, with senses controlled. Following Bhrigu's teaching he worshipped Shiva with one-pointed devotion: without shelter in the rains, standing in water in winter and among five fires in summer. Having conquered desire and the other inner enemies and the six waves of life, unshaken by heat and cold, practising the restraints and observances, he mastered the breath, the lotus posture, silence, withdrawal of the senses and concentration, and in meditation saw the Lord of gods. He stood unmoving like a lamp in a windless place, repeating the god's name and meditating on Shiva's form beyond qualities: the supreme, stainless, unthinkable light, eternal, pure, peaceful, beyond the senses, pure bliss, pervading all.

02-023.json.summary: Vasishtha continues. Hearing of Rama's penance, old and learned sages such as Bhrigu, Atri, Kratu, Jabali, Vamadeva and Mrikandu came to see him and praised his penance and knowledge. Shiva, well pleased, decided to test his devotion and came to him as a hunter: dark as collyrium, red-eyed, tall, carrying bow and arrows, with tawny beard and hair, smelling of flesh and fat, scratched by thorns, chewing raw meat and carrying two loads of meat, breaking trees as he walked like a moving mountain. He set down his load under a tree by the lake, then came to Rama with folded hands and said in a voice like thunder that he was the hunter who ruled this forest, ate the flesh of all creatures, made no distinctions of food, drink or conduct, feared not even Indra, and let no one stay there without his leave; he asked who Rama was and why he had come. Rama, wondering at his clear, refined speech and noticing good omens, said he was Rama, son of Jamadagni, come by his teacher's command to worship Shankara with penance until he appeared, and asked the hunter to go elsewhere, since living near a killer of creatures would harm his vow. The hunter angrily asked why he was despised like an ungrateful wretch when he had done no harm, and said he would not leave his own home; Rama could go if he liked. Rama replied that the hunter caste is cruel and scorned by all, that all creatures love their lives as the hunter himself shrinks from thorns, that non-violence is the eternal dharma, and that if he did not leave Rama would drive him off by force. The hunter, secretly pleased, mocked him: Shiva himself is a brahmin-killer, since he cut off Brahma's head, so it is fitting that such a worshipper should worship such a god; he accused Rama of having killed his own mother with his own hand, an act for which there is no atonement, and of now preaching non-violence and blaming others. He himself, he said, kills only as much as he needs to feed his parents and family, following the duty fate gave him, while Rama left his old father and killed his mother; such penance was useless, and Rama should go where no one knew him.

02-024.json.summary: Rama, amazed, said the hunter was no ordinary man: his body had the majesty of Indra and his speech the depth of one who knows all; he must be one of the gods, or Vishnu, or Shiva himself come in this form to test him, and he begged him with folded hands to show his true form. He sat in the lotus posture, controlled his breath and senses, and in meditation saw the Lord of the world in the form of the hunter. Opening his eyes, he saw the god standing before him in that form, fell at his feet with tears of joy, crying 'Be my refuge, Sharva, Shankara.' Shiva, pleased, raised him with his own hands, and Rama praised him (as Shankara, Sharva, Nilakantha, lord of beings, the manifest and unmanifest, three-eyed) and asked pardon for his harsh words. Shiva said he was pleased with his penance and devotion and would grant what he wished, but Rama did not yet have the strength to bear the fierce weapons; he should do more penance, go round the whole earth and bathe in all the holy places, and then he would receive all the weapons. Shiva vanished. Rama travelled round the earth, bathing in the holy places, offering to gods and ancestors and fasting, and with a purified body returned to his hermitage and went on worshipping Shiva. At that time a long war broke out between gods and demons; the demons defeated Indra and the gods and took their power, and the gods took refuge with Shiva and asked him to kill the demons. Shiva sent his attendant Mahodara to fetch Rama from the south side of the Himalaya. Brought to Kailasa, Rama saw Shiva among the gods and sages, wearing an elephant skin, smeared with ash, three-eyed, moon-crested, with tawny matted hair and snake ornaments, and fell at his feet. Shiva told him to kill the demons for the gods. Rama said that if Indra and all the gods could not, how could he, who knew no weapons or warfare? Shiva gave him his own Shaiva weapon power, bright as the fire of doomsday, and his own axe (parashu), which overcomes all weapons, and blessed him with invincible strength. Holding the axe, Rama, born of a portion of Vishnu and full of devotion to Rudra, shone like the sun; he went with the gods into battle and killed the demons in thousands with blows like thunderbolts, like a second Death; the rest fled. The gods returned to heaven, and Rama went back to his hermitage, made an image of Shiva in the hunter's form and worshipped it with scents, flowers, offerings and hymns.

02-025.json.summary: Pleased by Rama's devotion, Shiva appeared before him with his hosts, riding his bull. Rama bowed again and again and praised him in a long hymn: lord of gods, destroyer of Tripura, protector of devotees, dweller in cremation grounds and on Kailasa, drinker of the Kalakuta poison, crowned with the Ganga and the crescent moon, wearing serpents and ash, with sun, moon and fire for eyes, destroyer of Andhaka, Tripura and Daksha's sacrifice, known by the Vedanta, the creator as Hiranyagarbha, preserver and destroyer at the end of the kalpa, unknown even to Brahma and pure yogis; until one reaches his feet one wanders in the round of birth, and only one whose mind is fixed on them is truly wise. Shiva, pleased by his valour, penance, devotion and hymn, offered any boon. Rama asked for all the weapons, so that no one would surpass him in missiles, arms or learning and no one would defeat him in battle. Shiva gave him all the weapons with their mantras, how to use and withdraw them, a chariot with white horses and a fine banner, two quivers with endless arrows, an unbreakable bow named Vijaya, armour that resists all weapons, invincibility in war, unmatched valour, the power to hold his life at will, world-wide fame and great power of penance, together with devotion to himself, and vanished. Rama asked Mahodara to keep the chariot, bow and the rest, and to send them whenever he called. Setting out to see his elders, Rama entered a cave in the Himalaya and saw a brahmin boy fleeing, terrified, from a tiger; he chased it shouting 'stop', and when the boy fell and the beast ran at him, Rama charged a blade of grass with the Kusha weapon and burnt the tiger to ash before it could wound him. The tiger rose in the sky as a gandharva, saying he had been made a tiger by a brahmin's curse and was now freed, and went to heaven. Rama revived the frightened boy, who said he was the son of the sage Shanta, on his way from Shalagrama to Gandhamadana and Badarika, and had strayed from the path. Because he had been knocked down by the tiger but not wounded, he was named Akritavrana ('unwounded'), and from then on followed Rama like his shadow as his close friend. With him Rama visited Bhrigu and Khyati, Chyavana and Sukanya, Aurva, and Richika and Satyavati, telling each his story, and finally returned home to his parents, who embraced him with tears of joy and asked what he had done all this time and who his companion was.

02-026.json.summary: Vasishtha continues. Rama told his parents all he had done: his penance at the command of the family teacher, his pilgrimage at Shiva's command, the killing of the demons for the gods, and meeting Akritavrana; they rejoiced, and he served them and his brothers. At that time the Haihaya king (Kartavirya Arjuna) set out to hunt with his fourfold army. The dawn on the Narmada is described: birds calling, sages bathing and reciting, wives busy at housework, cows milked for the fire rite, offerings made as the sun rose. The king left his city with his priest, ministers, allied kings and army, entered the Vindhya forest and with his soldiers killed tigers, boars, deer, lions, bears, sharabhas and many other animals, young and old, with arrows, swords and spears, until the forest looked as at the end of an age. At midday, tired, hungry and thirsty, they bathed in the Narmada, drank, ate lotus shoots and rested. On the way back the king saw Jamadagni's hermitage on the Narmada bank; leaving the army at a distance he went in with a few attendants and his priest and bowed to the sage, who honoured him with water, a seat and the other courtesies and invited him to stay as a guest. The king asked leave to go, saying a forest hermit living on wild food could not feed his whole army, unless he could do so by his penance; otherwise the soldiers would trouble the ascetics. Jamadagni asked him to wait, called his sacred milk cow (homa-dhenu) and told her to honour the guest. By her power the hermitage at once became like Indra's city: a city of palaces with jewelled walls, golden altars, gateways, galleries, pillars, thrones, stores of food and drink, every comfort fit for gods, and lovely women.

02-027.json.summary: The cow then created the people of the city: countless beautiful, richly dressed and skilled women, servants and men; royal roads, markets, mansions, temples and squares full of contented citizens; houses for horses, elephants, chariots and cattle; homes for kings, vassals, soldiers, generals, brahmins, charioteers, bards and courtesans; jewelled gateways, flags and pavilions; lakes and ponds full of lotuses and water birds; gardens of mango, jackfruit, jambu and other fruit trees and flowering groves; and breezes carrying the scents of all seasons. Jamadagni sent a pupil to tell the king that the hospitality was ready. The king entered the city with his army and, though steady by nature, was amazed; the city women showered him with parched rice, flowers and pearls from the balconies as he passed along the royal road, shining like the Mandara mountain in moonlight. Seeing the riches, he praised the power of brahmin penance, yet thought that the wealth of kings was far greater, and that brahmin glory could not equal a hundredth of it. Received in a palace by the women of the household with lamps, curd, mirrors, flowers and durva grass, he sat on a jewelled seat, spent the day in pleasures, held court in the evening with music, dance and the company of courtesans till midnight, and then slept on a jewelled bed. His soldiers, lodged in fitting houses and fed with every food and drink, honey, meat, milk and ghee, said to one another that they had no need of their own homes and wished to stay there for good.

02-028.json.summary: At dawn bards and singers woke the king with songs and praise; he rose like Vishnu from his bed on Shesha, did his morning duties, worshipped his chosen deity, gave gifts, bowed to cows and brahmins and greeted the sun. With his ministers and vassals he went to Jamadagni and bowed. The sage asked whether he had slept well, saying that forest life is hard for townsmen. The king laughed and said the sage's greatness had amazed the world; his soldiers, captivated by the wealth, did not want to leave; and he asked leave to go. On the way he thought how wonderful was the cow, worth more than his whole kingdom and more than a sixteenth of Indra's wealth. His minister Chandragupta said the kingdom was empty without that jewel of a cow; he had also seen that all the palaces, women and wealth vanished in a moment into the cow and the place became a hermitage again; since the king is entitled to all jewels, he should take the cow. The king hesitated, saying a brahmin's property must not be taken. The priest Garga agreed: a brahmin's property must never be taken even in distress; it is a poison that destroys the whole family to the sons and grandsons, like a fire from a fire stick; ministers drunk on the king's favour drown their master like an iron boat; a generous king should not do a deed that ruins his fame. The minister answered that a brahmin cares only for his own caste and cannot judge royal affairs, which kings must decide; brahmins should be honoured but not given more; patience belongs to brahmins and force to kshatriyas, so taking it would be no sin, or the king could pay for it with cows and horses; the sage, peaceful and fond of the king, would surely give it if asked, or take wealth in exchange. The king told the minister to go himself, please the brahmin, give him what he wanted and bring the cow. Driven by fate, the minister went back to the hermitage, while Rama and Akritavrana had gone to the forest for fuel. Chandragupta asked for the cow in return for jewels or gold, then ten thousand cows, then half or all the kingdom; Jamadagni refused each time, saying his sacred cow was not for sale, he would not give her even to Indra while he lived, and if the king took her by force, what could a brahmin do, since he gives only freely. Enraged, the wicked minister began to take the cow by force.

02-029.json.summary: Jamadagni angrily warned that a wise man never takes a brahmin's property; taking his cow by force would bring sin, and he saw the king's life running out; who but Arjuna, wishing to live, would rob ascetic brahmins without their gift? The minister, driven by Time, tied the cow with strong ropes and dragged her. Jamadagni, moved by what was to come, held her neck tightly in his arms, saying he would not let her go while he lived. The cruel Chandragupta ordered his soldiers to drive him off, and they beat the sage with sticks, whips, clubs and fists until he was far from the cow. Though in pain, he did not become angry, for freedom from anger is the true wealth of the good; he could have destroyed or protected the whole world by his penance, but he thought of its ruin and stayed calm, having been calm ever since Rama had pacified him over the matter of his mother. Beaten until his limbs and bones were broken, he fell senseless to the ground. The minister then had the cow and her calf bound and dragged away with whips and clubs; the cow, enraged, broke her strong ropes, bellowed, struck the king's men on every side with horns, hooves and tail, scattered them, and rose into the sky before everyone's eyes. The beaten, defeated men took the calf by force instead, and the wicked minister brought it to the king, praised him and, fearful, told him all that had happened.

02-030.json.summary: Hearing that Jamadagni had been struck down, the king grieved, thinking how cruel and shameful it was to want a brahmin's property and to cause his death, and that he should have heeded the brahmin; he went back to his city. Renuka came out of the hermitage, saw her husband lying senseless, wounded and covered in blood, fainted as if struck by lightning, and on waking wept and lamented, crying 'Rama, Rama'. Rama, returning from the forest with Akritavrana and a load of fuel, saw evil omens and hurried home. Renuka, seeing him, beat her breast with both hands, twenty-one times in all. Akritavrana urged Rama not to grieve, since grief dries up the senses and blocks all aims, and to comfort his mother, for what is past does not return. Rama steadied himself and told his mother: because you have struck your breast twenty-one times, I will kill the kshatriyas on earth that many times; this I swear. Renuka calmed herself a little. Rama and his brothers began to prepare their father's body for the fire. Renuka called her sons and asked leave to follow her husband into the fire, saying she could not bear the scorned life of a widow, and told them not to oppose her. Then a deep voice from the sky told her not to do this rash deed: one who lives sees good things; her husband would soon come back to life and she would long enjoy happiness. Comforted, they carried the body into the hermitage, laid it in a sheltered place and sat around it, and good omens appeared. Then, by fate, Bhrigu arrived, master of the Atharva rites and the Vedas, honoured by the asuras, who knew the life-restoring knowledge (mrita-sanjivani) and wrote the political treatise of Ushanas still followed by kings. They honoured him and told him all; he sprinkled water over Jamadagni with the reviving mantra, saying 'If I have any merit of sacrifice and penance, let him live', and Jamadagni rose as if from sleep. He bowed to Bhrigu, washed his feet and sprinkled the water over his family, and asked what sin the king had committed. Bhrigu explained that the king had long ago been cursed by Vasishtha that his power would be destroyed for wronging a brahmin; that curse must come true, and Rama, who had vowed to clear the earth of kshatriyas twenty-one times for his mother's twenty-one blows, would surely kill him even if his father tried to stop him. Yet the king was devoted to elders, had gained wisdom from Dattatreya, a portion of Hari, and was a great devotee, so killing him would be a sin. Saying this, Bhrigu left.

02-031.json.summary: King Sagara asks what Rama did in his anger. Vasishtha says that after Bhrigu left, Rama, breathing hard, said: see the folly of Kartavirya, who tried to kill a brahmin; fate is strong and deludes creatures; let the sages hear my vow: I will kill Kartavirya in battle and avenge my father, even if all the gods and demons protect him. Jamadagni told him the eternal dharma of the good: the good who seek liberation are never angry even when blamed or beaten; those rich in patience gain imperishable worlds; one who strikes back at a striker is not good but sinful; brahmins are worthy of honour because of their patience; killing a king is a great sin; so forgive and do penance. Rama replied that calm is fitting toward the good, the poor and the elders, not toward the wicked; Kartavirya must be killed, and asked his leave. Jamadagni said whatever was fated would happen, and told him to go to Brahma and ask what was right. Rama went to Brahma's golden world and saw him on a jewelled throne, surrounded by siddhas and sages, watching vidyadhari dancers and teaching yoga; he bowed and told him everything. Brahma said that his vow was hard to fulfil: the world, which Brahma had made with great labour at Hari's command, would be destroyed by it, and to clear the earth of kings twenty-one times for one king's fault and his father's humiliation was a terrible thing; yet because of past deeds his vow would not fail, but would succeed only with effort. Many kings on earth were servants of Shankara and wore protective armour (kavacha) and powers, and could not be killed without Shiva's leave; Rama should go to Shiva's world, ask his permission and obtain from him the mantra and armour of Shri Krishna called Trailokyavijaya, for Vishnu's power cannot be overcome; Shiva, compassionate to the humble, would also give him the divine Pashupata weapon.

02-032.json.summary: Rama went to Shiva's world, a hundred thousand yojanas above Brahma's world, beyond description and reached only by yogis, with Vaikuntha on its right and Gauri's world on its left: a place of yogis, siddhas and Pashupatas, with parijata trees, wish-granting cows, a hundred jewelled lakes, golden jewelled walls with four gates, made by Shiva's own yoga beyond even Vishvakarma's dreams. At the lion gate he saw two fearsome doorkeepers with tridents, smeared with ash and dressed in tiger skins; he bowed and asked leave to see Shankara, and they let him in. In the fragrant hall full of siddhas he saw Shiva: calm, three-eyed, moon-crested, holding a trident, in a tiger skin, smeared with ash, wearing a snake as his sacred thread, bright as crores of suns, five-faced and ten-armed, teaching yoga with the gesture of reasoning, praised by yogis, pramathas, bhairavas, yoginis and Rudra hosts; Kartikeya on his left, Ganesha on his right, Nandishvara, Mahakala and Virabhadra before him, and the hundred-armed Durga in his lap. Rama bowed and praised him as the all-pervading lord who creates, keeps and destroys in the forms of Brahma and the others, beyond the reach of the Vedas, speech and mind, unknown even to the gods, from whose slightest anger fire burns all, whose eight forms are earth, wind, fire, water, sky, the sacrificer, moon and sun, and who is Time. Shiva raised him, placed his hand on his head, seated him before Ganesha and asked who he was. Rama said he was Rama son of Jamadagni of the Bhrigu line, told how Kartavirya, after being entertained, had struck down his father, how the cow went to the world of cows, how his mother wept, how Bhrigu revived his father, and how he had vowed to make the earth kingless twenty-one times; he asked Shiva to fulfil this. Shiva looked at Durga's face and pondered; Durga laughed and said: you, an ascetic brahmin's son, want to make the earth kingless twenty-one times and kill, unarmed, the thousand-armed Arjuna, who drove off even Ravana with a frown, and who holds the armour of Hari given by Dattatreya and a mighty power; only Shankara can do the impossible. With her consent, Shiva said: from today be equal to Skanda for me; I will give you a divine mantra and armour by which you will easily kill Kartavirya and make the earth kingless twenty-one times. He gave him the rare mantra and the wonderful Trailokyavijaya armour, and the Nagapasha, Pashupata, Brahmastra, Narayanastra, Agneya, Vayavya, Varuna, Gandharva, Garuda and Jrimbhana weapons, a mace, spear, axe, trident and staff. Rama bowed to Shiva, Durga, Skanda and Ganesha, went to the holy Pushkara, perfected the mantra and armour as Shiva had taught, and accomplished his purpose: he killed Kartavirya with his army and family and returned to his father's home.

02-033.json.summary: Sagara asks Vasishtha to tell the Trailokyavijaya armour (kavacha). Vasishtha gives the ten-syllable mantra addressed to Krishna, the beloved of the cowherd women, ending in svaha, which gives enjoyment and liberation; its seer is Sadashiva, its metre Pankti and its deity Krishna. The armour's seer is Prajapati, its metre Jagati and its deity the king of kings, used to win the three worlds. It then assigns mantras to protect each part of the body: Om and 'salutation to Shri Krishna' the head; 'svaha to Krishna' the forehead; 'Krishna' the eyes; 'salutation to Hari' the brows; 'Om svaha to Govinda' the nose; 'salutation to Gopala' the cheeks; 'klim salutation to Krishna' the ears; 'shrim salutation to Krishna' the lips; and so on with names such as Gopisha, Rameshvara, Radhikesha, Gopiganesha, Kishoravesha, Mukunda, Vishnu, Bhagavan, Narayana, Padmanabha, Sarveshvara, Madhava, Rasikesha, Gopijanesha, Daityanasha, Yashodanandana, Rasarambhapriya and Vrindapriya for the throat, shoulders, back, belly, hands, arms, nails, navel, hair, crown, forehead, waist, thighs, knees, shanks and all limbs. It also asks Krishna to protect in each direction: Krishna in the east, the lord of Goloka in the south-east, the complete Brahman in the south, Krishna in the south-west, Hari in the west, Govinda in the north-west, the lord of rasa in the north, the one who sports in Vrindavana in the north-east, the lord of Vrinda's life above, the destroyer of Bali below, Narasimha in water, land and sky, Madhava in sleep and waking, and the all-pervading inner Self everywhere. Vasishtha says he heard it from Shiva and it must not be told to anyone; one who worships his teacher and wears it on the neck or right arm becomes like Vishnu; Sarasvati and Lakshmi stay where such an adept lives, and one perfected in it is liberated while alive; it is worth more than crores of years of worship, thousands of Rajasuya and hundreds of Vajapeya sacrifices, great gifts, circling the earth, vows, fasts, study and bathing at all holy places; it gives success, immortality and service of Hari. It is perfected by ten lakh repetitions and brings sure victory. One may give a kingdom, one's head or one's life, but never this armour, even in danger; Vasishtha reveals it to Sagara for his protection and at his own bidding, and tells him to wear it and become emperor.

02-034.json.summary: Sagara thanks Vasishtha for revealing the armour, says he had learnt weapons by the grace of Aurva, and asks how Rama and Kartavirya, both favoured (by Shiva and by Dattatreya), met in battle. Vasishtha tells that Rama, having received the armour and mantra, practised them devotedly at Pushkara for a hundred years, sleeping on the ground and bathing three times a day, while Akritavrana brought fuel, flowers and kusha; he meditated on Krishna, but did not reach success. One day at the middle Pushkara lake he saw a stag and a doe, fleeing a hunter, tired and thirsty, come to drink fearfully; the hunter, seeing Rama there, stood far off, afraid to shoot in his presence. The two deer rested under a tree and talked. The doe said they should stay near Rama, since any hunter who attacked them there would be burnt to ash by his look. The stag agreed and told her Rama's story: his father had been insulted by Kartavirya, he had vowed to kill kings, Brahma had sent him to Shiva, and Shiva had given him Krishna's mantra and armour, the Pashupata and other weapons; he had been reciting for a hundred years without success because devotion is of three kinds, highest, middling and lowest. The highest belongs to Shiva, Narada, Shuka, Ambarisha, Rantideva, Hanuman, Bali, Vibhishana, Prahlada, the gopis and Uddhava; the middling to Vasishtha and the sages, Manu and others; Rama has only middling devotion, being given to rules, and so had not succeeded. Asked how he knew all this, the stag said knowledge comes from merit, and the sight of the pure Rama, a devotee of Krishna, had given it to him, so that he knew past and future. Without the highest devotion the armour and mantra will not succeed even in countless years; but if Rama received the grace of Agastya and learned from him the hymn called Krishna-premamrita ('nectar of love for Krishna'), which strings together all Krishna's deeds through his names, he would succeed, kill the Haihaya king with his sons, ministers, friends and army, and make the earth kingless twenty-one times. The stag then fell silent, also knowing why he himself had been born a deer.

02-035.json.summary: Sagara asks what else the deer said. Vasishtha says the doe praised her mate and asked by what deed they had been born as animals. The stag said that in a past life he was Suri, youngest of the four sons (Rama, Dharma, Prithu and Suri) of the learned brahmin Shivadatta of the Kaushika clan in the rich Dravida land; their father taught them the Vedas and they served him, fetching fruit, water, fuel and kusha from the forest. One day the brothers bathed in the Kritamala river and climbed the Audbhida mountain, which is described with its many trees, wild animals, fragrant flowers, jewelled peaks and roaring waterfalls; lost in wonder, they wandered apart. A thirsty doe came to drink at a waterfall, a tiger seized her, and Suri, fleeing in fear, fell from a height and died thinking of the doe; she was reborn as this doe and he as this stag, and he did not know where his brothers had gone. He also foretold that the hunter who had followed them, kept off by fear of Rama, would now be killed by a lion and go to heaven; that by drinking at the middle Pushkara and seeing Rama, a form of Vishnu, the sins of many births were destroyed; and that by seeing Agastya and hearing the hymn they would go to good worlds. Rama and Akritavrana heard all this in amazement. Rama set out for Agastya's hermitage; on the way he saw the hunter lying dead, killed by a lion. After a yojana and a half he bathed and did his midday prayer at the lowest Pushkara, and the pair of deer, following, drank and bathed there and went ahead toward Agastya's hermitage. Rama passed Vishnu's footprints, the pool of the nagas and the seven sages' pool, where the Sarasvati, Brahma's daughter, fills three pools for the fire rite, and came to Agastya's hermitage, where deer and lions lived together in peace. He found Agastya, son of the jar, calm as a still lake, meditating on Brahman in a leaf hut, bowed and gave his name. Agastya welcomed him with a seat and madhuparka and asked after him. Rama told him about the deer that had told his past and future, and that he had practised Krishna's mantra and Shiva's armour for over a hundred years without success, and asked for help. Agastya, meditating, understood what the deer had said and that they had come to hear the hymn, and comforted Rama.

02-036.json.summary: Agastya tells Rama that one who knows the three kinds of devotion and strives soon succeeds. Once he went to the nether world to see Ananta (Shesha), where the siddhas Sanaka and others, Narada, Gautama, Jajali, Kratu, Ribhu, Hamsa, Aruni, Valmiki, Shakti, Asuri, Vatsyayana and others sat around the serpent king to learn, and the Earth goddess sat before him asking questions; there he heard the 'Krishna-premamrita' hymn. The Earth, having heard the deeds of the Boar and other incarnations, asked Shesha for the chief names of Krishna. Shesha said he would tell the hundred and eight names, which give liberation, the eight powers, the fruit of all holy places and sacrifices, and destroy crores of great sins; one recitation of one name of Krishna gives the fruit of three recitations of the thousand names. He himself is its seer, the metre Anushtubh. The names follow: Shri Krishna, lord of Kamala, Vasudeva, eternal, son of Vasudeva, taking a human form in play, bearing the Shrivatsa and Kaustubha, dear to Yashoda, Hari, four-armed with discus, sword, mace and conch, son of Devaki, lord of Shri, beloved son of Nanda, who stopped the Yamuna's flood, younger brother of Balabhadra, taker of Putana's life, breaker of the cart demon, joy of Nanda's people, of the form of being, consciousness and bliss, smeared with butter, the butter-dancer and butter-thief, who blessed Muchukunda, lord of sixteen thousand women, bent in three places, sweet in form, Govinda, who grazed the calves, killer of Dhenuka, Trinavarta, the Yamalarjuna trees and the Tala demons, dark as the tamala, lord of cowherds and gopis, yogi, bright as crores of suns, Yadava lord, wearing the forest garland and yellow cloth, who took the parijata tree, who lifted Govardhana, Gopala, protector of all, unborn, stainless, lotus-eyed, slayer of Madhu, lord of Mathura and Dvaraka, who roamed Vrindavana, adorned with tulasi, who took the Syamantaka jewel, Nara-Narayana, who wore cloth from Kubja, the supreme Person, skilled in wrestling Mushtika and Chanura, enemy of Kamsa, Mura and Naraka, eternal celibate, remover of Draupadi's distress, who cut off Shishupala's head, destroyer of Duryodhana's family, giver of boons to Vidura and Akrura, who showed the cosmic form, true in word and resolve, delighting in Satyabhama, elder brother of Subhadra, Vishnu, giver of liberation to Bhishma, guru and lord of the world, master of the flute, destroyer of the bull demon and Baka, who cut Bana's arms, who established Yudhishthira, wearing a peacock feather, Partha's charioteer, the ocean of the nectar of the Gita, whose feet are coloured by the gems of Kaliya's hoods, Damodara, enjoyer of sacrifice, Narayana, the supreme Brahman, riding Garuda, who took the gopis' clothes at their water play, of holy fame, whose feet are holy, known by the Vedas, ocean of mercy, the essence of all holy places and planets, beyond the highest. This hymn, made by Krishna's devotee after hearing the Gita, removes calamities, lengthens life, multiplies the merit of all gifts, vows and pilgrimages crores of times, gives sons to the sonless, wealth to the poor, victory, protection of children and cattle, cures children's illnesses, and at death the remembrance of Krishna; a mantra of salutation to Krishna, lord of Rukmini, is also given. Shesha fell silent, and the sages praised him and returned home. Agastya says this rare hymn makes all mantras, hymns and armours succeed. As he finished, a heavenly car with four siddhas arrived; the stag and doe bowed at Agastya's feet, climbed in, took divine bodies marked with conch and discus, and went to Vishnu's world as all beings, Rama and Agastya watched.

02-037.json.summary: Parashurama told Agastya the story of the two deer, and Agastya, pleased, advised him: not far from here is the rare place of Vishnu's footprints, where the Ganga arose from the toe of Vamana's foot when he strode across the worlds to subdue Bali; he should go there and recite this hymn for one month with a controlled mind and diet, and the armour he had practised to overcome his enemies would then succeed. Rama bowed and went with Akritavrana to the place where the heavenly river came forth from the footprint, lived there and practised the Krishna-premamrita hymn. Pleased, Hari came to see him in person: Krishna, lord of the four forms, lotus-eyed, with a sun-bright crown, earrings and the Kaustubha jewel, in yellow cloth, dark as a cloud, playing the flute, the enchanting form. Rama fell before him like a stick and praised him: the cause of all, protector of those who take refuge, whom the Vedas and the gods cannot define, who takes many bodies among gods, men and animals to remove the earth's burden, devoted to his devotees and detached even from Lakshmi, bound by love even to those whose minds are faulty; others torment their bodies or perform sacrifices but do not see him even in dreams, while those who remember him, bow to him and speak of him to one another cross over and save others, for his name is the medicine for worldly life; Rama, bound by desire, had worshipped him with many efforts, and he knew everything. Krishna said: your task is done by the power of the armour and the hymn; kill the proud king Kartavirya, avenge your father and rid the earth of kshatriyas; Kartavirya is an incarnation of my discus on earth and has fulfilled his purpose, so end him. From now on you will move in the world with a portion of my power. In the twenty-fourth Treta age I will be born as Rama of the Raghu line, son of Dasharatha and joy of Kausalya; after protecting Vishvamitra's sacrifice with Lakshmana I will go to Janaka's city, break Shiva's bow and marry Videha's daughter, and on my way to Ayodhya I will take away your proud power. Having said this, Krishna vanished before Rama's eyes.

02-038.json.summary: When Krishna vanished, Rama felt filled with power by Krishna's grace and, blazing like fire, went with Akritavrana to Mahishmati on the Narmada, the holy river that purifies even sinners by its sight and where Shiva once prepared to destroy Tripura. He bowed to the Narmada, born of Shiva's body, praying that she quickly destroy his enemies, and sent a messenger to Kartavirya Arjuna: 'Relying on your strength you insulted the sage Jamadagni; his son has come to fight; come out quickly, give battle to Rama and go to the next world.' The king, a devotee of Atreya (Dattatreya), grew angry and replied that he had conquered the earth by the strength of his arms given by Datta, bound kings and brought them to his city, and would now give battle. He had his general prepare the fourfold army and mounted his chariot, surrounded by vassal kings with many akshauhinis, crores of elephants and countless horses, chariots and foot soldiers like an ocean, all eager to be first; dust covered the sky and the noise of instruments, horses and elephants filled it. On the way the king saw evil omens foretelling death: a weeping, naked woman with loose hair and cut nose in black clothes, a ragged, fallen, naked or ochre-robed man, a cripple, an iguana, a hare, a porcupine, an empty pot, a reptile, cotton, a tortoise, oil, salt, a piece of bone, a jackal howling on his right, a sick man, an outcaste, a bull, a hawk and a bear; yet, bound by the noose of Time, he went on. Rama, sitting with Akritavrana under a banyan on the north bank of the Narmada, saw Kartavirya coming with a hundred crore kings and a thousand akshauhinis, and rejoiced that his long-awaited task had come; he rose with his axe like an angry lion. Wherever he hurled the axe, elephants, horses and warriors fell with arms, thighs and necks cut off, as a rutting elephant crushes a reed bed. The king of the Matsyas, Mangala, attacked him with fiery arrows; Rama checked them with the wind weapon, Mangala answered with the mountain weapon, and Rama released the Narayana weapon, which set all quarters ablaze and made the Matsya king tremble; Rama killed his four horses with four arrows, cut his banner with one, his bow with two, felled his charioteer with one and smashed the chariot with three, and when Mangala stood on the ground split his head with the axe; he died vomiting blood, and his army was burnt to ash by the weapon.

02-039.json.summary: After the Matsya king fell, Kartavirya sent other great kings against Rama: Brihadbala, Somadatta, the kings of Vidarbha, Mithila, Nishadha and Magadha, showering arrows. Rama, holding the Pinaka and blazing like fire, threw the Nagapasha (serpent noose) weapon; Somadatta cut it with the Garuda weapon; then Rama killed Somadatta with the trident given by Rudra, Brihadbala with his mace, the Vidarbha king with his fist, the Mithila king with a hammer, the Nishadha king with a spear, the Magadha king with kicks, and the soldiers with a net of weapons, and ran at Kartavirya. Other kings, Kanyakubjas, Saurashtras and Avantis by the hundred, put Kartavirya behind them and covered Rama with arrows until he could not be seen; Akritavrana remembered what the deer had foretold and prayed to Hari for Rama's safety. Rama blew away the arrows with the wind weapon and rose like the sun from mist; he fought them for three days and nights and cut down twelve akshauhinis like a grove of banana stems. Then Suchandra of the solar line came with a hundred thousand kings and seven akshauhinis; Rama destroyed their weapons and mowed down the army like a farmer harvesting ripe grain. Suchandra fought him, cutting every weapon Rama threw; Rama, after touching water, fired the irresistible Narayana weapon, bright as a hundred suns, but Suchandra got down from his chariot and bowed to it, and since it is honoured by all weapons it left him and returned to Narayana. Amazed, Rama hurled spear, club, lance, axe and mace, and Suchandra caught them all in play; Rama threw Shiva's trident, and it became a garland of flowers on the king's neck. Then Rama saw before Suchandra the goddess Bhadrakali, mother of the world, wearing a garland of skulls, fearsome-faced, riding a lion, three-eyed, holding a trident. He laid down his weapons and praised her in a hymn as Shankara's beloved, daughter of Daksha and of Himavan, half of Maheshvara's body, Kali, Tara, Tripura, Bagalamukhi, Lalita, Rama, giver of kingdom and of all learning, mother and father of the three worlds, asking her to protect the vow he had made. Pleased, she offered a boon; Rama asked that he might conquer Suchandra, her devotee. She told him to send Suchandra to her house with the fire weapon, since she wanted him as her attendant. Rama controlled his breath, sipped water and fired the fire weapon at Suchandra; it burnt his body of elements and took him to the world of the supreme goddess. Bhadrakali, bowed to by Rama, vanished, and he stood on the battlefield eager to kill more kings.

02-040.json.summary: When Suchandra fell, his son Pushkaraksha attacked Rama from his chariot and covered him with arrows for a moment. Rama broke free and, blazing with anger, released the Varuna weapon; terrible clouds rose and flooded the earth with rain; Pushkaraksha blew them away with the wind weapon; Rama then set the Brahma weapon, and Pushkaraksha drew the same. Hissing like a struck snake, Rama ran at him with his axe; Pushkaraksha shot five fiery arrows into his heart, head, two arms and topknot and held him for a moment; then Rama brought the axe down on his head and split him in two from crown to foot, to the wonder of men and gods, and burnt up his army like fire in a forest; in a moment nine akshauhinis with many royal houses were destroyed, the soldiers crying 'father, mother' as they turned to ash. Then Kartavirya Arjuna himself came in a golden chariot ten nalvas long, drawn by a hundred horses and full of weapons, with his thousand arms holding many weapons, his hundred sons arraying the army behind him. Holding five hundred arrows in his right hands and five hundred bows in his left, he rained arrows on Rama like a cloud on a mountain, and Rama answered with his divine bow; they fought a hair-raising battle. Kartavirya fired the Brahma weapon and Rama, after touching water, did the same; the two weapons grew in the sky, blazing like fire and sun, and the three worlds thought the end had come. Remembering what the Lord of the world had told him, that he must protect the world, Rama drew both weapons into his two eyes, meditated for a moment, and by the power of his meditation they lost their force and fell; the world was at peace again. Though able to create, protect and destroy, he hid his power and acted as a man. Then Rama took two arrows and cut off both the king's ears, intending to take his crest jewel; the king felt his power gone, grew pale like a painted figure, remembered his victories over Ravana and others, and meditated on Datta, by whose grace he had subdued the world guardians; but Datta did not appear in his mind, because he had wronged an innocent, self-controlled ascetic. Seeing him sunk in grief, Rama said: do not grieve; I who gave you boons at the beginning have come to end you; everyone eats the fruit of his own deeds, which no one can change; your merit from many births made you worthy of Datta's boons, and now enjoy the fruit of your misdeed, for you wronged my father; therefore I cut your ears; see me take your crest jewel and your fame. He shot an arrow that cut the jewel off and it came back to him. Kartavirya attacked again with trident, spear, mace, discus, sword, pattisha, lance and other weapons, which Rama cut in mid-air; Agneya was met with Varuna, Gandharva with Vayavya, Naga with Garuda. Then the king hurled the unfailing trident given by Datta, bright as a hundred suns, with all his might; it struck Rama on the head and he fell senseless, remembering Hari. The frightened gods came with Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara; Shiva, conqueror of death, revived Rama with the life-giving knowledge; Rama bowed to them, and they vanished. Rama touched water, recited the armour, rose blazing with anger, remembered the Pashupata weapon Shiva had given and at once destroyed the mighty Kartavirya; the king, a devotee of Datta, entered Vishnu's discus Sudarshana, and his body became ash.

02-041.json.summary: Seeing their father killed, Kartavirya's hundred sons, each with an akshauhini, attacked Rama; with his axe he destroyed their hundred akshauhinis in two muhurtas. The sons then surrounded him in a circle hurling divine weapons, and Rama in the middle shone like the hub of a wheel, or like Krishna dancing among the circling gopis; the gods led by Brahma watched from their cars and showered flowers, and the clash of weapons sounded like music, the wounds like love marks and the cries like songs. Rama broke their circle and killed them one by one; five of them, Shura, Vrishasya, Vrisha, Shurasena and Jayadhvaja, lost heart and fled to the forests at the foot of the Himalaya. Having killed the kings and their allies, Rama bathed in the Narmada with Akritavrana, did his daily rites, worshipped Shiva, and went to Kailasa to see Shiva, his teacher's wife Uma, and their sons Skanda and Vinayaka. He passed Kubera's city Alaka, with jewelled houses, yakshas, groves, lakes, the Alakananda river where elephants drink saffron-tinged water left from the bathing of goddesses, and music of gandharvas and apsaras; above it, under a great banyan, he found Shiva's abode, a jewelled wall a hundred yojanas round with four gates, guarded by Nandishvara, Mahakala, Virabhadra, Chanda, Bhringi and many attendants, bhutas, pretas, pishachas, yoginis and others. Let in by Nandi, he saw Shiva's palace, four yojanas wide, with Kartikeya on the left and Vinayaka on the right of the eastern door, and bowed to them. As he went to enter, Vinayaka asked him to wait a moment, since Mahadeva was asleep with Uma, and said he would get leave and take him in. Rama said he only wished to bow to Parvati and Shankara and go home, since by Shiva's grace he had killed Kartavirya, Suchandra and their sons, armies and kin, and thousands of other kings, Kambojas, Pahlavas, Shakas, Kanyakubjas and Koshalas. Vinayaka said that one who disturbs a man and woman sitting together goes to hell, especially a son seeing his father, teacher or king so; one who sees a couple about to unite loses his wife for seven births, and one who looks at the hips, breast or face of another's wife, or of his mother, sister or daughter, is the lowest of men. Rama said these rules were for the lustful, not for a child free of desire, and that the two were the parents of the world; he would go in and do what was fitting. Vinayaka rose to stop him; they argued and pulled each other by the hands, and Skanda separated them. Then Rama, angry, raised his axe to throw at Ganesha; the elephant-faced god quickly lifted Rama with his trunk and, carrying him up, showed him all the worlds, Bhu, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapas and Satya, Vaikuntha and Goloka above it, and the seven lower worlds; then he dropped him into the waters of the cosmic ocean, and drew the terrified Rama, struggling for life, back out and set him down where he had been.

02-042.json.summary: Shaken and ashamed after being whirled around by Ganesha, and seeing him standing calm, Rama angrily hurled his axe at him. Ganesha, recognising the axe as his father's gift and wishing not to make it useless, caught it on his left tusk; the tusk was cut off and fell to the ground covered in blood, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt; the earth with its seas and islands shook, the worlds trembled, the gods cried out and Kartikeya and the others wailed. Hearing the noise, Parvati and Shiva came; seeing Heramba with one tusk, Parvati asked Skanda what had happened, and he told her everything in Rama's hearing. Angry, she told Shiva: this Bhargava, your pupil equal to a son, got power and the world-conquering armour from you, defeated Kartavirya, and has paid you his teacher's fee by knocking out your son's tusk; keep this pupil, he will do all your work; I will not stay where I am slighted, but will go with my sons to my father's house; the good honour even a servant's son as their own, but you have not said a word for your own son. Shiva said nothing, but remembered Krishna, who removes the distress of those who bow to him. Krishna came at once, dark as a cloud, smiling, in jewelled ornaments and lightning-bright clothes, with makara earrings, a peacock-feather crest and the Kaustubha jewel, together with Radha and Shridama, outshining all. Shiva bowed and seated him with Radha on a jewelled throne; Parvati and her sons bowed to them; Rama fell at Parvati's feet, but she did not greet him. Krishna then spoke to Parvati, asking her to take Rama into her lap, and told her the names of her great son Vinayaka given in the Vedas, Smritis and Puranas: Ganesha, as lord of the ganas; Lambodara, because all universes past, present and future are in his belly; Gajanana, because his cut head was joined again with an elephant's head; Bhalachandra, because he bore on his forehead the moon cursed on the fourth day; Shurpakarna, because he revived Agni when the seven sages had cursed him; Vighnanasha, because he removed obstacles for the gods in the war with the demons; Ekadanta, because today Rama's axe has broken his tusk; and Vakratunda, because his trunk will be curved in a future cycle of Brahma. In an earlier kalpa Krishna gave him the boon of being worshipped first among the gods: whoever worships Gajanana at birth rites and other sacraments, journeys, trade, war, worship of the gods, in trouble or for any wish succeeds in all. Parvati, amazed, did not answer; then Radha said: Prakriti and Purusha depend on each other and appear as two; there is no difference between you and me; you are Vishnu and I am Shiva become two; Vishnu dwells in Shiva's heart in your form and Shiva in Vishnu's heart in mine; Rama is a Vaishnava who has become a Shaiva, and Ganesha is Shiva who has become a Vaishnava; there is no difference between them. Radha took Gajanana in her lap, smelt his head and touched his cheek, and the wound healed. Parvati, pacified, raised Rama from her feet, took him in her lap and kissed his head; Krishna took Skanda in his lap and Shiva took Shridama in his.

02-043.json.summary: Rama rose from Bhavani's lap and with folded hands praised the One who is without and with qualities: Bhava (Shiva) and his consort who fulfil all wishes, the mother who is the cause of all, the six-faced Skanda who destroys demons, Ganesha who lives near Hara, loves serving Krishna, sits in Radha's lap and removes obstacles, asking him to forgive his great offence; Radha, worshipped in creation, preservation and dissolution, queen of the rasa dance, whose womb bore the cosmic person and in whose pores the universes shine; and Krishna, the all-pervading ocean of being, consciousness and bliss, shining with Radha, the most complete, asking him to be always merciful. Krishna said: you have become perfected by my grace; be the greatest in this world from today; the boon I gave you at the hermitage of Vishnu's footprints will come true in time over many years; show kindness to the poor, practise yoga and subdue enemies; no one equals you in power, strength, knowledge or fame; now go home, serve your parents and do penance in due time, and success will be in your hand. Krishna raised Ganesha from Radha's lap, embraced him and made him and Rama friends, and they became close at his command. Radha gave both a boon: they would be honoured by the whole world, unconquerable and her special devotees, and whoever begins a task uttering their names would succeed by her grace. Bhavani offered Rama a boon; he asked that in all his thousands of births he be a devotee of both Krishnas (Radha and Krishna) and both Bhavas (Shiva and Parvati), seeing no difference between them. Parvati granted it and made him long-lived (chiranjivi). Shiva said all he had promised would come fully true and no one would be stronger or more powerful than Rama. Krishna took leave of Shiva and Parvati and went to Goloka with Shridama and Radha. Rama worshipped Bhavani and Bhava, walked around them, bowed to Ganesha and Kartikeya, and left with Akritavrana, saluted by Nandishvara and the ganas, and went home joyfully.

02-044.json.summary: Rama travelled home through many countries with Akritavrana; wherever kshatriyas saw him on the road they hid to save their lives. He came to his father's hermitage, full of peaceful creatures where lions, deer, cows, snakes, cats and mice played together without fear, peacocks danced at the smoke of the fire rite, brahmins offered water to the setting sun and pupils studied the Vedas. Greeted by cries of 'victory' and 'salutation' from brahmins and their sons, he entered his house, saw his father Jamadagni, like Bhrigu himself, able to curse and to bless, and fell at his feet with all eight limbs touching the ground, saying 'I am Rama, your servant', and then bowed to his mother. He told them: by the power of your penance Kartavirya, who wronged you on the advice of a wicked minister, has been killed with his sons, army and mounts; he recounted going to Brahma, to Shiva's world, receiving the Trailokyavijaya armour, perfecting it at Pushkara, killing Kartavirya, returning to Shiva's world, the quarrel with Ganesha at the door, being whirled about, throwing the axe and breaking the tusk, Parvati's anger, and Krishna's coming with Radha, his reconciling Parvati, granting him a boon and making him Ganesha's friend. Jamadagni said that since Rama was now stained by the killing of kshatriyas he must perform an atonement; asked what, he told him to do penance for twelve years, wearing down his body with vows and observances, living on greens, roots and fruits. Rama bowed to his father and mother and went with Akritavrana to the Mahendra mountain, made a hermitage there and spent some years in hard penance, vows and worship of the gods.

02-045.json.summary: Some time later the brave Shurasena and the other surviving sons of Kartavirya went hunting with a fourfold army; after killing many animals they came, thirsty at midday, to the Narmada, bathed and drank, and on the way saw Jamadagni's hermitage. Driven by fate, they asked sages passing by whose it was, and were told it belonged to the calm, ascetic Jamadagni, whose son is Rama, best of warriors. At Rama's name they felt fear, then anger at the old enmity, and said to one another: 'What better revenge for our father's killer than to kill his father?' Swords in hand, they entered the hermitage while the sages were away, killed Jamadagni, cut off his head and, merciless as Nishadas, went back with their army to their city. His sons gathered round their slain father and wept. Renuka, seeing her husband dead on the ground, fell senseless like a vine struck by lightning, burning in the fire of grief, and her life left her at once. When she did not speak, her sons too fell senseless, sunk in sorrow. The other ascetics of the forest, sharing their grief, comforted them, and at their word the sons of Jamadagni cremated both parents and performed the rites that follow, tormented day and night by their deaths. When twelve years had passed, Rama finished his penance and returned with his friend to his father's hermitage.

02-046.json.summary: On the way Rama heard from sages all that the princes had done: his father's killing and beheading and his mother's death from grief. He wept, and Akritavrana, sharing his pain, calmed him with reasons from scripture, examples from the world and reminders of his strength. Rama went to see his brothers, greeted them in their sorrow and stayed three days, but remembering his father's death he was seized by a great anger able to destroy the world; he renewed in his heart the vow made for his mother and resolved to kill all kshatriyas and offer the funeral water to his parents with their blood. Telling his brothers his intention and taking their leave, he completed his father's rites and went with Akritavrana to Mahishmati. In a garden outside the city he called Mahodara, who sent him the chariot, bow and other arms; Rama mounted, armed, took his bow and blew the conch given by Rudra and twanged his bowstring so that heaven and earth shook, with Mahodara (Sahasaha) as his charioteer. The whole city was thrown into turmoil, and the princes, knowing that Rama, destroyer of all kshatriya families, had come, prepared for battle. The five heroes Shurasena and the others, with other kings and a fourfold army, came at Rama like moths to a flame. Alone in one chariot he fought them all, killed a hundred kings, killed Shurasena and the others with their armies and mounts, and laid low the circle of kshatriyas in a moment; the survivors fled in all directions. Then, in anger, he released a weapon bright as the fire of doomsday and burnt the whole city with its walls, elephants, horses and men; Vitihotra fled in fear to save his life. Having burnt the city and killed his enemies, like Death himself, Rama went on with Akritavrana and Mahodara, making the earth shake with the noise of his chariot, killing kshatriyas all over the earth, and then went to Mahendra to do penance. Each time kshatriyas grew up again, including those born of brahmins in kshatriya wives, he returned and killed them by the hundred thousand, making the earth kshatriya-less in two years and then doing penance for twenty-four years, again and again. Remembering his father's death, Rama made the earth empty of kshatriyas twenty-one times, as many times as his mother had struck her breast.

02-047.json.summary: Vasishtha tells Sagara that Rama took twelve thousand consecrated kings alive and brought them with sages to Kurukshetra; there he had five lakes dug, killed the kings and filled the lakes with their blood; he bathed in them, offered water to his ancestors and performed the shraddha for his father and mother with brahmins. The place became the famous ford Samantapanchaka, the best of holy places, where his ancestors received lasting satisfaction; bathing there equals bathing in all holy places, sins fall away like dry leaves in the wind, and the wicked cannot reach it even in a hundred births. After a year Rama went with brahmins to Gaya, to the Shaiva place called Chandrapada, which satisfies the ancestors like no other, and offered rice balls. His ancestors, led by Jamadagni, came from their world and, invisible in the sky, said: you have done a great deed and honoured us properly, but we cannot gain the imperishable fruit because you are stained by killing kshatriyas; perform atonement, keep eternal dharma and stop killing kshatriyas; they are not really guilty toward your father, for the world is not free and his death was ordained long ago; no one kills or protects anyone, all are only instruments of Time and their own deeds; give up your anger at the kshatriyas for our sake and become calm, for that is our greatest strength. Rama accepted this, went with Akritavrana to the Siddhavana hermitage, sent back the chariot, Mahodara and the weapons with a sign to recall them, bathed at all holy places, went round the earth three times worshipping gods and ancestors, and returned to Mahendra to do penance. Sages came to see him there, calm like a fire that has burnt up the forest of kshatriyas, and with their consent he performed a horse sacrifice with Kashyapa as his teacher and adhvaryu, Gautama as udgatri, Vishvamitra as hotri, Markandeya as brahman, Bharadvaja, Agniveshya and others as priests, and Bhrigu with his sons and pupils as overseer. At its end he adorned the Earth like a beautiful maiden, with her hundreds of towns and villages, seas, mountains and forests, and gave her all to Kashyapa, keeping only the Mahendra mountain for himself; he gave away his wealth, granted safety to all beings and resumed penance there. The Earth, now belonging to Kashyapa, suffering under many kings, observed with Kashyapa's consent the Dipa-pratishtha vow taught by Vishnu, and was freed from her sorrows. This is the account of Jamadagni's son, and hearing it frees from all sins; Kartavirya's power was told along the way: no man like him was or will be; he had chosen from Dattatreya the boon of death at the hands of the highest Person, and so reached liberation when killed by Rama. His fifth son Jayadhvaja had a son Talajangha, who had a hundred sons, the Talajanghas, eldest Vitihotra; they hid long in the Himalayan forests, living on greens and roots; Talajangha, once struck in the back by Rama's arrow while fleeing, was carried off by Vitihotra. When Rama turned to penance, Talajangha regained his kingdom, and later, remembering the old enmity, attacked Sagara's city Ayodhya with a fourfold army. Sagara's father (Phalgutantra) fought them bravely though old, was defeated and fled to the forest with Sagara's pregnant mother; living near Aurva's hermitage, he died of grief and age. His wife placed his body on the pyre and resolved to enter the fire, but Aurva stopped her, saying a son who would be the greatest of emperors was in her womb; she lived near his hermitage and there bore Sagara, whose birth rites Aurva performed and who grew up under his care. Vasishtha says he has told Sagara this best of vows with its mantras and rites, by which Kartavirya became famous and which grants any of the four aims. The narrator Jaimini relates that Sagara asked to undertake the vow; Vasishtha initiated him in the prescribed way, Sagara performed it, worshipped the Lord, vowed to keep it all his life, and Vasishtha returned to his hermitage.

02-048.json.summary: Jaimini continues. After Vasishtha left, Sagara ruled the earth from Ayodhya, young in years but mature in deeds, yet he could neither eat by day nor sleep by night, sighing hotly, remembering how enemies had seized his kingdom and his father had gone to the forest and died. Burning with the insult, the Ikshvaku king vowed to destroy all his enemies. After auspicious rites he set out with thousands of chariots, elephants, horses and soldiers, an army like a stormy ocean, with white umbrellas and banners, the dust of its march filling the low places and making the land rise; every king whose country he approached at once submitted. Conquering the kings and making them his followers, he turned south, remembered the old enmity and attacked the Haihayas; in a hair-raising battle he killed thousands of kings with their armies, defeated the Haihayas, broke and burnt their city, and reduced their kingdom to dust. The surviving kings fled in all directions; Sagara pursued and killed them like angry Death, and released the terrible Bhargava weapon (fire weapon) at them; burnt, blinded by the smoke of the wind weapon and rolling in the dust, they wandered helpless, throwing off clothes, weapons, armour and ornaments, with loose hair, like madmen. He then attacked the Kambojas, Talajanghas, Shakas, Yavanas, Kiratas, Pahlavas and Paradas, his old enemies, who abandoned kingdoms, cities and wives and fled to forests and caves; he killed the Talajanghas with their armies and destroyed their kingdom, proclaiming in battle that he was the son of the man whose kingdom they had taken and had come to take revenge. The surviving Paradas, Pahlavas and others, with women and children, took refuge with Vasishtha, the family teacher of the Ikshvakus, begging him to save them from Sagara's fire weapons, since he alone could restrain the king, who never crossed his teacher's word as the sea never crosses the shore. Vasishtha, moved by pity for the old men, women and children, told them not to fear, made them agree to terms, went to Sagara, calmed him and asked leave to let them go alive. Sagara, though angry, honoured his teacher's word: he spared their lives but made them give up the dharma and dress of their royal families, so that they were cut off from Vedic rites and rejected by brahmins, as good as dead: he made the Shakas half-shaven, the Pahlavas wear beards, the Yavanas shave their beards and the Kambojas wear only chin-beards, and disfigured other royal lines in the same way. So these enemies, having lost their own customs, became vratyas (outcastes) despised by all classes, cruel and shameless, and formed the outsider (mleccha) peoples; the Shakas, Yavanas, Kiratas and others went to live in mountains, forests and caves, and to this day they are scorned by the good and live by wrong conduct, keeping the king's terms.

02-049.json.summary: With Vasishtha's leave Sagara marched against Vidarbha; the king of Vidarbha gladly gave him his peerless daughter Keshini, whom he married before the fire at an auspicious moment. After staying some days as an honoured guest he went to the Shurasenas, where his mother's brothers, the Yadavas, honoured him and gave him wealth, and then left Mathura. Having conquered the whole earth, made all kings pay tribute and come at his call, he dismissed the kings to their kingdoms and returned slowly with his army, without troubling the lands, receiving gifts on the way. The citizens of Ayodhya decorated the city for a great festival: the streets sprinkled and swept, hundreds of full pots and tall banners, agaru incense, flowers, jewelled arches, gateways and towers, parched rice and flowers on the highways, and worship in every house and shrine. Ministers, palace people, courtesans and citizens came out to meet him; amid shouts of victory, music, Vedic chanting, bards' praise, singers and dancing women, under a white umbrella and showered with parched rice and flowers, he entered Ayodhya as Indra enters his city. Getting down from his chariot with his two wives, he went to his mother's house, bowed at her feet, and she rose, embraced him and blessed him and her two daughters-in-law. Then, fanned with white whisks, he went to the assembly hall, bowed to the elders and sat on the throne among the kings, having fulfilled his vow and conquered the world; he followed dharma, wealth and pleasure in proper measure and ruled the whole earth with its seven continents under one umbrella. In time Vasishtha came to see him; Sagara went out with the kings to receive him, honoured him and bowed. Vasishtha asked after the welfare of his kingdom, ministers and people, praised him for defeating his enemies without effort and for sparing those who gave up their dharma at his request, and said he had come out of affection after hearing he had returned victorious. Sagara, conqueror of the Talajanghas, said all was well, since the gods favour him on whom Vasishtha thinks well; everything he had achieved was by Vasishtha's grace, for how else could he have killed such enemies? Vasishtha took leave and returned to his hermitage. Sagara ruled from Ayodhya and enjoyed life with his two lovely, devoted wives, Sumati and Keshini; no other king on earth was even called king beside him, and he followed dharma always, pursuing wealth without greed and pleasure without harming dharma.

02-050.json.summary: Jaimini says Sagara ruled the seven-continent earth like a second Dharma, keeping each class in its own duty.
