In his reign no child died before an elder, the kingdoms were prosperous and untroubled, no twice-born man lived outside a stage of life, all undertakings bore fruit, cities and villages held festivals, no one was blamed, poor, sick, greedy or mean; people loved one another's virtues, bowed to elders, loved learning, feared slander, were faithful to their wives, avoided the wicked and believed in dharma; the seasons came in time and the earth was rich in rice. His hall shone like Indra's with hundreds of consecrated kings from eighteen provinces, who camped around the city with gifts waiting to see him, and his feet were calloused from the crowns of bowing kings. Yet he had no son, and grieved: his ancestors would lose their offerings, a son saves the ancestors even from hell, the gods do not open heaven's door to the sonless, and his kingdom would pass to others. He resolved to go with his wives to Aurva and do whatever he said. Leaving the kingdom with his chief minister, he drove with his two wives through a lovely forest, showing them peacocks, deer, flowering trees, cuckoos, bees, monkeys, vidyadhari singers, kinnara pairs and lakes full of lotuses and water birds. At the hermitage he got down, told the charioteer to rest the horses, and, hearing from Aurva's pupils that the sage had finished his daily rites, entered and bowed with his wives. Aurva seated them, honoured them with water and forest food, and asked about the welfare of his kingdom, whether he pursued the three aims well, praised him for conquering his enemies and ruling by dharma, since dharma protects one who protects it, and asked why he had left his kingdom and come with his wives.

02-051.json.summary: Sagara told Aurva that all was well, since Aurva had trained him in weapons and thought of his welfare; Aurva was his teacher, friend, god and only father; by the weapon Aurva taught him he had conquered all kings. He praised the power of Aurva's penance, seen in the hermitage where a fawn drinks from the water at his seat, a thin doe lets others suckle, a ruru deer scratches its cheek on another's horn, a tigress feeds the fawns of the doe she killed, a lion and the elephant it chased stand together, and mongoose, cat, peacock, hare, snake, wolf, boar, tiger, sharabha, bear, monkey, jackal, gavaya, cow, deer and buffalo live in friendship. But he had no child, and so no one to offer rice balls to his ancestors or protect the earth; this grief no one but Aurva could remove. Aurva told him to stay there for a time with his wives under restraint, and he would gain his wish. They stayed long, serving him devotedly, and the queens pleased him with their humility and devotion. Aurva called the queens and offered them a boon; they asked for sons. He said: by my grace both of you will have sons: one will bear a single son, not very righteous, but his line will last till the end of the kalpa; the other will bear sixty thousand sons, who will die soon without fulfilling their purpose; let each choose. The Vidarbha princess (Keshini) chose the one son who would continue the line, and the other (Sumati) the many sons. Aurva sent Sagara home. Both queens conceived; Keshini bore a brilliant son named Asamanjasa; Sumati bore a gourd-like lump, which the king wanted to throw away, but Aurva came and told him not to, since it held the seed of sixty thousand sons; it should be divided and kept in covered pots of ghee, and the sons would break out in time. After a year the sons broke out of the pots one by one, day after day, sixty thousand of them, strong, cruel, acting as one; the king did not love them, but honoured Keshini's son, married him, and Asamanjasa had a son, Amshuman, who pleased everyone. Then Asamanjasa was possessed by a pishacha. In a former life he had been a rich vaishya who found a buried treasure in a forest; its guardian pishacha, long starving, let him take it on his promise to give it cow's flesh, but he never gave it, and the pishacha died of hunger; the vaishya was reborn as Sagara's son, and the bodiless pishacha, remembering the wrong, entered him as wind. He became cruel and mad, killed children, youths, old men and women and threw them into the Sarayu; the citizens complained; Sagara warned him many times, but could not turn him from evil, and, fearing public blame, banished him from the kingdom.

02-052.json.summary: Having given up his son, Sagara gave his love to the righteous child Amshuman. Meanwhile Sumati's sixty thousand sons grew up as one body: hard as diamond, cruel, merciless, shameless, unrighteous, angry and foolish, harassing all beings like demons; sacrifice and Vedic study ceased, the earth trembled under them and ascetics' meditation was broken. The gods and ancestors, deprived of their offerings, went with Shiva and others to Brahma and told him what Sagara's sons were doing. Brahma said they would soon perish; one should wait for Time, which governs all, others being mere instruments; Kapila, a portion of Vishnu and best of yogis, born for the world's good, was meditating for a hundred divine years in a lonely place in the ocean that Agastya had drunk dry; the gods should wait near him until he came out of meditation, tell him their wish, and arrange that Sagara's sons break his meditation. The gods went to Kapila and with folded hands begged him to save the world from Sagara's sons, praising him as a portion of Vishnu who took a body only to relieve suffering and could create and destroy by thought. Kapila opened his eyes and said: Sagara's sons, burnt by their own deeds, will perish when their time comes; I will be the cause of their destruction; they will be burnt in the fire of my anger; go home without fear and wait a little. The gods bowed and returned to heaven. Then Sagara resolved to perform a horse sacrifice; with Vasishtha's consent and with Aurva and other brahmins he was consecrated, and he sent all his sons to lead the horse around the earth and bring it back quickly. Driven by fate, the horse wandered over the earth, not for conquest or tribute, since Sagara had already conquered all kings; and the princes, surrounding it, entered the dry bed of the salt ocean.

02-053.json.summary: Prompted by Indra, the Wind carried off the horse unseen into the nether world (Rasatala) and left it near the sage Kapila. The princes searched the whole earth with its towns, mountains and forests and, not finding it, went to Ayodhya and told their father that while they watched over it near the ocean someone had stolen it. Sagara angrily told them to go and not return without the horse. They decided to dig through the earth from the ocean down to the nether world, and dug on every side from the ocean shore; the earth cried out in distress and creatures wailed; they dug out and scattered a thousand yojanas of the land of Bharata into the ocean, and digging down to Patala they saw the horse grazing there. They laughed and danced with joy; then they saw the great Kapila, old and shining, sitting in the lotus posture with eyes on the tip of his nose, back and neck straight, chest forward, lit by his own radiance like a lamp in a windless place, absorbed in meditation, calm as a still ocean (one verse here is garbled in the source). Afraid for a moment, then, driven by Time, they surrounded him, saying 'This is the thief who took the horse; he must be killed', and assaulted the sage as if he were an ordinary man. Kapila, his meditation broken, was shaken with great anger; it blazed up from his ocean-deep body like the fire of doomsday fanned by winds; he opened his eyes, red as the sun and moon rising together, and looked at the princes like Death at the end of an age; flames poured from his eyes in all directions with smoke and sparks, like the mare's-mouth fire from the ocean, filling the sky. In front of all the world the fire of his anger burnt Sagara's sons, all but the horse, to ashes, like dry trees in a forest fire. The gods and sages, amazed, said that the fruit of terrible sins comes quickly: those cruel, mountain-like oppressors of creatures had been destroyed in an instant like grass; no one who harms others finds happiness; the wise should do good, avoid what the world condemns, never harm anyone, and not trust the fleeting body, wealth and world. The princes, struck by the brahmin's power, went to hell for their deeds. Then the fire, having burnt them all, began to burn the whole world, and the frightened gods praised Kapila to calm it.

02-054.json.summary: The gods begged Kapila to withdraw his fire of anger before it burnt the world out of time, and he at once calmed it, and the world and the gods were at peace. Then Narada came from heaven to Ayodhya; Sagara honoured him, and Narada told him that his sons, sent to guard the sacrificial horse, had been destroyed by a brahmin's power: the horse had been taken by fate, they had searched for it, dug down through the earth, found it in Patala near Kapila, angered him calling him a thief, and been burnt to fuel by the fire of his eyes; since they were cruel, sinful and harmful to all, Sagara should not grieve, but stay steady, for the wise do not mourn what is gone; he should send his young grandson Amshuman to bring back the horse. Narada vanished. Sagara sat long in grief; Vasishtha told him that men of steadiness like him should not let grief in, but accept what is fated and do what must be done next. Sagara called Amshuman before the assembly and told him: your fathers, struck by the brahmin's power, have fallen into hell forever for their sins; you alone are my line and the protector of this kingdom; go to Kapila in Patala, please him, ask for the horse and come back quickly. Amshuman bowed, went to Kapila, bowed humbly and begged him to calm his anger, which could destroy the world, and to look kindly on him, the grandson of Sagara and descendant of those burnt by his anger, come to ask for the horse. Kapila, pleased, welcomed him, told him to take the horse to Sagara so the interrupted sacrifice could continue, offered him any boon, and told him to tell his grandfather that he should not grieve for the death of these sinners. Amshuman asked as his boon that his fathers, burnt by Kapila's anger and doomed to hell forever, since those struck by a brahmin's power receive no rice balls or water and so cannot reach the world of the ancestors, might gain lasting heaven, and asked how they could be raised. Kapila said Amshuman could not raise them from hell; they must stay there until his grandson was born: the wise King Bhagiratha, who out of reverence for his ancestors would do great penance and bring the Ganga down from heaven; when her water washed their ashes and bones, all of them would go to heaven, and she would be known as Bhagirathi; whoever's bones, ashes, hair or nails are touched by her water goes from hell to imperishable heaven. Amshuman bowed and returned to Saketa (Ayodhya), told Sagara everything, gave him the horse and asked what he should do next.

02-055.json.summary: The opening of this chapter is damaged in the source; it begins with Sagara greeting and praising Amshuman. With priests and assembly members versed in the Vedas, Sagara resumed the horse sacrifice, conducted by Aurva, Vasishtha and other sages, with a golden altar and every kind of vessel, and the priests completed it in order. He gave the priests their fees and gave the brahmins and petitioners more wealth than they wished, asked pardon of his teachers and the assembly, and then, followed by the classes, priests, courtesans and bards, with his wives, under a white umbrella and fanned with whisks, went to the bank of the Sarayu with music and took the final bath of the sacrifice with his kin. He re-entered the decorated city to Vedic chanting, praise of bards and showers of parched rice from the women, received gifts from merchants, honoured his friends and the brahmins, and sat in his hall among kings like a second Indra. With Vasishtha's consent he made his grandson Amshuman crown prince; Amshuman, though young, was loved by citizens, kin and friends for his noble qualities, like the new moon. Sagara lived long and happily with him, his friends and his two wives, ruling the earth like Dharma himself, and the lord of northern Koshala, jewel of the solar line, rejoiced with all his subjects.

02-056.json.summary: Jaimini says he has told Sagara's story in brief and in full. The land of Bharata stretches north to south and is nine thousand yojanas wide; Sagara's sons, digging for the horse, dug out and sank eight (or a thousand) yojanas of it into the sea, and because the sons of Sagara enlarged the ocean it became known as Sagara. The sea flooded the land with its holy places, fields and forests as far as Brahmapada, and the gods, demons and men living there scattered in distress. The famous holy field of Gokarna, a yojana and a half wide on the shore of the western sea, full of countless fords, shrines and siddhas, where sages reached final liberation and where Shankara lives with the goddess and his hosts, fell into the sea in the south-west. Its glory is told: sins vanish like dry leaves in the wind for pilgrims, the wicked never wish to go there even if they live nearby, only great merit brings the wish, all beings who die there go to eternal heaven, even remembering it frees from sin, and gifts, offerings and recitation there give crores of times more fruit. When it sank, its ascetics climbed the Sahya mountain to live, and decided together to go to Rama (Parashurama), doing penance on Mahendra. The king (the listener) asks what the people did when the coastal lands were destroyed and how and when the ocean was filled. Jaimini says the people scattered, some staying on with hardship. Meanwhile Amshuman's son Dilipa became king; Amshuman went to the forest; Dilipa's son was Bhagiratha. When Bhagiratha learned that all his ancestors, struck by the brahmin's power, had fallen into hell, he lost interest in kingdom, kin and pleasure, left the kingdom to his chief minister and went to the forest to raise them to heaven. By penance he first won from Brahma as long a life as he wished, then pleased the Ganga and asked her to come down from heaven, then pleased Shiva to hold her on his head. Shiva caught the Ganga, with her crocodiles and sea monsters, falling from the top of Meru, and she vanished in his matted hair like a palmful of water; Bhagiratha worshipped him again to release her. Following the king, she flooded the sacrificial ground of the royal sage (Jahnu), who angrily drank her up like a mouthful of water; after a hundred years of service Bhagiratha won her back, and because she came out of his belly she is called Jahnavi. Following Bhagiratha, the heavenly river washed the bones and ashes of his ancestors, and at once all the sons of Sagara were freed of sin and went from hell to heaven. Then she went to the eastern sea; from the top of Meru she split into four streams, Sita, Alakananda, Suchakshu and Bhadravati, flowing in four directions, and filled again the four oceans that Agastya had drunk dry. As the ocean, enlarged by Sagara's sons, filled, many coastal lands and holy places disappeared, including Gokarna, and its people went to see Rama to ask him to raise it.

02-057.json.summary: The sages led by Shushka and Sumitra travelled through many lands, forests and rivers to Mount Mahendra and climbed to Rama's hermitage, a calm grove with peaceful wild animals, fruit trees of every season, cool shade and fragrant breezes, filled with Vedic chanting. They found Rama seated on a black antelope skin among his pupils, like the fire of doomsday that had burnt the three worlds at will and was now doing penance to atone for it; they bowed, and he honoured them and asked what he could do. They said they were sages of Gokarna; when Sagara's sons dug the earth, that great holy field with its fords had sunk in the sea; they wished to get it back by driving back the ocean's water; Rama, born of a portion of Vishnu in Bhrigu's line, could do anything and was known to grant wishes. Rama said he knew all this and would do it, but it required taking up weapons, and he had laid down his weapons, given safety to all beings and vowed before the good at his father's command never to take up arms again; so his mind wavered. Shushka replied that taking up weapons to protect the good does not break one's word, as Brahma said long ago; he should take them up for their sake and it would be a great act of dharma. Persuaded, Rama went with them to the south-west, came down the Sahya and reached the shore of the ocean, which is described: wind-tossed, mine of all jewels, unfathomable like the mind of the great, hard to cross, full of sea creatures, home of all beings and rivers, with countless restless waves breaking into foam on the rocks and a deep roar. After resting a moment, Rama stood facing south and called in a voice like thunder to Varuna to show himself; Varuna did not stir or answer though called again and again. Taking this as an insult, Rama grew angry and decided to dry up the ocean; touching water and bowing in his mind to Shiva, he strung his great bow Vijaya and twanged it so that the earth with its seven continents and seas shook; he fitted a gold-feathered arrow charged with the fierce Bhargava fire weapon. The earth shook, gods, demons and nagas were alarmed, the quarters were covered with burning clouds, harsh dusty winds blew, the sun grew dim and red, meteors and thunderbolts fell and it rained blood. Drawing the bow to his ear, Rama looked like the fire of doomsday, like Vishnu as Narasimha, like Shiva about to burn Tripura; the sages cried 'Be gracious, victory to Rama.' The smoke of the weapon filled the ocean's depths, the waters boiled, whales, crocodiles, fish, snakes and turtles suffered, the waves leapt to the shore and the Sahya trembled. Seeing Rama with the bow drawn, the ocean despaired like a sinner seeing Yama, gave up his natural steadiness, took his own form, adorned with ornaments, rose from the water and hurried to Rama with folded hands and offerings, fell at his feet and begged: protect me, I have come for refuge; I offended without knowing; command me.

02-058.json.summary: Seeing Varuna fallen at his feet, Rama withdrew the weapon, his anger gone, and told him with a smile that these Gokarna sages had come to him on Mahendra because their holy field, dear to Shiva, had sunk into the sea when Sagara's sons dug the earth, and he asked Varuna to draw back his water and give back the field as before. Varuna said that no one could drive back his water, for Brahma had given him that boon, but since Rama's power had overcome his steadiness, and Rama asked for the sake of these sages, he would withdraw his water as far as Rama decided. Rama agreed and, to show the boundary, took a sacrificial ladle (sruva), whirled it and threw it into the salt sea toward the north-west; it flew two hundred yojanas and fell beyond the holy ford of Shurparaka, which is famous in the three worlds and removes all sins; there was the limit of the land Rama made. The ocean drew back its water that far and gave the land to Rama, never again to cross that limit, and Rama, with Varuna's consent, set up the boundary and gave the land back; the gods were amazed at his prowess. Towns and village boundaries reappeared here and there, and near the Sahya the land rose again as before, as the sea withdrew. Rama gave the sages the places they wished, and they blessed him; he took leave and returned to his hermitage. The sages went to the shore, walked over the land and found that the holy field which had long lain under the sea had not been greatly damaged, because the gods are always present there and by Rudra's power; it emerged from the water as before, a power of the gods beyond thought. So Rama made again four hundred yojanas of land from north to south (or six hundred, as said later), and the ocean still keeps that limit. Such was the power of Rama and of Sagara, whose sons sank the land of Bharata a thousand yojanas into the sea, and since then the ocean is called Sagara. Jaimini says he has told the story of the great Rama, Kartavirya and King Sagara.

02-059.json.summary: The chapter opens with the frame speaker named as Brihaspati, but the account is given by the bard Lomaharshana to the sages, who ask about the royal lines in order. He begins with Varuna's wife Stuta (or Sura), whose sons were Kali and Vaidya; Kali's sons Jaya and Vijaya and Vaidya's sons Ghrini and Muni devoured each other and perished; Kali's son by Sura was Mada; Kali's wife Himsa bore four man-eating sons, Naka (bodiless), Vighna (headless), Bhadrama (one-handed) and Vidhama (one-footed), whose wives and children are the rakshasas called Nairritas, seizers of children, wandering at the two twilights, with Skanda appointed by Brahma as their lord. Brihaspati's sister, the yogini Bhuvana, wife of Prabhasa the eighth Vasu, bore Vishvakarma, patriarch of craftsmen, who made the gods' celestial cars and by whose crafts men still live; Tvashta's wife was Virochana, Prahlada's daughter, mother of Trishiras Vishvarupa; Vishvakarma's son was Maya, and his sister Surenu (Samjna), daughter of Tvashta, was the wife of Vivasvan (the Sun) and bore Manu, the eldest, and the twins Yama and Yamuna; later, as a mare among the Northern Kurus, she bore the Ashvins, Nasatya and Dasra, from her nostrils. Asked why the Sun is called Martanda, the bard says that when the egg was split in two, (Kashyapa) said out of love 'he is not dead (mrita) in the egg (anda)', hence Martanda (one line is unclear in the source). Vivasvan's radiance was too fierce; Samjna could not bear it, created a shadow-self (Chhaya) of the same colour, told her to look after her children and not tell the Sun, and went to her father Tvashta, who sent her back to her husband; she became a mare and grazed in the Northern Kurus. The Sun, thinking Chhaya was Samjna, had by her two sons, Shrutashravas, who will be the Savarni Manu, and Shrutakarman, the planet Saturn (Shanaishchara), also called Savarni. Chhaya loved her own son more than the elder children; Manu bore it, but Yama, angry, raised his foot at her, and she cursed him that his foot would fall off. Yama told his father he had only raised his foot, not struck her, and asked protection; the Sun said the curse could not be false, but worms would take flesh from his foot to the earth, and so the curse would be fulfilled and he would be saved. The Sun asked Chhaya why she favoured one child; she would not say, but when he was about to curse her she told the truth. Angry, he went to Tvashta, who calmed him, explained that Samjna could not bear his fierce form and was grazing as a mare, and with his leave put him on his lathe and trimmed away his excess radiance. Then, handsome, the Sun found his wife by yoga, approached her in the form of a horse, and she, fearing another male, expelled his seed through her nostrils, from which the Ashvins, the best of physicians, were born. He showed her his lovely form and she was pleased. Yama, by his righteous deeds, became the king of dharma, lord of the ancestors and a world guardian; the Savarni Manu does penance on Meru and will be Manu in a future age; Saturn became a planet; Tvashta made Vishnu's discus from the trimmed radiance; and Yamuna became the purifying river. One who hears or reads this birth of the gods and the seven sons of Vivasvan is freed from danger and gains great fame.

02-060.json.summary: The bard says that after the Chakshusha manvantara Brahma gave the rule of the earth to Vaivasvata Manu, who had sons like himself: Ikshvaku, Nriga, Dhrishta, Sharyati, Narishyanta, Pramshu, Nabhaga, Dishta, Karusha and Prishadhra. Urged by Brahma, Manu wished to perform a horse sacrifice, and for the sake of a son made an offering into the fire to the portion of Mitra and Varuna; from it was born Ila, in divine clothes and ornaments. Manu told her to follow him, but she replied that since she was born of the portion of Mitra and Varuna she would go to them, so that dharma would not be harmed. She went to them and asked what she should do; pleased by her modesty, self-control and truthfulness, they said she would become famous as their child and would be known as Sudyumna, honoured in the three worlds, righteous and continuing Manu's line. Sudyumna, Manu's son, became a woman; Ila, having received the boon, was returning to her father when Budha (son of Soma) invited her to union, and from Budha she bore Aila Pururavas; after that she became Sudyumna again. Sudyumna had three righteous sons, Utkala, Gaya and Vinata; Utkala ruled the Utkala country, Vinata the west, and Gaya the east with the city of Gaya. When Manu entered the Sun, he divided the earth into ten parts among the kshatriyas; Ikshvaku received a tenth share; Sudyumna, because he had been a woman, got no share, but on Vasishtha's word ruled at Pratishthana. Asked how Sudyumna became a woman, the bard says Sanaka and the other Kumaras once came to Ilavrita to see Shiva and found him making love with Uma; they turned back, and Shiva's consort, embarrassed, declared that any man who entered her grove would become a woman, beautiful as an apsara; there all beings, even pishachas and animals, are female and play like apsaras with Rudra, who himself takes a female form. King Sudyumna entered Uma's grove while hunting and so became a woman, and by Mahadeva's grace became a man again.

02-061.json.summary: The bard describes the descendants of Manu's sons. Prishadhra killed his teacher Chyavana's cow at night and through his curse became a shudra. From Karusha came the Karusha kshatriyas, fierce in war, a thousand strong. Nabhaga, son of Dishta, had the learned Bhalandana, whose son was the mighty Pramshu; Pramshu's only son (Marutta) was taken to heaven with his friends and kin by Samvarta; a great quarrel arose between Samvarta and Brihaspati, who, seeing the splendour of the sacrifice Samvarta performed for Marutta, grew angry, and the gods had to calm him to save the worlds. The emperor Marutta had Narishyanta, whose line ran through Dama, Rashtravardhana, Sudhriti, Nara, Kevala, Bandhuman, Vegavan and Budha to Trinabindu, a king at the start of the third Treta age, whose daughter Idavida was mother of Vishravas. Trinabindu's son Vishala founded Vishala; his line runs through Hemachandra, Suchandra, Dhumrashva, Srinjaya, Sahadeva, Krishashva, Somadatta, Janamejaya and Pramati; by Trinabindu's power all the Vaishala kings were long-lived, mighty and righteous. Sharyati had twins, Anarta and Sukanya, the wife of Chyavana; Anarta's son Reva ruled the Anarta country with its city Kushasthali; Reva's son Raivata Kakudmi, eldest of a hundred brothers, went with his daughter to Brahma's world to hear the gandharva music; a moment for Brahma was many ages for men, and when he returned, still young, his city had become Dvaravati, guarded by the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas led by Vasudeva; he gave his daughter Revati to Baladeva and went to Mount Meru to do penance, and Balarama lived happily with Revati. Asked how they did not age over so many ages, the bard says that in Brahma's world there is no old age, hunger, thirst, fear of death or disease. He then begins to explain gandharva music: there are seven notes (shadja, rishabha, gandhara, madhyama, panchama, dhaivata and nishada), three scales (grama), twenty-one modes (murchhana) and forty-nine tones (tana); he names modes of the middle and shadja scales, lists of musical forms named after sacrifices (Agnishtoma, Vajapeya and others) and after gods and sages, and the presiding deities of various modes. Much of this technical passage is corrupt in the source and only names can be made out.

02-062.json.summary: This chapter continues the account of music (gandharva) following the teachers of old, but most of its verses are badly corrupt in the source, so only the general outline is clear. It speaks of musical ornaments (alankaras) to be used with their own 'colours' (varnas), produced in three places, chest, throat and head. There are four kinds of varna: steady (sthayi), moving (sanchari), descending (avaroha) and ascending (aroha), and the ornaments depend on them; thirty or so ornaments are said to have been described by the gods, defined by placement, measure, change and character. Ornaments must be used in their proper place: just as a woman's jewels are fitting only where they belong, and no one wears an earring on the foot or a girdle on the neck, so a misplaced musical ornament is to be condemned. The chapter then touches on the notes used in the gandhara and madhyama scales, song forms such as the Madraka and Kaushiki with their measures and divisions, and ends with mention of the combinations of styles, modes and note-branches.
